She then pursued higher education, earning a Bachelor of Fine Arts in Theatre from the Carnegie Institute of Technology, now Carnegie Mellon University. 

Thompson began her career working in regional theatre, performing in productions of plays like *The Seagull*, *Pygmalion*, *Our Town*, *Arms and the Man*, and *Blithe Spirit*. She honed her skills further with training at the Pittsburgh Playhouse, appearing in numerous of their shows. Her professional debut came Off-Broadway in 1955 with *Under Milk Wood*, followed by a television appearance in *Goodyear Television Playhouse* the next year. She made her Broadway debut in 1959 with the musical *Juno*.

Throughout her stage career, Thompson garnered significant critical acclaim, winning an Obie Award, a Tony Award for Best Actress in a Play for her performance in *Twigs* in 1972, three Drama Desk Awards, and two Sarah Siddons Awards for her work in Chicago theatre. In 2005, she was inducted into the American Theater Hall of Fame.

Her success on Broadway led to opportunities in television. She was initially cast as Irene Lorenzo on *All in the Family*, but was quickly replaced by Betty Garrett due to creative differences with producer Norman Lear regarding the character's portrayal. Thompson then found lasting recognition as Kate Lawrence in the television series *Family*, from 1976 to 1980. Her realistic and nuanced performance earned her an Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series in 1978, along with three Golden Globe nominations. In total, she was nominated for an Emmy nine times, including for her guest role as Carla's mother on *Cheers*.

Beyond these prominent roles, Thompson had a substantial television career, appearing in shows such as *Owen Marshall: Counselor at Law*, *The Love Boat*, *Father Dowling Mysteries*, *Andre's Mother*, *Indictment: The McMartin Trial*, *ER* and *Law & Order*. She also appeared in several films, including *The Pursuit of Happiness*, *Desperate Characters*, and *Pollock*.

Thompson was married to Donald E. Stewart from 1949 until her death. They resided in Southbury, Connecticut, and had one daughter, Liza Stewart, who works as a costume designer. Sada Thompson passed away on May 4, 2011, in Danbury, Connecticut, at the age of 83, due to complications from lung disease.

title: Michael L. MacDonald
text:
Michael L. MacDonald, born May 4, 1955, is a Canadian politician currently serving as a Conservative member of the Canadian Senate. He was appointed to the Senate on January 2, 2009, following a recommendation from then-Prime Minister Stephen Harper. 

Born in Louisbourg, Nova Scotia, MacDonald grew up as the youngest of ten children. He pursued higher education at the University of King's College in Halifax, graduating with an Honours degree in political science in 1977. Following his studies, MacDonald embarked on a career in politics, beginning as a researcher for the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada Research Office from 1978 to 1980. 

He continued to gain experience working within Nova Scotia’s provincial government, initially serving in the office of Member of the Legislative Assembly Gerald Sheehy between 1980 and 1982. He then progressed to the role of Executive Assistant to Premier John Buchanan from 1982 to 1984.  Further roles followed as Executive Assistant, first to Thomas McMillan from 1984 to 1985, and then to Stewart McInnes from 1985 to 1987.

Alongside his political work, MacDonald has been a business owner, running the Fortress Inn in his hometown of Louisbourg since 1988. He also sought elected office on multiple occasions, though without success.  He first ran for federal office in 1988 in the riding of Cape Breton—East Richmond, achieving second place with 7,173 votes. He then contested a provincial seat in 1993 in Dartmouth-Cole Harbour for the Progressive Conservative Association of Nova Scotia, again finishing second, this time with 2,905 votes. He ran in the same provincial riding in 1998, placing third with 2,084 votes, and later ran federally in Dartmouth—Cole Harbour in 2004, finishing third with 8,739 votes.

In February 2022, MacDonald became embroiled in controversy during the convoy protest in Ottawa. A video surfaced showing him making critical and dismissive comments about the city and its residents, specifically referencing perceived entitlement and high salaries coupled with limited work hours. He also voiced support for the protesting convoy, stating his desire for them to remain in Ottawa. He further made a personal comment about his wife, referring to her as "a Karen" due to her wanting the protest to end. Following the public reaction to the video, MacDonald delivered an apology in the Senate chamber for his remarks.

Michael MacDonald currently resides in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, with his wife, Marilyn, and their two sons, Lauchlan and Liam.

title: Neil Googe
text:
Neil Googe is a British comic artist with a career spanning several decades and multiple publishers. He began his work in the late 1990s with contributions to titles like *Shotgun Mary* and *2000 AD*, where he worked on several *Judge Dredd* stories. A significant early project was a graphic novel adaptation of the video game *Silent Hill*, completed in 1999, but it was never published due to disagreements with Konami, despite being finished, advertised, and assigned an ISBN. Googe reportedly lost the only copy of the completed work on a CD.

In 2000, Googe co-founded the independent British comic publisher Com.x, where he created *Bazooka Jules*, though only three issues were released. He then transitioned to the American comic book market, collaborating with Gail Simone on *Welcome to Tranquility* for Wildstorm, after previously working on *Majestic*. Further American projects included *Wildcats: World's End* with Christos Gage and the *World of Warcraft* graphic novel *Dark Riders* with Mike Costa, published by DC Comics following the Wildstorm merger. 

Googe continued to contribute to DC Comics with one-shot issues such as *Rose and Thorn*, a *Detective Comics* Harley Quinn issue, a *Legends of the Dark Knight* Harley Quinn installment, and *The Flash*. He also returned to *2000 AD* to work on *Survival Geeks*. Currently, Googe is developing a creator-owned project called *Welcome to the Hood*, planned as both a pen-and-paper role-playing game and a comic series. He is also revisiting *Bazooka Jules* under the name *Bazooka Jules: Tales from Caliber Bay*, reimagining it as a world setting for role-playing games with accompanying comic short stories, and working on other tabletop and RPG products, including a Pathfinder supplement. He intends to continue working on regular comic projects alongside these new ventures.

His extensive bibliography includes work on titles like *Mercy Heights*, *Pulp Sci-fi: “Coy’s Big Score”*, and *Hondo-City Justice*. Several of his works, including *Majestic* and *Welcome to Tranquility*, have been collected into trade paperbacks.

title: Cédric Bakambu
text:
Cédric Bakambu, born on April 11, 1991, is a professional footballer who currently plays as a forward or winger for Real Betis in La Liga, and represents the DR Congo national team. He began his career at Sochaux, joining their youth system at age 14 and making his professional debut in 2010. Over five seasons with Sochaux, he appeared in 107 official matches, scoring 21 goals, including a goal in the 2010 Coupe Gambardella Final.

In 2014, Bakambu moved to Bursaspor in Turkey for a fee of €1.8 million. He quickly became a key player, finishing as the team’s top scorer and helping them reach the Turkish Cup final, though they ultimately lost to Galatasaray. He also earned recognition for his goal-scoring prowess in the cup competition, being the top scorer with eight goals.

A year later, in 2015, he signed with Villarreal in Spain. He made his La Liga debut for Villarreal, and quickly established himself as a prolific scorer. He played in the UEFA Europa League, becoming a standout performer and being named to the competition’s Squad of the Season after scoring nine goals. He also earned La Liga Player of the Month in October 2017. 

In January 2018, a transfer to Beijing Sinobo Guoan in the Chinese Super League materialized after some complications regarding tax regulations. He joined for a reported €40 million, becoming the club’s all-time top scorer. He won the Chinese FA Cup with Beijing Guoan in his first season.

Bakambu returned to Europe in January 2022, signing for Marseille in France. He then moved to Olympiacos in Greece in September 2022, where he was named Super League Greece Top Scorer for the 2022-23 season and was selected for the Team of the Season. A brief spell with Al-Nasr in the UAE followed in June 2023, before returning to Turkey with Galatasaray in July 2023. He scored a late goal in a Champions League match for Galatasaray against Bayern Munich in November 2023. As of February 2024, he plays for Real Betis.

Internationally, Bakambu represented France at youth levels, winning the 2010 UEFA European Under-19 Championship. He later switched his allegiance to the DR Congo in 2015, expressing pride in representing his parents’ homeland. He has since become a key player for the Congolese national team, qualifying for the 2019 Africa Cup of Nations and participating in the 2023 edition. He briefly retired from international football in 2022 before reversing his decision.

Throughout his career, Bakambu has received numerous individual accolades, including being named to the UEFA Europa League Squad of the Season and winning the La Liga Player of the Month award. He is known for his goal-scoring ability and has consistently been a threat in front of goal for every club he has represented.

title: Jose Canseco
text:
José Canseco was a Cuban-American professional baseball player who enjoyed a 17-season Major League Baseball (MLB) career, primarily known for his powerful hitting. Born in Havana, Cuba in 1964, he and his twin brother Ozzie were brought to Miami as young children after their family left Cuba following Fidel Castro’s rise to power. Canseco excelled in high school baseball, though he didn’t make the varsity team until his senior year. He was drafted by the Oakland Athletics in 1982 and spent several years in the minor leagues before debuting with the A’s in 1985.

Canseco quickly became a star with the Athletics, winning the American League Rookie of the Year award in 1986. He was a six-time All-Star and won the Most Valuable Player award in 1988, a year he achieved the unprecedented feat of hitting 40 home runs and stealing 40 bases – the first player in MLB history to do so. He secured World Series championships with the Athletics in 1989 and the New York Yankees in 2000. Alongside teammate Mark McGwire, he formed the formidable “Bash Brothers” duo, known for their combined power hitting. 

Throughout his career, Canseco played for seven different teams, accumulating impressive statistics. He ranks fourth in Athletics history with 254 home runs and is one of only 14 players in MLB history to achieve 400 home runs and 200 stolen bases. Despite battling injuries, he averaged a remarkable 40 home runs, 120 RBIs, and 102 runs scored per 162 games over his 17 seasons. He finished his career with 462 home runs, the 12th-highest total in the American League and the second most for a player with fewer than 2,000 games played. He also won four Silver Slugger Awards.

Later in life, Canseco admitted to using performance-enhancing drugs during his career and detailed widespread steroid use in MLB in his controversial 2005 book, *Juiced*. After retiring from baseball, he briefly pursued careers in boxing and mixed martial arts. His early life was marked by his family’s emigration from Cuba, and he quickly established himself as a dominant force in baseball, known for his exceptional power and speed.

title: Thirayuth Boonmee
text:
Thirayuth Boonmee, born on January 10, 1950, is a prominent Thai social scientist, public intellectual, and former student activist. He rose to national prominence as a student leader at Chulalongkorn University in 1973, spearheading the National Student Center of Thailand (NSCT) in opposition to the military dictatorship led by Thanom Kittikachorn and Praphas Charusathien. The NSCT organized large-scale public protests, including a ten-day boycott of Japanese products to protest Japanese investment in Thailand, drawing tens of thousands of participants.

In October 1973, Thirayuth was arrested alongside twelve other student activists for sedition after distributing leaflets calling for a new constitution. False rumors of their deaths ignited widespread anti-government demonstrations culminating on October 13th with approximately 400,000 protesters assembling near the Democracy Monument and parliament. The students were subsequently released, and the king agreed to oversee the drafting of a new constitution within a year. Thirayuth also played a part in revealing the involvement of the Internal Security Operations Command in the Ban Na Sai village massacre.

Following the violent crackdown on students at Thammasat University in 1976, Thirayuth, like many others, sought refuge with the Communist Party of Thailand (CPT) in the country's jungles. During this period, he became increasingly critical of the monarchy, publicly stating in 1977 that it was “obsolete and deteriorating” and suggesting its abolition would have no negative consequences. However, after the CPT disbanded in the early 1980s, Thirayuth returned to mainstream Thai intellectual life, retracting his socialist views and disavowing his earlier anti-monarchical statements.

Thirayuth pursued higher education in the Netherlands, earning a degree equivalent to a Master of Arts in Philosophy, Sociology, and Anthropology from the International Institute of Social Studies in The Hague and the University of Nijmegen. He returned to Thailand in 1985 and has since been a long-standing faculty member in the Faculty of Sociology and Anthropology at Thammasat University. Recognized for his influence, he was named one of Thailand’s ten most influential public intellectuals in 1997. 

He served as director of the Sanya Dharmasakti Institute for Democracy at Thammasat University from 2008 and was appointed Professor of Anthropology in 2012. In 2015, he transitioned to Thammasat University's College of Interdisciplinary Studies. Throughout his career, Thirayuth has been a vocal critic of political figures; notably, he coined the term "Thaksinocracy" to describe the rule of Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra between 2001 and 2006.

title: Brianna Keilar
text:
Brianna Keilar is an American journalist born on September 21, 1980, in Canberra, Australia. Her father, Glenn, is Australian, while her mother, Miriam, is American. The family relocated to Orange County, California in 1982. She graduated from Mission Viejo High School in 1998, having been voted homecoming queen, and then went on to earn dual bachelor's degrees in mass communications and psychology from the University of California, Berkeley in 2001.

Keilar began her broadcasting career in Yakima, Washington, working at the CBS affiliate KIMA and co-hosting a morning radio show on KFFM. She then moved to CBS News, where she worked as an anchor, reporter, and producer for a newscast on MTVU, MTV's college network. She also filled in as an anchor for the CBS News overnight program, *Up to the Minute*, and contributed reporting to the weekend edition of *CBS Evening News*.

She joined CNN as a correspondent for CNN Newsource, covering breaking news for its partner stations.  She later became a general assignment correspondent for CNN, reporting on stories such as the 2007 Virginia Tech massacre, where she was the first CNN correspondent to arrive on the scene. While covering Congress, Keilar received the 2009 National Press Foundation Everett McKinley Dirksen Award for her reporting on the $700 billion bank bailout.  Later, while reporting on the Obama White House, she was awarded the 2014 Aldo Beckman Memorial Award from the White House Correspondents’ Association for her coverage of the rollout of the Affordable Care Act, often referred to as Obamacare.

In 2019, Keilar began writing a column called “Home Front,” focusing on the experiences of military families and aiming to connect civilian and military communities. She hosted the CNN program *CNN Right Now with Brianna Keilar* before joining *New Day* in 2021, co-anchoring the show with John Berman until September 2022. Following the cancellation of *New Day*, she continued to co-anchor until it was replaced by *CNN This Morning* in November 2022. 

As of April 2023, Keilar is a co-anchor of *CNN News Central*, alongside Boris Sanchez and Jim Sciutto, specifically hosting the afternoon edition of the program, which airs from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m. 

In her personal life, Keilar was first married to Dave French, but they later divorced. She married Fernando Lujan, an active-duty Green Beret and National Security Council director, in Las Vegas on December 30, 2016, after becoming engaged in July 2016. They have a son, born on June 8, 2018.

title: Jeffrey Satinover
text:
Jeffrey Satinover, born in 1947, is an American psychiatrist, psychoanalyst, and physicist whose work often touches upon controversial subjects, particularly regarding homosexuality and religion. He received a broad education, beginning with a National Merit Scholarship and culminating in a PhD in physics from the University of Nice in France in 2008, after earning degrees from MIT, Harvard, the University of Texas, and the C. G. Jung Institute of Zürich, where he became their youngest graduate and a certified Jungian analyst. He is currently a visiting scientist at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology and teaches at the Jung Institute in Zürich, while also managing his investment advisory firm, Quintium Analytics, LLC.

Satinover gained public attention for his involvement in the 1991 Clarence Thomas Supreme Court confirmation hearings. He suggested to President Bush’s nephew that Anita Hill’s accusations of sexual harassment could stem from erotomania, a delusional disorder, even if untrue, a notion he later questioned after hearing testimony from a witness. He has also provided commentary for the documentary films *What the #$*! Do We (K)now!?* and *What the Bleep!?: Down the Rabbit Hole*. 

His 1996 book, *Homosexuality and the Politics of Truth*, published by Baker Books, is a central component of his public profile. In it, he argues that homosexuality can and perhaps should be treated, a position contrary to mainstream psychological and psychiatric views. He draws parallels between homosexuality and other conditions like alcoholism and pedophilia, framing it as involving compulsive impulses and a “soul sickness.” He posits that “gay activism distorts the truth” and ultimately harms homosexual individuals. The book extensively explores the biological and genetic origins of homosexuality and the possibility of change, dedicating a portion to Jewish and Christian perspectives on sexuality, ultimately concluding that the debate rests on moral and religious grounds.

Satinover testified as an expert witness in the 1997 Florida case *Amer v. Johnson*, challenging the state’s ban on gay and lesbian adoption. While he expressed no objection to same-sex couples adopting, he maintained that children ideally need both a mother and a father. He refused to support the argument that homosexuals would be bad parents, a position the State of Florida allegedly wanted him to take. He has also testified before the Massachusetts Judicial Committee in 2003, asserting that homosexuality is not immutable and that environment plays a role in sexual orientation. His research is frequently cited by organizations opposing the expansion of LGBTQ+ rights. 

Satinover identifies as Jewish but describes his worldview as eclectic. He is also the author of several other books, including works on Jungian psychology, the Bible Code, and quantum physics.

title: Yehuda Lindell
text:
Yehuda Lindell, born in 1971, is an Israeli computer scientist and professor at Bar-Ilan University, specializing in cryptography, particularly secure computation. He currently leads the cryptography team at Coinbase, but his career trajectory includes both significant academic contributions and substantial industry experience.

Lindell’s education began at Bar-Ilan University, where he earned both his BSc and MSc in computer science. He then completed his PhD at the Weizmann Institute of Science in 2002. Following his doctoral studies, he was a Raviv Fellow and spent two years conducting research at IBM’s T.J. Watson Research Center. He returned to Bar-Ilan University in 2004, where he continues to hold an academic position. His research has been recognized with both an ERC starting grant in 2009 and an ERC consolidators grant in 2014, and in 2021 he was appointed an IACR Fellow.

Beyond academia, Lindell has been heavily involved in the cryptographic industry. He worked as a cryptographic consultant for Safenet (formerly Aladdin) from 2004 to 2014. He co-founded Unbound Security, serving first as Chief Scientist from 2014 to 2019, then taking on the role of CEO, during which time he took a leave of absence from Bar-Ilan. In 2022, Unbound Security was acquired by Coinbase, leading to his current position heading their cryptography team.

Lindell’s research focuses primarily on secure multiparty computation. Initially, he concentrated on the theoretical aspects of protocol composition. He has made significant contributions to efficient two-party secure computation using the Yao garbled circuit construction and multiparty computation based on secret sharing. A particularly influential paper co-authored with Benny Pinkas proposed using secure computation for privacy-preserving data mining, specifically with the ID3 algorithm. He’s credited with providing the first security proofs for both the Yao and BGW protocols. He has also worked on protocols resistant to active adversaries and the development of covert adversarial models. He received the IBM Pat Goldberg Memorial Best Paper Award in 2006 and the ACM CCS best paper award in 2016. In 2021, he published a review article on secure multiparty computation in *Communications of the ACM*. He is also a co-inventor of the AES-GCM-SIV mode of operation, a standard for symmetric encryption.

Lindell is also a textbook author, collaborating with Jonathan Katz on *Introduction to Modern Cryptography*, a widely used reference in universities. He has authored and edited several other books on cryptography, including works on protocol composition and proceedings from the Theory of Cryptography Conference, and tutorials on the foundations of cryptography.

title: Bobby Fischer
text:
Robert James Fischer, born in Chicago in 1943, was an American chess grandmaster who became the eleventh World Chess Champion. A child prodigy, he displayed exceptional chess ability from a young age, winning his first of a record eight US Championships at just 14 years old. In 1964, he achieved a historic perfect score of 11-0 in the US Championship, a feat unmatched in the tournament’s history. His path to the World Championship involved dominating qualifying matches, including sweeping victories against Mark Taimanov and Bent Larsen with 6-0 scores, and defeating Tigran Petrosian.

The 1972 World Championship match against Boris Spassky in Reykjavík, Iceland, was a globally publicized event, framed as a Cold War contest between the United States and the Soviet Union. Fischer’s victory in this match garnered unprecedented worldwide attention for chess. However, in 1975, Fischer refused to defend his title due to disagreements with FIDE, the international chess governing body, over match conditions. As a result, Anatoly Karpov was declared the World Champion by default.

Following this, Fischer largely withdrew from public life, with occasional reports surfacing regarding his increasingly erratic behavior. He reemerged in 1992 to play an unofficial rematch against Spassky in Yugoslavia, which was then under a United Nations embargo. This decision brought him into conflict with the US government, which warned him against violating sanctions. A warrant was issued for his arrest, leading him to live as an exile. In 2004, he was arrested in Japan for traveling on a revoked US passport and eventually granted Icelandic citizenship through a special act of the Althing, where he resided until his death in 2008. Throughout his life, Fischer was known for making numerous antisemitic statements, including Holocaust denial, despite his Jewish heritage, and his views and behavior fueled speculation about his psychological state.

Fischer left a lasting legacy on the game of chess. His book, *My 60 Memorable Games*, published in 1969, remains a cornerstone of chess literature. He also innovated chess timing systems, patenting a method of adding time increments after each move – a now-standard practice in tournaments. Furthermore, he invented Fischer Random Chess (Chess960), a variant where the starting position of the pieces is randomized, offering a new dimension to the game.

Fischer’s early life was marked by instability. His mother, Regina Wender Fischer, a physician, raised him and his sister as a single parent after separating from Hans-Gerhardt Fischer. It was later revealed, through investigative reporting, that Paul Neményi, a Hungarian mathematician, was Fischer’s biological father. He learned to play chess at the age of six and quickly became engrossed in the game, eventually finding guidance from Brooklyn Chess Club President Carmine Nigro. He then studied with John Collins at the Hawthorne Chess Club, playing countless games and absorbing knowledge from Collins’ extensive chess library. 

His rise through the chess world was rapid. He won the US Junior Championship in 1956 and the US Open Championship in 1957, becoming the youngest ever to achieve both titles. In 1957/58, at just under 15 years old, he won the US Championship, qualifying him for the 1958 Interzonal tournament, and earning him the title of International Master. He became a Grandmaster, the youngest at the time, showcasing remarkable talent and dedication to the game.

title: Djimon Hounsou
text:
Djimon Gaston Hounsou, born in Cotonou, Benin in 1964, is an actor who has achieved recognition in both American and international cinema. He immigrated to France with his brother at age 12, experiencing homelessness before beginning a successful modeling career in Paris after being discovered by a photographer and encouraged by designer Thierry Mugler. He moved to the United States in 1990, initially appearing in music videos for artists like Paula Abdul, Tina Turner, Janet Jackson, and Madonna.

Hounsou’s film career began in 1990 with *Without You I'm Nothing*. He gained wider attention with roles in *Stargate* (1994) and *Gladiator* (2000), but his breakthrough came with his critically acclaimed performance as Cinqué in Steven Spielberg’s *Amistad* (1997), earning him a Golden Globe nomination. He has since received two Academy Award nominations for Best Supporting Actor, for *In America* (2002) and *Blood Diamond* (2006), winning a National Board of Review Award for the latter.

He has become a recognizable face in major franchises, notably portraying Korath the Pursuer in the Marvel Cinematic Universe films *Guardians of the Galaxy* (2014) and *Captain Marvel* (2019), as well as the animated series *What If...?* (2021). He also joined the DC Extended Universe, playing the Fisherman King in *Aquaman* (2018) and taking over the role of the Wizard Shazam in *Shazam!* (2019), *Black Adam* (2022), and *Shazam! Fury of the Gods* (2023). Other significant film roles include appearances in *The Island* (2005), *Furious 7* (2015), *The Legend of Tarzan* (2016), *A Quiet Place Part II* (2021) and *Rebel Moon* (2023 & 2024) among many others.

Beyond acting, Hounsou has explored other creative avenues. He directed the documentary *In Search of Voodoo: Roots to Heaven* (2018), focusing on the history and religious practices of West African Vodun. He has also lent his voice to animated projects like *How to Train Your Dragon 2* (2014) and been involved in advertising, serving as a Calvin Klein underwear model in 2007, and narrating ESPN’s commercials for the 2010 FIFA World Cup.  He's also contributed to discussions on global issues, speaking at the United Nations on climate change. 

In his personal life, Hounsou had a long-term relationship with model Kimora Lee Simmons, with whom he has a son. They participated in a traditional commitment ceremony in Benin but were never legally married. He has expressed frustration with challenges faced by Black actors in Hollywood, including typecasting and unfair compensation, attributing these issues to systemic racism.

title: Kathleen A. McGrath
text:
Kathleen Anne McGrath, born June 4, 1952, in Columbus, Ohio, was a pioneering figure in the United States Navy, most notably becoming the first woman to command a US Navy warship. She was the daughter of Colonel James H. McGrath and Martha McGrath. Prior to her naval career, McGrath worked for the United States Forestry Service until 1980. She received a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science from California State University, Sacramento in 1975, and later earned a Master of Arts degree in Educational Management from Stanford University in 1987. She completed Officer Candidate School in Rhode Island as part of her training.

McGrath’s naval career included deployments to the Western Pacific, the Persian Gulf, and the Mediterranean and Caribbean seas. In 1993 and 1994, she commanded the rescue and salvage ship USS Recovery. While Lieutenant Commander Darlene Iskra had commanded a similar ship, the USS Opportune, in 1990, McGrath’s command of the frigate USS Jarrett in December 1998 marked a significant milestone, as the Jarrett was a combatant ship – a vessel with the capacity to engage in warfare – making her the first woman to achieve this distinction. She was selected as one of five women, alongside Michelle J. Howard, Maureen Farren, Ann O'Connor, and Grace Mehl, to break barriers as the first female combatant commanders in the Navy.

In March of 2000, McGrath led the USS Jarrett on a deployment from San Diego, California, to the Persian Gulf. The mission focused on intercepting vessels suspected of illegally smuggling Iraqi oil, in violation of United Nations sanctions. This deployment occurred only six years after Congress lifted restrictions preventing women from serving on combat ships and aircraft. McGrath was promoted to the rank of Captain in May 2002. Following her command of the Jarrett, she served at the Joint Advanced Warfighting Unit in Alexandria, Virginia.

Throughout her career, Captain McGrath received numerous accolades, including the Legion of Merit, the Meritorious Service Medal with three gold stars (representing four awards), the Navy Commendation Medal with two gold stars, the Navy Achievement Medal, the Joint Meritorious Unit Award, the Meritorious Unit Citation, the Navy E Ribbon, the National Defense Service Medal with a star, the Armed Forces Expeditionary Medal, the Southwest Asia Service Medal with a star, the Sea Service Deployment Ribbon, the Navy Overseas Service Ribbon, and the Kuwait Liberation Medal. 

Kathleen McGrath passed away on September 26, 2002, at the age of 50, succumbing to lung cancer at the National Naval Medical Center in Bethesda, Maryland. She was married to Gregory H. Brandon and had two children. She is interred at Arlington National Cemetery, a testament to her dedicated service to the nation.

title: Benjamin Lawrence Reid
text:
Benjamin Lawrence Reid was born in Louisville, Kentucky, on May 3, 1918, and spent some of his childhood in Texas. He was a dedicated athlete in his youth, initially playing baseball and later transitioning to basketball during his teenage years. Reid pursued higher education, beginning with a Bachelor of Arts degree from the University of Louisville in the 1940s. He continued his studies, earning a Master of Arts from Columbia University and a Doctor of Philosophy from the University of Virginia, both in the 1950s.

Reid’s career as an English professor spanned from the 1940s to the 1980s. He began teaching in 1946 at Iowa State College as an English lecturer for two years, followed by a position at Smith College from 1948 to 1951. He then moved to Sweet Briar College, starting as an instructor in 1951 and eventually becoming an assistant English professor there until 1957. The majority of his academic life, however, was spent at Mount Holyoke College. He joined Mount Holyoke in 1957 as an assistant professor and steadily rose through the ranks, becoming an associate professor in 1959, a professor in 1963, and finally an English professor in 1970. He remained at Mount Holyoke until his retirement in 1983.

Beyond his teaching responsibilities, Reid was a prolific writer. He began publishing books in the late 1950s and early 1960s, drawing upon the material from his university theses focusing on the works of Gertrude Stein and William Butler Yeats. He then turned his attention to biographical writing, publishing a biography of New York lawyer John Quinn in 1968 and another on Irish politician Roger Casement in 1976. In the later years of his life, between 1988 and 1990, Reid dedicated himself to writing his autobiographies.

Reid received significant recognition for his writing. He was awarded the 1969 Pulitzer Prize for Biography or Autobiography for his work, *The Man from New York: John Quinn and His Friends*.  He was also a finalist for the National Book Award for Biography and Autobiography in 1977 for *The Lives of Roger Casement*.  His research was also supported by prestigious grants; he received a Fulbright Program research grant in 1963 to study at the University of London and a fellowship from the National Endowment for the Humanities in 1971 to support his work on Bertrand Russell.

Benjamin Lawrence Reid died on November 30, 1990, in South Hadley, Massachusetts, as a result of a heart attack and multiple strokes. Prior to his academic career, during World War II, he served as a conscientious objector, working as both a bridge constructor and a psychiatric hospital orderly.

title: Ahsee Tuala
text:
Ahsee Tuala, born on August 23, 1989, is a rugby union player currently playing as a fullback for Northampton Saints in the Aviva Premiership. Though originally from Samoa, his family moved to New Zealand when he was two years old, and he was raised in South Auckland. He began his professional rugby career with the Counties Manukau Steelers in New Zealand, making his debut during the 2009 Air New Zealand Cup season at the age of 20. He quickly became a valuable player for the Steelers, accumulating over 50 ITM Cup appearances due to his versatility across the backline. He also participated in development squads for the Chiefs in both 2010 and 2011.

Tuala transitioned to English rugby in February 2015, initially signing with Northampton Saints for the remainder of the 2014-15 season. He subsequently agreed to a permanent contract with the club, establishing himself at Franklin's Gardens. While he had been with the Saints for a couple of seasons, the 2016/17 season marked a significant step forward in his career. He consistently secured a starting position, initially while George North was fulfilling international commitments, and continued to do so even upon North’s return. During that season, he scored five tries for the Saints, becoming a key component of their attacking backline. 

His contributions were recognized with the Saints’ Supporter’s Breakthrough Player of the Year award at the end of the 2016/17 season, surpassing fellow nominees Nic Groom and Juan Pablo Estelles. More recently, Tuala played a crucial role in securing Northampton Saints’ qualification for the European Rugby Champions Cup, scoring the decisive try in a narrow one-point victory against Stade Francais.

Tuala’s international representation began with New Zealand. He was initially involved with the New Zealand Under-20 wider squad in 2009, and later included in the New Zealand sevens wider training group in 2012. However, he chose to pursue international opportunities with Samoa, withdrawing from the New Zealand sevens squad in January 2012 to focus on achieving recognition with his birth nation. This ambition was fulfilled in 2014 when he was selected for the Samoan squad for the end-of-year rugby union tests. He made his debut for Samoa on November 14, 2014, in a match against Canada, which Samoa won 23-13, played in Vannes, France. He was again called up to represent Samoa, alongside teammate Ken Pisi from Northampton Saints, for the 2017 internationals.

title: Vance Joy
text:
Vance Joy, born James Gabriel Keogh on December 1st, 1987, is an Australian singer-songwriter and musician who rose to prominence with his 2013 hit single “Riptide.” He initially signed a five-album deal with Atlantic Records that same year and quickly followed it with his debut EP, *God Loves You When You're Dancing*. His musical journey began after a period playing Australian rules football; he played as a key defender for the Coburg Football Club in 2008 and 2009, but ultimately felt his potential in the sport was limited and pursued music instead.

Joy’s breakthrough came with “Riptide,” which topped the 2013 Triple J Hottest 100 and achieved significant commercial success both in Australia and the United States, becoming the longest-charting song in ARIA Charts history and earning 5x platinum certification in the US. The song’s inspiration stemmed from childhood family holidays and a motel called “Riptide.” His debut studio album, *Dream Your Life Away*, released in September 2014, earned him the ARIA Award for Best Male Artist in 2015, along with six further nominations. This album included singles like “Mess Is Mine,” “First Time,” “Georgia,” and “Fire and the Flood.”

Beyond his own tours, Joy supported Taylor Swift on her 1989 World Tour across North America, the UK, and Australia, and was featured on NBC’s *Today* show. He also performed a duet of “Riptide” with Quentin Alexander on *American Idol*. In 2018, he released his second studio album, *Nation of Two*, which debuted at number one in Australia and won the ARIA Award for Best Adult Contemporary Album. Singles from this album included “Lay It on Me,” “Like Gold,” “We’re Going Home,” and “Saturday Sun.” He also released a live album, *Live at Red Rocks Amphitheatre*, capturing a performance from his world tour.

His third studio album, *In Our Own Sweet Time*, was released in June 2022. Prior to this, he collaborated with Benny Blanco and Marshmello on the single “You” in 2021 and released “Missing Piece,” which achieved platinum status in Australia and won an ARIA Award for Best Video. More recently, in 2023, he collaborated with Noah Cyrus on the single "Everybody Needs Someone."

Joy’s personal life includes his marriage to Selen Us, whom he engaged to in November 2022 and married in June 2023. They welcomed their daughter, Gigi, in early 2024. He revealed that his song "Missing Piece" was inspired by his wife. Throughout his career, he has consistently toured, both headlining his own shows and as an opening act for major artists like Taylor Swift and P!nk.

title: Michael Collins (astronaut)
text:
Michael Collins was an American astronaut, test pilot, and U.S. Air Force Major General best known for piloting the Apollo 11 command module *Columbia* during the first crewed lunar landing in 1969, while Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon. Born in Rome, Italy, in 1930 to a military family, Collins followed in the footsteps of his father, brother, and other relatives by pursuing a career in the armed forces. He graduated from the U.S. Military Academy at West Point in 1952 and subsequently joined the Air Force, becoming a fighter pilot flying F-86 Sabres in France.

Driven by a fascination with aeronautics and a desire to avoid accusations of nepotism, Collins applied to and was accepted into the U.S. Air Force Experimental Flight Test Pilot School at Edwards Air Force Base in 1960. This led to his selection as one of the fourteen astronauts in NASA’s third group in 1963. His first spaceflight was aboard Gemini 10 in 1966, where he and John Young successfully rendezvoused with two spacecraft and completed two spacewalks, making him the fourth person and first American to perform more than one spacewalk.

The culmination of his career came with the Apollo 11 mission. While Armstrong and Aldrin descended to the lunar surface, Collins piloted the *Columbia* in lunar orbit, completing 30 orbits around the Moon. He was the second person to orbit the Moon alone, following Jim Lovell on Apollo 8.  His role, though often described as solitary, was critical to the mission’s success, as he maintained communication with Earth and prepared for the return journey. 

Following his retirement from NASA in 1970, Collins transitioned to public service, holding positions within the Department of State as Assistant Secretary of State for Public Affairs, and later as director of the National Air and Space Museum until 1978. He then became undersecretary of the Smithsonian Institution and later worked in the private sector as vice president of LTV Aerospace before starting his own consulting firm. Throughout his life, Collins remained a prominent figure, sharing his experiences and insights. Alongside his Apollo 11 crewmates, he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1969 and the Congressional Gold Medal in 2011. He passed away in April 2021, leaving behind a legacy as a dedicated astronaut and a pivotal figure in the history of space exploration.

title: Jimmy Tompkins (priest)
text:
James John “Jimmy” Tompkins was a Roman Catholic priest born in 1870 in Margaree Forks, Nova Scotia, who dedicated his life to improving the economic and social conditions of rural communities in eastern Nova Scotia. He died in 1953 and is best known as the spiritual founder of the Antigonish Movement, a progressive initiative focused on adult education, cooperative businesses, and community development, particularly within fishing and mining areas. This movement eventually became the Extension Department of St. Francis Xavier University, now known as the Coady International Center.

Tompkins’s belief in the power of education to uplift individuals led him to promote study groups and cooperative efforts as a means to address poverty. He famously stated, “It is not enough to have ideas, we have to put legs on them,” reflecting his pragmatic approach to social improvement. He was a pioneer in establishing community resources, founding the first regional library in Nova Scotia, as well as the first credit union and a cooperative housing association in Reserve Mines, which became known locally as “Tompkinsville.”

His path to becoming a champion of the working class was somewhat circuitous. Tompkins attended St. Francis Xavier University intermittently while also teaching Greek and Mathematics to fund his studies, graduating in 1895. He then pursued theological studies in Rome at the Urban College of the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide from 1897 to 1902, and was ordained in the Lateran Basilica in 1902. Returning to St. Francis Xavier, he served in various administrative roles, including vice-rector.

He was involved in an ultimately unsuccessful attempt to consolidate colleges in the Maritime Provinces into a single, nondenominational university centered around Dalhousie University. Despite support from the Archbishop of Halifax, the Bishop of Antigonish opposed the plan, and Tompkins was subsequently reassigned in 1923 to the small fishing village of Canso, Nova Scotia, to serve as parish priest for Canso, Little Dover, and Queensport. 

It was in Canso that he directly witnessed the hardships faced by fishing communities, which spurred him to organize the cooperative initiatives that formed the core of the Antigonish Movement. While he spearheaded the movement, its institutionalization and continued success was largely due to the work of his double-cousin, Father Moses Coady, along with collaborators like Father Hugh MacPherson and A.B. MacDonald, who headed the Extension Department at St. Francis Xavier. 

Tompkins continued his priestly duties, serving as chaplain at Bethany, the motherhouse of the Sisters of Saint Martha, and later as parish priest of St. Joseph’s Church in Reserve Mines until his retirement in 1948 due to ill health. He spent his final years at St. Martha’s Convent in Margaree Forks, and died in St. Martha's Hospital in 1953, being buried in Reserve Mines. His life and work have been the subject of multiple biographies, including works by Jim Lotz, Michael R. Welton, and George Boyle.

title: Don DeLillo
text:
Donald DeLillo, born November 20, 1936, is a highly regarded American author known for his novels, short stories, plays, screenplays, and essays. His work frequently explores themes of consumerism, nuclear anxieties, language, art, television, the digital age, mathematics, politics, economics, and sports. While respected within literary circles for some time, he achieved widespread recognition with the 1985 publication of *White Noise*, which won the National Book Award. He followed this success with *Libra* (1988), a novel focusing on the assassination of John F. Kennedy, and later received the PEN/Faulkner Award for *Mao II* and the William Dean Howells Medal for *Underworld*. Further accolades include the Jerusalem Prize (1999), the PEN/Saul Bellow Award (2010), and the Library of Congress Prize for American Fiction (2013). DeLillo views his writing as a form of opposition, believing writers should challenge power structures – corporations, the state, and the prevailing culture of consumption.

Born and raised in the Bronx, New York City, DeLillo grew up in an Italian-American Catholic family with roots in Molise, Italy. He recalls a childhood filled with imaginative play, particularly pretending to be a baseball announcer, and a multilingual household where English and Italian were frequently mixed. His serious engagement with reading began during a summer job as a parking attendant, a period he describes as a “golden age.” Influenced by modernist writers like James Joyce, William Faulkner, Flannery O’Connor, and Ernest Hemingway, he also found inspiration in jazz music – artists like Ornette Coleman and Miles Davis – and European and Asian cinema, particularly the works of Antonioni, Godard, and Truffaut. He credits his parents’ support for allowing him to pursue a literary career.

DeLillo graduated from Fordham University in 1958 with a degree in communication arts and initially worked as a copywriter at Ogilvy & Mather, writing advertisements for companies like Sears Roebuck. He published his first short story in 1960 and began working on his first novel in 1966, but only truly committed to writing after leaving advertising in 1964. He described his initial foray into novels as a slow process, acknowledging a lack of ambition and a developing sense of what constituted serious writing. William Gaddis’s *The Recognitions* proved a particularly formative influence.

The 1970s were DeLillo’s most prolific period, with six novels published between 1971 and 1978. These included *Americana*, *End Zone*, *Great Jones Street*, *Ratner's Star*, *Players*, and *Running Dog*.  He supported his writing through a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1978, which allowed him to travel and write in Greece. DeLillo later reflected that while he doesn't regret the work of the 70s, he might have benefited from a slower, more deliberate pace. He also published *Amazons* under a pseudonym, later requesting it be removed from his bibliographies.  The 1980s brought further success with *The Names* (1982) and the breakthrough novel *White Noise* (1985), solidifying his reputation as a major contemporary novelist. *Libra* followed in 1988, sparking both acclaim and controversy for its depiction of Lee Harvey Oswald and the Kennedy assassination.

title: Susan Sarandon
text:
Susan Sarandon, born Susan Abigail Tomalin in 1946 in Queens, New York City, is a highly acclaimed American actor with a career spanning over five decades. She has earned an Academy Award and a British Academy Film Award, alongside numerous nominations for Primetime Emmy and Golden Globe Awards. Sarandon began her acting journey with a debut role in the 1970 film *Joe* and appearances in television soap operas like *A World Apart* and *Search for Tomorrow*. She gained wider recognition for her performance in the 1975 musical horror film *The Rocky Horror Picture Show*.

Throughout her career, Sarandon has delivered memorable performances in a diverse range of films, including *Pretty Baby* (1978), *The Hunger* (1983), *The Witches of Eastwick* (1987), *Bull Durham* (1988), *Little Women* (1994), *Stepmom* (1998), and more recent works like *Enchanted* (2007) and *The Meddler* (2015). She received multiple Academy Award nominations for roles in *Atlantic City*, *Thelma & Louise*, *Lorenzo’s Oil*, and *The Client*, ultimately winning the Best Actress award in 1995 for her portrayal of Helen Prejean in *Dead Man Walking*. 

Beyond film, Sarandon has a notable stage presence, making her Broadway debut in *An Evening with Richard Nixon* in 1972 and returning in 2009 for a revival of *Exit the King*. She has also appeared in television shows such as *Friends*, *Malcolm in the Middle*, and starred in HBO films like *You Don't Know Jack* and *Bernard and Doris*, and the FX miniseries *Feud*, portraying Bette Davis.

Sarandon is equally well-known for her dedicated social and political activism. She was appointed a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador in 1999 and received the Action Against Hunger Humanitarian Award in 2006. Born into a large family – the eldest of nine children – her father worked in advertising and television, and her mother was active in local clubs. She grew up in New Jersey, attending Catholic schools and demonstrating athletic ability in swimming competitions. She attended Catholic University of America, earning a Bachelor of Arts in drama.

Her political involvement has been consistent and outspoken. She actively supports progressive causes and has been involved in anti-war movements, notably opposing the 2003 invasion of Iraq. She supported Ralph Nader’s presidential campaigns in 2000 and, later, Barack Obama in 2008 and Bernie Sanders in 2016. She has also been a vocal advocate for civil rights, speaking out on issues like the death penalty, mass incarceration, and LGBTQ+ rights, and actively working to raise awareness about these issues.  She continues to work on projects reflecting her beliefs, and in recent years has appeared in films like *Blue Beetle* (2023) and is slated to star in *Nonnas* (2025).

title: Elizabeth Inglis
text:
Elizabeth Inglis, born Desiree Mary Lucy Hawkins on July 10, 1913, was a British actress who achieved recognition for her work in film and theatre, and is also known as the mother of actress Sigourney Weaver. She passed away on August 25, 2007, in Santa Barbara, California, at the age of 94. Her parents were Margaret Inglis, born Hunt, and Alan George Hawkins.

Inglis began her film career with a role in *Borrowed Clothes* in 1934. A year later, she appeared in a small part as Hilary Jordan in Alfred Hitchcock’s renowned film, *The 39 Steps* (1935). A significant early role came with the original British production of Patrick Hamilton’s play *Gas Light*, where she portrayed the young maid Nancy. The play ran successfully for 141 performances, opening on December 5, 1938, and closing on June 10, 1939. The success of the stage production led to a live television adaptation for BBC Television in 1939, in which Inglis reprised her role alongside the original cast. 

Following her work in British productions, Inglis moved to Hollywood and took on the stage name Elizabeth Earl. There, she played Adele Ainsworth in William Wyler’s 1940 film *The Letter*, a role for which she became well known. This film marked a high point in her career.

In 1942, she married Pat Weaver, an American television executive. Shortly after their marriage, she chose to retire from acting. The couple remained together until Weaver’s death in 2002. They had two children together, one of whom was the acclaimed actress Sigourney Weaver. 

Interestingly, a connection to her daughter’s most famous role occurred in 1986 with the film *Aliens*. A photograph of Inglis herself was utilized in a deleted scene to depict Amanda Ripley, the elderly mother of Sigourney Weaver’s character, Ellen Ripley. This served as a visual representation of the family history woven into the narrative of the *Alien* franchise.

title: Ramli Sarip
text:
Ramli Sarip, born on October 15, 1952, is a Singaporean musician widely recognized as a pioneer of the nation’s rock scene and known affectionately as “Papa Rock.” He is a multifaceted artist, functioning as a singer, songwriter, arranger, and record producer. His musical career began in 1964 with the formation of the Malay rock band Sweet Charity, where he served as the frontman and lead vocalist for over two decades, remaining with the group until 1986. Sweet Charity achieved significant success throughout the 1970s and 1980s, reportedly sparking a widespread “rock explosion” across both Singapore and Malaysia.

Following his departure from Sweet Charity, Ramli embarked on a solo career, eventually signing with Warner Music. He distinguished himself as the first Malay rock singer to perform two solo concerts at the prestigious Istana Budaya in Kuala Lumpur. His contributions to the arts were acknowledged with the COMPASS Artistic Excellence Award in 1998. To support his solo work, Ramli formed the band Sangkakala, which functioned as his backing group.

Beyond music performance, Ramli has ventured into other creative areas. He hosted a Malaysian Hari Raya Puasa television special, *Bersama Ramli Sarip*, broadcast in 1990. However, his career faced a setback in 1993 when Radio Televisyen Malaysia imposed a seven-year ban on his appearances due to his long hair, which violated the broadcaster’s performance standards at the time. He contributed vocals to the 2011 remake of the song "Home" and, as of that year, had released a total of twelve solo albums. He also showcased his acting skills in the 2002 Singaporean satirical film, *Talking Cock the Movie*.

In 2019, Ramli Sarip performed a rendition of Singapore’s national anthem, "Majulah Singapura," at the National Day Parade. This performance drew considerable criticism, including a strong rebuke from Dr. Rohana Zubir, the daughter of the anthem’s original composer, Zubir Said, who publicly stated the rendition lacked the necessary quality and respect for the original composition. 

In 2013, Ramli Sarip was bestowed with the title of ‘Datuk’ by the Yang di-Pertua Negeri of the State of Malacca, in recognition of his contributions. He holds the Companion Class II of the Exalted Order of Malacca (DPSM), granting him the honorific Datuk.

title: Fifi Cooper
text:
Fifi Cooper, born Refilwe Boingotlo Moeketsi on October 24, 1991, is a South African recording artist who began her career as an R&B singer before finding success in rap. She grew up in Montshiwa, Mahikeng, as the youngest of three children, developing her singing and dancing abilities from a young age. She completed her secondary education at Batswana High School and later studied Media at Boston Media House.

Cooper’s professional music journey began in 2008 with a guest appearance on Mo'Molemi’s album. Her breakthrough arrived in 2010 with the release of the rap single “Chechela Morago,” which gained significant radio play and established her in the South African music scene. Before achieving solo success, she contributed vocals to remixes of songs by artists like AKA, Mo'Molemi, Khuli Chana and Lection.

In 2015, she signed with Ambitiouz Entertainment and released the AB Crazy-produced song “Kisses,” accompanied by a music video. Later that year, she released her debut studio album, *20FIFI*, which proved highly successful, winning three awards at the 15th Metro FM Music Awards and earning nominations for “Best Newcomer of The Year” and “Best Female Artist of The Year” at the South African Music Awards. 

Cooper’s time with Ambitiouz Entertainment ended in 2017 when she, along with A-Reece and B3nchMarQ, left the label. This departure led to a legal battle, with Ambitiouz successfully suing her for copyright infringement after she resigned without a clearance certificate. The court ruled she forfeited ownership of music recorded under the label and ordered her to remove or return all copies, as well as pay damages and legal fees. However, Julius Malema and the Economic Freedom Fighters intervened, negotiating an out-of-court settlement that restored her rights to her music.

Following the resolution of her legal issues, Fifi Cooper established her own record label, Mo Cooper Records, and released the 21-track album *Take Me Back*, featuring collaborations with artists like Thabsie and Moozlie. In 2020, she released the single “Net So” from her upcoming album, *Chapters*, and followed with “Motlogeleng” in March 2021. 

Known as the “Motswako first lady” by local media, Fifi Cooper is recognized for her versatility, seamlessly blending rap and singing. She is particularly known for her work in hip hop and Motswako, including her contribution as a vocalist on Khuli Chana's hit "Mnatebawen." She describes her rap style as “unpredictable, punchy and hearty.” Fifi Cooper is also a single mother to a son named Resego.

title: Francis Nicholson (painter)
text:
Francis Nicholson was a British artist born in Pickering, North Yorkshire, on November 14, 1753, and who died in London on March 6, 1844. He primarily worked as a landscape artist, utilizing both watercolour and oil paints. He initially received artistic training from a local artist in Scarborough before establishing his career in his hometown of Pickering. There, he began by creating sporting pictures and portraits, gaining patronage from various individuals throughout Yorkshire. 

As his artistic development progressed, Nicholson transitioned to painting country houses, which ultimately led to his focus on landscape painting, particularly using watercolour. By the mid-1780s, his work began to gain wider recognition, with contributions to exhibitions at the Royal Academy starting in 1789. These early exhibited pieces featured views of both Yorkshire and Scotland. He also provided topographical views for publication in the *Copper Plate Magazine*, broadening his reach.

A significant collaborative project involved “Views of England”, which Nicholson created alongside engraver Francis Jukes for inclusion in the multi-volume work *The Beauties of England and Wales*, authored by John Britton and Edward Wedlake Brayley, published between 1801 and 1815. While his market expanded and became centered in London, Nicholson continued to reside in Yorkshire for some time, moving between Whitby, Knaresborough, and Ripon before finally relocating to London around 1803. 

In 1804, Nicholson became a founding member of the Society of Painters in Watercolours, and he remained an active and productive exhibitor with the society. Demonstrating his expertise and commitment to the medium, he authored a handbook titled *The practice of drawing and painting landscape from nature, in water colours*, published in 1820. The book proved popular, selling out and necessitating a second edition in 1823.

Nicholson is remembered as a significant figure in British art, often referred to as the “Father of water colour painting” and recognized as an early pioneer of lithography. His work was highly regarded by the prominent artist J.M.W. Turner. A self-portrait, created around 1837, is held in the National Portrait Gallery. In 2012, the Pickering and District Civic Society honored his legacy by erecting a Blue Plaque at 3 Hungate in Pickering, commemorating his birthplace. His influence extended to his family, as his daughter, Marianne Croker, also became an artist, poet, and author, and was married to Thomas Crofton Croker.

title: Josiah Maduabuchi
text:
Josiah Maduabuchi is a Nigerian footballer, born on April 16, 1988, who currently plays as a midfielder for Lobi Stars. He began his football career in his home country, originating from Lagos, Nigeria. His professional journey started with Wikki Tourists F.C., where he first established himself as a player. 

His career progressed in 2007 when he transferred to the well-known Nigerian club, Enyimba International. He spent several years with Enyimba, gaining experience and further developing his skills as a footballer. Details regarding his specific achievements or time spent at Enyimba are not provided.

In 2015, Maduabuchi moved to Lobi Stars, another prominent Nigerian football club. As of the information available, he remains a player for Lobi Stars and continues to contribute as a midfielder for the team. title: Lali Espósito
text:
Mariana “Lali” Espósito, born in Buenos Aires in 1991, is a multi-talented Argentine artist working as a singer, actress, dancer, and model. Her career began in 2003 with a role in the children’s telenovela *Rincón de Luz*, followed by supporting parts in popular series like *Floricienta* and *Chiquititas*. She achieved widespread fame with her leading role in *Casi Ángeles*, which propelled her to recognition throughout Latin America, the Middle East, and Europe. This success led to her becoming a member of the teen pop band Teen Angels from 2007 to 2012, touring extensively with the group.

In 2014, Espósito launched her solo music career by signing with Sony Music Argentina and releasing her debut album, *A Bailar*, a pop and EDM-influenced record that spawned hit singles like “Asesina,” “Mil Años Luz,” and “Histeria.” Both *A Bailar* and her subsequent albums, *Soy* (2016) and *Brava* (2018), were certified gold in Argentina. *Soy* featured the singles “Soy,” “Boomerang,” and “Ego,” while *Brava* included “Una Na,” “Tu Novia,” and “100 Grados.” Her fourth studio album, *Libra*, was released in 2020 with singles “Laligera”, “Como Así” and “Lo Que Tengo Yo”. 

Alongside her musical pursuits, Espósito has continued to build a successful acting career. She garnered critical praise for her stage performance as Abigail Williams in *The Crucible* and for her roles in the crime thriller *The Accused* and the Netflix action series *Sky Rojo*. She has starred in several telenovelas including *Solamente vos* and *Esperanza mía*. 

Throughout her career, Espósito has accumulated numerous awards and nominations. These include six Gardel Awards, five MTV Europe Music Awards, thirteen Argentina Kids' Choice Awards, a Billboard Latin Music Award, and seven MTV Millennial Awards. She has also been nominated for the Lo Nuestro Awards and the Seoul International Drama Awards. In 2015, *Infobae* recognized her as one of the ten most influential women in Argentina.

Born into a family with connections to the entertainment industry – her mother manages her tours, and her siblings work as a makeup artist and former athlete – Espósito’s early life included a childhood appearance on the television program *Caramelito y Vos*. She inadvertently auditioned for Cris Morena, leading to her role in *Rincón de Luz*.  She has since become a prominent figure in Latin American entertainment, consistently achieving commercial success and critical acclaim in both her music and acting endeavors.

title: Maddy Crippen
text:
Madeleine Marie Crippen, born July 10, 1980, is a former American competitive swimmer who competed for the United States at the 2000 Summer Olympics. Known as Madeleine Plankey after marriage, she achieved significant success throughout her swimming career, beginning with a silver medal at the 1997 Pan Pacific Championship in Fukuoka, Japan, representing Team USA. She continued to perform well on the international stage, placing fifth in the 400-meter individual medley and sixth in the 200-meter individual medley at the 1998 World Aquatics Championships in Perth, Australia, and securing fourth place in the 400-meter individual medley at the 1999 Pan Pacific Championships.

Crippen qualified for the 2000 Olympic Games by finishing second in the 400-meter individual medley at the U.S. Olympic Trials. At the Sydney Olympics that year, she finished sixth in the same event. She continued competing internationally after the Olympics, participating in the 2002 Pan Pacific Championships and the 2003 World Championships in Barcelona, Spain. Throughout her career, she was a three-time U.S. national champion, with two titles in the 400-meter individual medley and one in the 200-meter breaststroke. She benefited from the guidance of Hall of Fame Coach Dick Shoulberg, who served as an Advisory Women's Coach for the U.S. Olympic team in 2000.

Beyond her international achievements, Crippen was a prominent collegiate swimmer at Villanova University, swimming for the Villanova Wildcats. During her time there, she won an NCAA championship in the 400-yard individual medley and accumulated ten Big East championships. She was recognized as the Big East "Swimmer of the Year" in both 1999 and 2001, and was named Villanova “Swimmer of the Year” in 1999, 2001 and 2002. Her accomplishments led to her induction into the Villanova Athletic Hall of Fame in 2019.

Swimming is a family affair for the Crippens. She is the daughter of Peter and Patricia Crippen, and her siblings, Fran, Teresa, and Claire, were also competitive swimmers under coach Richard “Dick” Shoulberg. All four siblings qualified for the U.S. Olympic Team Trials. Her brother, Fran, tragically died in 2010 after collapsing from exhaustion during a race. He was a successful swimmer in his own right, earning a bronze medal at the 2009 World Aquatics Championships and achieving All-American honors at the University of Virginia. Her sisters, Claire and Teresa, also enjoyed collegiate success; Claire as an NCAA All-American at the University of Virginia, and Teresa as a Pan American Games Champion and U.S. National Team member who swam for the University of Florida.

Crippen retired from competitive swimming in 2004 and currently works in marketing. She remained involved in the sport by serving on the board of directors for USA Swimming and as a member of the Athletes Executive Committee. She is married to Sean Plankey, who is a commander in the U.S. Coast Guard.

title: Will Voigt
text:
William Voigt, born August 18, 1976, is an American basketball coach currently an assistant coach for Brigham Young University’s men’s basketball team. His career has spanned multiple levels of basketball, from professional leagues to international competition, and includes a diverse range of coaching positions.

Voigt’s basketball journey began in Cabot, Vermont, where he played both basketball and soccer at Cabot High School. He then attended Pomona College in California, participating in soccer while earning a degree in political science. While in college, he gained initial experience with an internship with the Los Angeles Clippers. After graduating, he joined the San Antonio Spurs as a video coordinator, transitioning into college coaching a year later as an assistant under Rick Barnes at the University of Texas. He continued his college assistant work at Metro State under Mike Dunlap.

His first head coaching opportunity came with Ulriken Elite in Norway, a position he held from 2003 to 2006. A unique fan-vote selection process led to him becoming the head coach of the Vermont Frost Heaves in the American Basketball Association. He successfully led the team to consecutive ABA championships during its first two seasons. 

In 2009, another fan vote secured him the head coaching position for the Bakersfield Jam of the NBA Development League, now known as the G League. He guided the Jam to three playoff appearances over five seasons before departing in 2014. Voigt then took his coaching skills internationally, serving as an assistant coach for the Shanxi Brave Dragons in the Chinese Basketball Association. 

A significant achievement came in 2015 when he was chosen to coach the Nigerian national team at AfroBasket. Under his leadership, Nigeria won its first AfroBasket title, earning automatic qualification for the 2016 Summer Olympics. He later signed a three-year contract in November 2017 to coach the Angola national basketball team, and also served as a consultant for a team in the Philippine Basketball Association that same year. 

Voigt’s international coaching continued with Telekom Baskets Bonn of the German Bundesliga, initially in February 2020, and then again from January 2021, before parting ways after the 2020-21 season. In 2022, he accepted a one-year deal to coach Zamalek in the Egyptian Basketball Super League and the Basketball Africa League, leading them to a third-place finish in the BAL Playoffs and the semi-finals of the Super League. Most recently, prior to his appointment at BYU, he was head coach of the Austin Spurs of the NBA G League, a position he held since June 2023.

Voigt’s mother is Ellen Bryant Voigt, a former Vermont Poet Laureate. His career demonstrates a breadth of experience and success across various basketball landscapes.

title: Loo Kum Zee
text:
Loo Kum Zee, born on December 2nd, 1974, is a Malaysian athlete specializing in the high jump. He is recognized as one of Malaysia’s prominent figures in the sport, having achieved a personal best jump of 2.24 meters. This record-setting jump occurred in December 1995 in Chiangmai, marking a significant achievement in his athletic career.

Throughout his competitive years, Loo Kum Zee consistently demonstrated his talent on the Asian stage. He secured bronze medals at the Asian Championships on four separate occasions: in 1995, 1998, 2002, and 2003. This repeated success highlights his enduring skill and consistency within the competition. 

His athletic pursuits extended to the highest level of international competition, as he represented Malaysia at the 1996 Olympic Games. While he participated in the Games, he unfortunately did not advance to the final round of the high jump event. Nevertheless, his presence at the Olympics signifies a peak in his career and a demonstration of his national representation.

Prior to his athletic achievements, Loo Kum Zee received his secondary education at SMJK Sam Tet, a school located in Ipoh, Perak, Malaysia. This information provides a glimpse into his early life and educational background. 

Beyond his athletic accomplishments, Loo Kum Zee has been recognized for his contributions to the nation. In 2013, he was awarded the Member of the Order of the Defender of the Realm (A.M.N.) by Malaysia. This honour acknowledges his service and dedication to the country, likely stemming from his representation in international sporting events and his achievements as an athlete. The award signifies national appreciation for his efforts and contributions to Malaysian sport.

Information regarding Loo Kum Zee’s career can be found on the World Athletics website, serving as a resource for further details about his competitive record and statistics. His career is defined by consistent performance at the Asian Championships, a notable appearance at the Olympic Games, and ultimately, national recognition through a prestigious honour.

title: Thomas Jack
text:
Thomas Jack, born Tom Jack Johnston, is an Australian DJ, record producer, and musician who is credited with popularizing and even coining the term “tropical house” in 2013. He grew up on a large dairy farm in rural New South Wales, working with thousands of cows before moving to Sydney to study music production. His initial foray into music production began with the PlayStation game eJay, before progressing to Ableton software, a gift from his father. Prior to achieving success, he experimented with various stage names including Dirty-D and Tom Foolery.

Johnston’s musical style, which he describes as summery and laid-back dance music, blends deep house with influences from acoustic rock and jam bands. His tracks frequently incorporate live instrumentation such as saxophone, flute, piano, and guitar, aiming for an uplifting and relaxed atmosphere, and often include sampled speeches. He initially worried about being pigeonholed by the “tropical house” label, wanting to maintain artistic freedom.

His career gained momentum after being discovered on SoundCloud by Myles Shear, who brought him to Miami. He launched a popular podcast mix series called *Tropical House*, featuring mixes from artists like Felix Jaehn and Robin Schulz. He became known for original tracks like "Symphony" and "The Final Speech," alongside remixes of artists such as Of Monsters & Men and OneRepublic. Extensive touring followed, leading him to spend significant time in the United States, particularly Florida.

In 2015, Johnston participated in the *We Are Your Friends* movie tour and launched the *Tropical Express Tour* with artists including Bag Raiders and Felix Jaehn. He released his debut single, "Rivers," featuring Nico & Vinz, which achieved chart success in Belgium, the Netherlands, and Norway, accompanied by a music video on his YouTube channel. He also expressed intentions to potentially launch a tropical house record label, though he prioritized completing his debut album. 

He released a second single, "Rise Up" with Jasmine Thompson in 2016, peaking at fourteenth in Belgium, and also had an accompanying music video released on Thompson’s YouTube channel. Though he planned to release an album in 2016, a busy touring schedule delayed production. 

Johnston’s influence extends beyond his own music; he inadvertently popularized the “tropical house” genre, which was then embraced by artists like Kygo and Klingande. He played a role in launching the careers of both Kygo and Klingande by introducing them to his manager, Myles Shear. He remains interested in the evolution of the genre, hoping to see it progress and avoid becoming overly commercialized, while also maintaining his own artistic identity.

title: Patoranking
text:
Patoranking, born Patrick Nnaemeka Okorie on May 27, 1990, is a Nigerian Afrobeats and reggae-dancehall singer and songwriter. He grew up in the Ebute Metta area of Lagos, sharing a single room with his parents and five siblings, a background that fueled his ambition. His early musical journey involved underground collaborations with artists like XProject, Konga, Slam, and Reggie Rockstone. He first signed a record deal with K-Solo's Igberaga Records in 2010, releasing “Up in D Club” and later recording tracks like “Iya Bisi” with Qdot and Kbaj, a fusion of dancehall and fuji music.

Patoranking’s career gained momentum after a collaboration with Timaya on the song “Alubarika” in 2013, which he described as a reflection of his personal journey and a catalyst for building his fanbase. This led to a mentorship under Dem Mama Records, though Timaya later clarified Patoranking was never officially signed to his label. In February 2014, he signed with Foston Musik, releasing the single “Girlie O,” produced by WizzyPro, which brought him wider recognition. He further expanded his reach with a remix of “Girlie O” featuring Tiwa Savage, which charted on MTV Base’s Official Naija Top 10.

He has collaborated with other artists including Seyi Shay on "Murda" and Stonebwoy on a remix of "Pull Up", demonstrating an effort to maintain connections with his fanbase in Ghana, where he once pursued education at the University of Cape Coast before dropping out due to financial difficulties. While in Ghana, he worked various jobs to support himself.

Patoranking cites musical influences including Buju Banton, Bob Marley, Fela Kuti, and Lucky Dube, describing his own music as morally conscious dancehall with socio-political commentary. He has released several successful singles, including “Daniella Whine” and “My Woman, My Everything,” both of which topped the MTV Base Official Naija Top 10 chart. 

He has released four albums: *God Over Everything* (2016), *Wilmer* (2019) – named after his daughter – *Three* (2020), and *World Best* (2023). Patoranking is currently managed internationally by Rickie Davies and in Africa by Chimdinma Maduforo. He has a son, Welda, in addition to his daughter Wilmer, and has been linked romantically to Joselyn Dumas and Yemi Alade. He reportedly found inspiration for a song while playing football.

title: Shaolin (humorist)
text:
Francisco Jozenilton Veloso, professionally known as Shaolin, was a Brazilian entertainer who worked as a cartoonist, caricaturist, humorist, comedian and television presenter. Born on May 8, 1971, in Coremas, Paraíba, he became a recognizable figure in Brazilian media before his death on January 14, 2016.

Shaolin began his career performing at the Teatro Municipal Severino Cabral in Campina Grande. He expanded his work into radio, hosting programs on Rádio Campina Grande, and further developed his artistic skills by creating cartoons for several publications, including the newspapers *A Palavra* and *Jornal da Paraíba*, as well as *Revista Nordeste*. 

He gained widespread recognition for his appearances on popular Brazilian television programs. He featured in shows like *Domingão do Faustão* and *Show do Tom*, but he is perhaps best remembered for his work on *Tudo è Possível*, hosted by Ana Hickmann. On this show, Shaolin specialized in satirical impressions of Brazilian celebrities. His targets included well-known figures such as the singer Leonardo, Joelma, of the band Banda Calypso, and Zezé di Camargo. 

In January 2011, Shaolin suffered life-altering injuries in a serious traffic accident. His car collided with a truck on the BR-230 highway near Campina Grande. The accident left him in a coma for several months, until May of that year, when he was discharged from the hospital. However, he did not fully recover from his injuries and continued to require care. Despite his severe condition, Shaolin showed remarkable resilience. By September 2012, he was able to begin communicating through deliberate movements of his eyelid, aided by a specialized machine.

Shaolin was married to Laudiceia Veloso in December 1994, and together they had two children. His death, occurring on January 14, 2016, was the result of a myocardial infarction, marking the end of a career that brought humor to many Brazilians. Information about his life and career can be found on the Internet Movie Database (IMDb) and through his previously active Twitter account.

title: Ziaur Rahman
text:
Ziaur Rahman was born in 1936 in Bogra, East Bengal, to a Bengali Muslim family. His father was a chemist, and he received his early education in Calcutta and later Karachi after the partition of India in 1947. He joined the Pakistan Military Academy, graduating in 1955 and eventually serving as a company commander in the 1965 Indo-Pakistani War, earning the Hilal-e-Jurrat for his bravery. He served in East Pakistan, becoming increasingly aware of the disparities and Bengali grievances within Pakistan.
