He maintained his lead, ultimately winning by a margin of 28 seconds over Pablo Urtasun of Euskaltel–Euskadi and his own teammate, Mikhail Antonov. This victory demonstrated his ability to perform strongly in international competition.

Later in his career, Shalunov achieved the recognition of being named to the start list for one of cycling’s three Grand Tours, the Giro d'Italia, in 2017. The article does not detail his performance *during* the Giro d'Italia, only that he was included amongst the riders at the start. 

The article provides links to further information about his career statistics and results on websites such as UCI, Cycling Archives, ProCyclingStats, Cycling Quotient, and CycleBase, allowing for a more in-depth exploration of his racing history.

title: Deyverson
text:
Deyverson Brum Silva, known simply as Deyverson, is a Brazilian professional footballer currently playing as a forward for Fortaleza, having joined the club in March 2025. Born in Rio de Janeiro in 1991, he began his career with Grêmio Mangaratibense in 2011, where he quickly established himself as a prolific scorer, netting 18 goals in 31 appearances over two seasons and becoming the team’s top scorer in the Carioca Série C twice.

In 2012, Deyverson moved to Benfica in Portugal, initially joining the reserve side. He made a quick impact, scoring eight league goals in his first season, despite starting only 12 matches. He then spent a year with Belenenses, where he scored a notable goal against Alvalade, before a six-month loan spell with 1. FC Köln in Germany in 2015, where he scored against Eintracht Frankfurt. 

Deyverson then moved to Spain, signing a four-year deal with Levante in 2015. He scored his first goal in La Liga against Eibar and later contributed a brace against Sporting de Gijón. Following Levante’s relegation, he joined Deportivo Alavés on loan in 2016, famously scoring the winning goal against Barcelona at Camp Nou.

He returned to Brazil in 2017, joining Palmeiras on a five-year contract. During his time with Palmeiras, he was a key contributor to their success, scoring seven goals in his first season and nine goals in 2018, helping them win the Campeonato Brasileiro Série A.  He later had loan spells back in Spain with Getafe and Alavés, though he didn’t find consistent success.

A highlight of his career came in 2021 when, playing for Palmeiras, he scored the winning goal in the Copa Libertadores Final in extra time against Flamengo, earning him the Man of the Match award. He also played a part in Palmeiras winning the Recopa Sudamericana in 2022 and the Campeonato Paulista in the same year.

After leaving Palmeiras, Deyverson joined Cuiabá in 2022, where he scored six goals and had a run of three goals in three consecutive matches. He then moved to Atlético Mineiro in 2024, where he quickly made an impact, earning Man of the Match awards for performances in the Copa Libertadores against Fluminense and River Plate, scoring multiple goals in both ties. He also helped Atlético Mineiro win the Campeonato Mineiro in 2025.



Deyverson’s honours include the Campeonato Brasileiro Série A, Copa Libertadores, Recopa Sudamericana, Campeonato Paulista with Palmeiras, and the Campeonato Mato-Grossense with Cuiabá, and Campeonato Mineiro with Atlético Mineiro.

title: Jean Muir (actress)
text:
Jean Muir, born Jean Muir Fullarton in 1911 in Suffern, New York, was an American actress who worked in both stage and film, and later became a college drama teacher. She is notably remembered as the first performer to be blacklisted in the entertainment industry, following her inclusion in the anti-Communist publication *Red Channels* in 1950. 

Muir’s early life included a period of study in Paris after attending school in New Jersey. She began her acting career in New York City, initially working as a model before making her Broadway debut in 1930. This led to a contract with Warner Bros. in 1933, where she appeared in fourteen films over three years alongside actors like Paul Muni and Warren William. However, her career at Warner Bros. was short-lived due to her outspoken nature and unwillingness to conform to studio expectations. She questioned directors and crew, refused to participate in typical publicity, and actively engaged in political activism, supporting striking workers and joining the Screen Actors Guild. Her persistent questioning earned her the nickname “the studio pest,” and ultimately led to the termination of her contract in 1937.

She returned to New York to continue working in theatre, eventually returning to Hollywood for a final film role in 1943, and was considered for the role of Melanie in *Gone with the Wind*. After a period focusing on raising her three children, she briefly returned to television in 1949 with *The Aldrich Family*, but was quickly dismissed after being named as a Communist sympathizer in *Red Channels*. Despite thousands of letters of support, NBC and its sponsor, General Foods, refused to reinstate her, citing public outcry and a policy against “controversial persons.” 

Muir voluntarily testified before the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1953, denying Communist affiliation but acknowledging past support for organizations later deemed subversive. She later deeply regretted this decision, feeling it betrayed her principles and was disturbed to discover she had named names during her testimony. After the blacklist eased, she resumed some television work in the late 1950s, but her on-screen career largely ended by 1962. 

She then transitioned to teaching drama, working at community centers in New York before moving to Missouri in 1968. There, she became a Master Acting Teacher at Stephens College, eventually earning her own degree from the institution in 1977. She continued teaching at the University of Missouri–Kansas City for a year following her retirement from Stephens. Jean Muir married attorney Henry Jaffe in 1940 and passed away in 1996 at the age of 85, leaving behind a legacy as a talented actress and a courageous advocate for her beliefs. She is honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

title: Ruth Fischer
text:
Ruth Fischer, born Elfriede Eisler in Leipzig in 1895, was a prominent figure in the early Communist movement in both Austria and Germany. She was a co-founder of the Austrian Communist Party (KPÖ) in 1918, and alongside her partner Arkadi Maslow, briefly led the Communist Party of Germany (KPD) in the mid-1920s. However, she ultimately became a fervent and lifelong critic of Stalinism.

Fischer’s political journey began in Vienna, where she studied philosophy, economics, and politics. Following the founding of the KPÖ, she quickly became involved in its leadership, even claiming to be its first member. Her early activism led to a brief arrest for alleged treason. She later moved to Berlin after disagreements over tactics within the Austrian party, becoming a key leader of the KPD’s left wing alongside Maslow. They criticized the party’s cautious approach and opposed collaboration with the Social Democrats. To secure her German citizenship and avoid deportation, she married fellow communist Gustav Golke.

In the early 1920s, Fischer and Maslow advocated for a revolutionary uprising in Germany, pushing for a strategy mirroring the Bolshevik revolution. They were vocal in their criticism of the existing KPD leadership, accusing them of opportunism and ideological weakness. Despite being a minority voice, Fischer was co-opted onto the Comintern’s Central Committee in 1923. She even controversially appealed to Nazi students, seeking common ground in their opposition to Jewish capital. 

Following the failure of the Hamburg Uprising, Fischer, Maslow, and Ernst Thälmann gained control of the KPD, ousting the previous leadership. Fischer and Maslow were elected as co-chairpersons in 1924, and Fischer was elected to both the Reichstag and the Prussian House of Representatives. However, their position was short-lived. During the power struggles following Lenin's death, they initially supported Grigory Zinoviev against Leon Trotsky. This alliance proved temporary, as Zinoviev and Stalin later turned against them, accusing them of unreliability.

In 1926, Fischer and Maslow were expelled from the KPD. They subsequently formed a splinter group, denouncing Stalin's regime as a new form of state capitalism. Fischer spent the following years in exile, first in Paris and then in the United States. During the Cold War, she even worked as an agent for the CIA’s predecessor, providing intelligence on communist movements.

Fischer authored a memoir, *Stalin and German Communism*, in 1948, which offered a critical account of her experiences. However, the accuracy of her recollections has been questioned by historians. She died in Paris in 1961, leaving behind a complex legacy as a committed revolutionary who ultimately rejected the Soviet model. She had one son, Friedrich Gerhart Friedländer, who became a mathematician. Her papers are now held by the International Institute of Social History.

title: Joe McGinniss
text:
Joe McGinniss, born in Manhattan in 1942 and passing away in 2014, was an American author known for his work in both non-fiction and novels, totaling twelve books. He first gained recognition with *The Selling of the President 1968*, a bestseller detailing the marketing strategies used in Richard Nixon’s 1968 presidential campaign. This book, published when he was 26, achieved significant success and established him as a notable figure in political reporting. He later became particularly known for a trilogy of true crime books – *Fatal Vision*, *Blind Faith*, and *Cruel Doubt* – all of which were adapted into television miniseries. His final published work was *The Rogue: Searching for the Real Sarah Palin*, a biography of the former Alaskan governor and 2008 Republican vice-presidential nominee.

McGinniss’s early life was spent in Forest Hills, Queens, and Rye, New York. He attended Archbishop Stepinac High School and later the College of the Holy Cross, graduating in 1964. Despite being proud of his rejection from the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism, he began his journalism career as a general assignment reporter for the *Worcester Telegram* before moving to the *Philadelphia Bulletin* as a sportswriter and then the *Philadelphia Inquirer* as a columnist. He later held a writer-in-residence position at the Los Angeles Herald Examiner and taught creative writing at Bennington College, where he had Donna Tartt and Bret Easton Ellis as students.

Following the success of *The Selling of the President 1968*, McGinniss dedicated himself to writing books full-time. He followed his initial success with a novel, *The Dream Team*, and then *Heroes* and *Going to Extremes*, the latter being a nonfiction account of his experiences in Alaska. The 1980s and early 90s saw him achieve further acclaim with his true crime trilogy. *Fatal Vision* centered on the Jeffrey MacDonald murder case, sparking a lawsuit from MacDonald alleging deception on McGinniss's part regarding his belief in MacDonald's innocence, which ultimately resulted in an out-of-court settlement. The case also became the subject of a book by Janet Malcolm, *The Journalist and the Murderer*, prompting a response from McGinniss himself. *Blind Faith* detailed the Marshall murder case, and *Cruel Doubt* focused on the Lieth Von Stein murder. 

However, his 1993 biography of Ted Kennedy, *The Last Brother*, was widely criticized for its sourcing, lack of attribution, and speculative nature, being described as “awful” and “rotten” by critics. He later returned to Alaska to research Sarah Palin, resulting in *The Rogue*, which generated controversy due to allegations and unnamed sources, and faced potential legal action, though a lawsuit never materialized.  He also briefly pursued a book about the O.J. Simpson trial, ultimately returning a $1 million advance after deciding he couldn't produce a satisfactory work. Later books included *The Miracle of Castel di Sangro* and *Never Enough*. 

In his later years, McGinniss battled alcoholism and depression. He was diagnosed with terminal prostate cancer in 2012 and died in 2014 at the age of 71, leaving behind a legacy as a distinctive and often controversial figure in American journalism and non-fiction writing.

title: Bobby Thomson
text:
Bobby Thomson, born in Glasgow, Scotland in 1923 and passing away in 2010, was a Major League Baseball outfielder known for a career spanning several teams including the New York Giants, Milwaukee Braves, Chicago Cubs, Boston Red Sox, and Baltimore Orioles. Though he achieved eight seasons with 20 or more home runs and was a three-time All-Star, he is overwhelmingly remembered for one singular moment: the “Shot Heard ‘Round the World.”

Thomson’s family moved to Staten Island, New York when he was two years old, and he signed with the Giants directly out of high school in 1942. His baseball career was interrupted by World War II, serving in the United States Army Air Forces as a bombardier, though he remained stateside. He began his professional baseball career in earnest in 1947, posting a .283 batting average with 29 home runs in his rookie season. He continued to be a productive hitter, achieving a career-best .309 average and 109 RBIs in 1949.

The 1951 season cemented Thomson’s place in baseball lore. Despite being 13 1/2 games behind the Brooklyn Dodgers in mid-August, the Giants rallied to tie for the National League pennant, forcing a three-game playoff. The deciding game, played at the Polo Grounds, saw the Dodgers leading 4-1 in the bottom of the ninth. After a series of hits, Thomson came to bat with the score 4-2 and runners on second and third. His dramatic walk-off home run off pitcher Ralph Branca won the pennant for the Giants and became instantly legendary, broadcast coast-to-coast as the first major sporting event to receive such coverage. However, the Giants lost the subsequent World Series to the New York Yankees, four games to two, with Thomson batting .238.

Later revelations brought controversy to the celebrated moment. It was discovered in 2001, and detailed in a 2008 book, that the Giants had been systematically stealing signs from opposing catchers using a telescope and a buzzer system. Though Thomson maintained he was unaware of the stolen signs, evidence suggested that information regarding the pitch was relayed to him before his famous at-bat. 

Thomson continued playing for several years, leading the National League in triples in 1952 and being traded back to the Giants in 1957. He finished his major league career in 1960 and played one final season in Japan in 1963. Throughout his 15-year career, he compiled a .270 batting average, 264 home runs, and 1,026 RBIs. Following his playing days, he worked in sales. He was honored with the naming of baseball fields in Scotland and Staten Island after him, and is a member of the Staten Island Sports Hall of Fame. A poignant letter received decades later from a Marine serving in Korea, whose dying friend had listened to the broadcast of Thomson’s home run, highlighted the profound impact of that moment beyond the confines of the baseball field.

title: Cris Cyborg
text:
Cristiane Justino Venâncio, known professionally as Cris Cyborg, is a Brazilian-American mixed martial artist and boxer currently competing in the Professional Fighters League (PFL), where she is the inaugural PFL Super Fights Women's World Featherweight Champion. She has achieved a remarkable career, becoming the only MMA fighter to win championships in five major promotions: UFC, Strikeforce, Invicta FC, Bellator MMA, and now PFL. She is widely considered one of the greatest female MMA fighters of all time.

Born in Curitiba, Brazil in 1985, Cyborg excelled in handball as a young athlete, earning athletic scholarships to universities. Her path shifted when a Chute Boxe Academy trainer recognized her physical potential and encouraged her to pursue fighting. She began her MMA career at age 19 in 2005, suffering an early loss to Erica Paes, which remained her only defeat for several years. She quickly improved, winning fights in Brazilian promotions like Storm Samurai and making her US debut with a win at EliteXC in 2008.

Cyborg rose to prominence in Strikeforce, winning the Women’s Featherweight Championship in 2009 with a first-round TKO victory over Gina Carano – a historic fight as the first major women's main event. She successfully defended this title twice, defeating Hitomi Akano and Marloes Coenen. A planned fight with Marloes Coenen at XMMA 7 was cancelled when she signed with Strikeforce. She also earned a BJJ Purple Belt during this time. 

After Strikeforce folded, she signed with Invicta Fighting Championships, winning and defending their Featherweight Championship before moving to the UFC in 2015. In the UFC, she won the Featherweight Championship, defeating Tonya Evinger, and successfully defended it against Holly Holm and Yana Kunitskaya. Her run in the UFC ended with a loss to Amanda Nunes in 2018.

Following her time in the UFC, Cyborg signed with Bellator MMA, where she once again became a champion, winning the Bellator Women's Featherweight Championship in 2020 against Julia Budd and defending it several times against Arlene Blencowe (twice) and Leslie Smith. After a period as a free agent, she joined the PFL in 2024, winning the inaugural PFL Super Fights Women's Featherweight Championship against Larissa Pacheco.

Throughout her career, Cyborg faced a one-year suspension in 2012 due to a positive test for stanozolol, resulting in a no-contest for her win over Hiroko Yamanaka. She has also pursued a professional boxing career, starting in 2022 and achieving multiple wins, including several by knockout. 

Beyond her athletic accomplishments, Cyborg has a notable personal life. She was previously married to Evangelista "Cyborg" Santos, adopting his nickname. She became a naturalized US citizen in 2016 and became engaged to Ray Elbe in 2017. Notably, she legally adopted her teenage niece in 2018, becoming the first mother to hold a UFC championship. She is also involved in charitable work with the organization Fight for the Forgotten.

title: Eric Winter
text:
Eric Winter, born on July 17, 1976, is an American actor who began his career in modeling before transitioning to television and film. He was raised in the Los Angeles area, specifically La Mirada and La Puente, and attended Los Altos High School before earning a psychology degree from UCLA. Initially, his involvement in modeling and taking on small acting roles was intended as a way to finance his college education. 

Winter’s early modeling work included a print campaign for Tommy Hilfiger and an appearance in a television commercial alongside Britney Spears promoting her fragrance, Curious. He gained recognition for his role as Rex Brady on the daytime soap opera *Days of Our Lives*, appearing on the show from 2002 to 2005. Following his departure from the soap, he took on numerous guest roles in various television series including *CSI*, *Love, Inc.*, *Charmed*, and *Just Legal*. He also had a five-episode arc on ABC Family’s *Wildfire*, where his character, R.J. Blake, met an untimely end. Further television appearances included roles on *The Parkers*, *The Ex-List*, and a recurring role on *Brothers & Sisters* as Jason McCallister. He also had regular roles in the short-lived series *Viva Laughlin* and *Moonlight*.

His film credits include appearances in *Harold & Kumar Escape from Guantanamo Bay* in 2008 and *The Ugly Truth* in 2009, as well as *The Good Doctor*. In 2010, he starred in the Lifetime television movie *Sundays at Tiffany's* as Michael Friend. He then joined the cast of *The Mentalist* in 2010, playing FBI agent Craig O'Laughlin and developing a relationship with Grace Van Pelt, culminating in an engagement.  He also had a recurring role on *GCB* in 2012 and appeared in the video game *Beyond: Two Souls*.

From 2013 to 2014, Winter starred as Dash Gardiner in the Lifetime series *Witches of East End* before the show was cancelled after two seasons.  Currently, he is widely known for his role as Officer Tim Bradford in the ABC drama *The Rookie*, a role he began in 2018 and continues to play.

In his personal life, Winter was married to actress Allison Ford from 2001 to 2005. He then had a two-year relationship with Roselyn Sanchez, leading to their engagement in Puerto Rico in 2007. The couple married in San Juan, Puerto Rico, in November 2008 and have two children together: a daughter born in January 2012 and a son born in November 2017.

title: Yuyan
text:
Yuyan, born with the courtesy name Yanrui and nickname Xiaoruizi on May 17, 1918, and passing away on January 18, 1999, was a Chinese calligrapher descended from the Manchu Aisin Gioro clan, the imperial family of the Qing dynasty. He was a distant cousin of Puyi, the last Emperor of China, and a central figure in the story of the potential succession to the throne after the dynasty’s fall.

Born in Beijing to Pucheng and Jinggui, Yuyan’s lineage traced back to the Daoguang Emperor through his grandfather, Zailian. In 1936, Puyi summoned Yuyan to his court in Manchukuo, a puppet state established by Japan, where they developed a close relationship – Puyi affectionately called him “Little Rui.” 

Following the collapse of Manchukuo, Yuyan’s life took a dramatic turn. He was arrested by the Soviets in 1945 and imprisoned in the Soviet Far East until 1950, alongside Puyi. After being sent back to China, he was incarcerated in the Fushun War Criminals Management Centre from 1950 to 1957. It was during their imprisonment that Yuyan claimed Puyi designated him as his heir, a claim Puyi himself only alluded to in his autobiography as a consideration. However, a formal succession law established in 1937 had already named Puyi’s brother, Pujie, as the next in line.

Life under the People’s Republic of China was marked by hardship. Released from Fushun, Yuyan worked as a teacher and in a factory, but was repeatedly arrested. He endured hard labour in 1959 near Beijing and again during the Cultural Revolution in 1966, being sent to Shanxi. He wasn’t fully released until 1979, after which he worked as a road sweeper in Beijing.

Despite his difficult circumstances, Yuyan continued to practice calligraphy and poetry. He was later recognized for his skills and appointed as a state consultant for the restoration of the Prince Gong Mansion in 1987. His story gained wider attention with the publication of Tony Scotland’s 1993 book, *The Empty Throne*, which details the British journalist’s search for a potential heir to the Chinese imperial throne, with Yuyan as its primary subject.

Yuyan married twice, first to Magiya Jinglan in 1943, and later to Zhang Yunfang after Jinglan’s death in 1948. He had three sons: Hengzhen, Hengkai, and Hengjun. He also had three grandchildren, Hengxing, Jin Yinghui, and Jin Qitong.

title: Maxime Masson
text:
Maxime Masson, born on October 15, 1867, in Saint-Justin, Quebec, was a Roman Catholic priest who profoundly shaped the religious landscape of Sainte-Thècle, a town in the Mauricie region of Quebec. He served as the parish priest of Sainte-Thècle for an impressive 52 years, beginning on February 6, 1903, and leaving a lasting legacy through his extensive building projects and pastoral work. 

Before arriving in Sainte-Thècle, Masson completed his studies in classics at Séminaire Saint-Joseph de Trois-Rivières and theology at the Grand Seminary Trois-Rivières, culminating in his ordination on July 8, 1894, by Bishop L.F. Lafleche. He initially served as a vicar in several parishes – Saint-Justin (1894–1899), Saint-Léon-le-Grand (1902), and Saint-Timothée of Hérouxville (1902–1903) – before taking on the role of pastor in Sainte-Thècle.

As pastor, Masson spearheaded the construction of numerous important buildings. He was the primary coordinator for the building of the Sainte-Thècle church between 1903 and 1905, and also oversaw the construction of the rectory and other buildings belonging to the Fabrique de Sainte-Thècle. He was also key to the establishment of the local monastery in 1912, built for the Daughters of Jesus, and the first college run by the Brothers of St. Gabriel in 1939.

Beyond large-scale construction, Masson possessed significant artistic and crafting skills. He designed and built the calvary in the cemetery in 1935, a cement lion placed outside the church in 1939, and painted the ceiling of the sacristy. He also personally carved the Stations of the Cross from stone imported from France and created decorative elements like cement flowerpots, balls, steps, and a fountain for the church and rectory grounds. He crafted a carved wood clock, mirroring the church’s tower design, and the high altar itself. 

During his time as pastor, Masson administered 2497 baptisms, recorded between February 7, 1903, and April 30, 1955. He was also a relatively early adopter of automobile technology, owning a Ford Model T in 1911, one of the first cars in Sainte-Thècle. A significant challenge during his tenure was the collapse of the church’s two towers during the hurricane of August 3, 1938. 

Masson also contributed to the community as the first president of the Sainte-Thècle School board, serving from July 19, 1915, to April 14, 1947. He concluded his service in Sainte-Thècle on July 1, 1955, and passed away on October 2, 1960, being buried in the local cemetery. His contribution to the town was recognized through the naming of School Masson and Masson Street in his honor. He was also a chaplain for Catholic Action and other pious associations.

title: Gopi Sundar
text:
Gopi Sundar C.S., born May 30, 1977, in Kochi, Kerala, is a versatile Indian artist working as a music director, programmer, playback singer, songwriter, actor, and performer across the Malayalam, Telugu, and Tamil film industries. He began his musical journey composing jingles, creating nearly 5,000 of them over several years, aided by guidance from Sudheer Kariat. He also gained experience as a keyboardist, collaborating with prominent Bollywood composers Vishal–Shekhar on songs like “Ek Main Aur Ek Tu Hai” and “Aankhon mein teri.”

Sundar’s formal musical education was brief, having dropped out of Government Music College in Chennai after feeling disillusioned. He found early support from his father, who connected him with Malayalam composer Ouseppachan, becoming his assistant for over a decade. His breakthrough came with the film *Notebook* in 2005, leading to his first independent film score. He quickly followed this with *Flash*, his first complete soundtrack composition. A pivotal moment in his career was *Big B*, a film that debuted several technicians and showcased Sundar's ability to create a fresh cinematic experience with his music. 

He expanded his work to Tamil cinema with *Poi Solla Porom* in 2008, and experienced success with *Sagar Alias Jackie Reloaded*, despite critical reception of the film itself. The film *Anwar* (2010) earned him his first Filmfare Award for Best Music Director. *Ustad Hotel* (2012) proved to be a major success, with the song “Appangalembadum” becoming a chart-topping hit and garnering him multiple awards, including Filmfare, Asianet, SIIMA, and Kochi Times Awards.

Sundar’s contributions extended to Bollywood with the song “Titli” for *Chennai Express* (2013). He continued to deliver successful soundtracks for films like *1983*, which won him the National Film Award for Best Background Score, and *Bangalore Days*, earning him further Filmfare and Asianet awards. He ventured into acting with a cameo in *Salalah Mobiles*. He further expanded his presence into the Telugu film industry with *Malli Malli Idi Rani Roju* and *Bhale Bhale Magadivoy*. 

In recent years, his work on *Pulimurugan* garnered international attention, being considered for Academy Award nominations for both Best Original Song and Best Original Score. He continues to be a prolific composer, with credits including *Oopiri*, *Devi*, and *Geetha Govindam*. Sundar launched his own recording label, Gopi Sundar Music Company, to support emerging musicians, and formed the live performance band “Band Big G” in Dubai. He frequently collaborates with directors like Rosshan Andrrews and Amal Neerad, and lyricists Rafeeq Ahamed, Santhosh Varma and B.K Harinarayanan.

title: James Tyrrell
text:
Sir James Tyrrell, born around 1455 and executed on May 6, 1502, was a knight who served King Richard III of England and became infamous for alleged involvement in the deaths of the Princes in the Tower. He was the eldest son of William Tyrrell of Gipping, Suffolk, and Margaret Darcy, and a descendant of Sir John Tyrrell. His father was beheaded in 1462 following accusations of plotting against Edward IV, though James was spared attainder and his father’s lands were initially placed under the guardianship of Cecily Neville, Duchess of York.

Tyrrell fought for the Yorkist cause at the Battle of Tewkesbury in 1471, where he was knighted by Edward IV. He soon entered the service of Richard, Duke of Gloucester, and after Richard became king, Tyrrell was appointed High Sheriff of Cornwall in 1484. He was abroad in France during the Battle of Bosworth Field, the decisive defeat for Richard III, and therefore did not participate. 

Following the establishment of the Tudor dynasty under Henry VII, Tyrrell was pardoned twice in 1486 and reappointed governor of Guînes, a possession in Calais, a position he had initially been granted by Richard III. However, his loyalty shifted in 1501 when he supported Edmund de la Pole, a Yorkist claimant to the throne, who was in exile. This led to his arrest in 1501 by Thomas Lovell, sent by Henry VII, and a subsequent trial for treason. He was convicted at the Guildhall in London on May 2nd, 1502, and executed four days later alongside Sir John Wyndham. Though initially attainted, this was reversed in 1507.

Tyrrell’s notoriety stems from claims made years after his death by Sir Thomas More, who wrote that Tyrrell confessed to murdering Edward V and his brother, Richard of Shrewsbury, under Richard III's orders. He allegedly implicated John Dighton in the act, and Dighton corroborated the story, though he couldn’t reveal the bodies' location. No original record of this confession exists, and other contemporary accounts, like that of Polydore Vergil, don’t mention it. It's also suggested the confession, if it occurred, was likely obtained through torture. Later Elizabethan chronicles elaborated on More’s narrative, detailing Tyrrell’s role in orchestrating the murders and the concealment of the bodies.

James Tyrrell married Anne Arundel in 1469 and had three sons – Sir Thomas, James, and William – and a daughter, Anne. His eldest son, Sir Thomas Tyrrell, continued the family line. Recent analysis of a chain mentioned in the will of Tyrrell’s sister-in-law has been presented as potential evidence supporting his involvement in the princes’ deaths, while historical research continues to debate the circumstances surrounding his trial, with questions raised about the King and Queen’s presence during the proceedings. He is also a significant character in Shakespeare’s play *Richard III*.

title: Imbolo Mbue
text:
Imbolo Mbue, born in 1981, is a Cameroonian-American novelist and short story writer currently residing in New York City. She is best known for her acclaimed debut novel, *Behold the Dreamers*, published in 2016, which brought her significant recognition including the PEN/Faulkner Award for Fiction and the Blue Metropolis Words to Change Award. Her writing frequently explores the experiences of immigrants, drawing heavily from her own life and the stories of others.

Mbue was raised in Limbé, Cameroon, in the English-speaking region, until her family supported her pursuit of higher education in the United States. She arrived in the U.S. in 1998 and earned an undergraduate degree in business management from Rutgers University in 2002, followed by a Master’s degree from Columbia University in 2006. She initially worked in the corporate sector in New York City, but lost her job during the economic downturn of the Great Recession. This experience, coupled with her observations of the economic disparities in the city – specifically witnessing the contrast between cab drivers and the executives they drove – provided the inspiration for *Behold the Dreamers*. 

The novel delves into the complexities of American immigration, the pursuit of the American Dream, and the financial and emotional struggles experienced by immigrants. Mbue herself has stated that the characters’ experiences mirror her own, encompassing financial hardship, feelings of hopelessness, and a reassessment of personal goals. She believes strongly in the power of literature to foster empathy, particularly in areas like immigration and politics where she feels it is lacking. Her second novel, *How Beautiful We Were*, published in 2021, shifts focus to the environmental crisis unfolding in Africa, attributing it to corporate greed.

Mbue became a U.S. citizen in 2014 and now lives in New York City with her husband and children. *Behold the Dreamers* was acquired by Random House in a million-dollar deal and was praised for its nuanced portrayal of the United States. Its release coincided with the 2016 presidential election and its accompanying anti-immigrant rhetoric, bringing attention to the obstacles faced by those seeking to achieve the American Dream. The novel’s impact was further amplified when it was selected for Oprah Winfrey’s book club in 2017. She also contributed to the anthology *New Daughters of Africa* in 2019. 

Her works have been translated into multiple languages, including French and German. Her published novels are *Behold the Dreamers* (2016), *How Beautiful We Were* (2021), and their respective translations.

title: Hoshiar Singh Dahiya
text:
Hoshiar Singh Dahiya was an Indian Army officer born on May 5, 1936, in Sisana village, Haryana, to Choudhary Hira Singh. He came from a Jat family belonging to the Dahiya clan. After completing his initial education and a year at Jat College in Rohtak, he joined the army and married Dhano Devi, who was still alive as of December 2021. He was commissioned into The Grenadiers Regiment on June 30, 1963, and promoted to lieutenant two years later, on June 30, 1965.

Singh’s early career included a posting in NEFA and participation in the 1965 Indo-Pakistan war in the Rajasthan sector, where his service was noted with a mention in despatches. He achieved the rank of captain by June 30, 1969. However, he is most renowned for his exceptional bravery during the 1971 Indo-Pakistani War, specifically the Battle of Basantar.

In December 1971, his battalion was tasked with establishing a bridgehead across the Basantar river in the Shakargarh Sector. As a major commanding the left forward company, he was ordered to capture the heavily fortified enemy locality of Jarpal. Despite facing intense shelling and machine-gun fire during the assault, he led the charge and successfully captured the objective after fierce hand-to-hand combat.  

The enemy launched three counterattacks on December 16th, two of which were supported by tanks. Throughout these attacks, Major Singh moved amongst his troops, encouraging them to hold their ground despite heavy fire. His courage inspired his company to repel all attacks, inflicting significant casualties on the enemy.  On December 17th, another enemy attack came, supported by artillery, and Singh was seriously wounded by shelling. Despite his injuries, he continued to rally his men, and when a shell rendered a medium machine gun post inoperative and injured its crew, he personally took over the gun, continuing to inflict heavy losses on the attacking forces. This final attack was also successfully repulsed, resulting in 85 enemy deaths, including their commanding officer and three other officers. Singh refused evacuation until the ceasefire, despite his severe wounds.

For his extraordinary courage, leadership, and fighting spirit, Major Hoshiar Singh was awarded the Param Vir Chakra, India’s highest military honour. He was promoted to substantive major in 1976 and later served as an instructor at the Officers Training School in Madras (now Chennai) for two years. He then became an instructor at the Indian Military Academy in Dehra Dun in 1981, earning promotion to lieutenant-colonel on April 8, 1983, and eventually commanding his battalion. He retired from the army on May 31, 1988, with the honorary rank of colonel, settling in Jaipur while maintaining ties to his village of Sisana, encouraging its residents to join the armed forces. He died of a cardiac arrest on December 6, 1998, at the age of 61, and received a full military funeral in Jaipur. He is survived by three sons, two of whom followed in his footsteps as commissioned officers in The Grenadiers, with one serving in the 3rd Grenadiers. His story was also portrayed in the 2017 Malayalam film *1971: Beyond Borders* through the character of Major Sahadevan, played by Mohanlal.

title: Deitrick Haddon
text:
Deitrick Haddon, born May 17, 1973, is an American gospel singer, songwriter, pianist, arranger, record producer and pastor known for his work in progressive and contemporary gospel music. He began his solo career in 2002 with the album *Lost & Found* on Tyscot/Verity, which reached number one on the Billboard Top Gospel Charts and included the successful single “Sinner’s Prayer.” His follow-up album, *Crossroads* (2004), featured the upbeat single “God is Good” and notably included a performance on the television program *Soul Train* as part of its promotion, a strategy uncommon for gospel albums at the time. 

Haddon continued to expand his musical reach with *7 Days* in 2006, largely produced by R&B producers Tim & Bob, and featuring the traditionally gospel-influenced lead single “Heaven Knows,” which he produced himself. He also collaborated with his brother, Gerald, to produce a comeback album, *Brand New Day*, for veteran gospel singer Vanessa Bell Armstrong.

His work with Deitrick Haddon & Voices of Unity resulted in the album *Live the Life* earning awards from the Gospel Music Workshop of America, specifically “New Artist of the Year—Urban Contemporary” and “Album of the Year—Urban Contemporary.” The album *Revealed* followed in 2008, featuring the popular single “Love Him Like I Do” with contributions from Mary Mary and Ruben Studdard. In 2010, Haddon made his acting debut in the direct-to-DVD movie *Blessed and Cursed*. 

He released *Church on the Moon* in 2012, achieving another number one debut on the Billboard Top Gospel chart and reaching number 65 on the Billboard 200.  He gained further public recognition as a cast member on the Oxygen network’s reality television show *Preachers of L.A.*, which premiered in 2013 and documented the lives of six Los Angeles preachers. In 2019, he appeared in the TV One movie *Sins of the Father* as Clarence Burnett.

On a personal note, Haddon was married to Damita Chandler from 1996 to 2011, and together they pastored Kingdom Culture Church in Detroit, founded by his father, for two and a half years starting in 2009. He is currently married to Dominique Haddon (née McTyer), and they have three children: Destin, Denver, and Deitrick II.  Together, Deitrick and Dominique are the Founders and Senior Pastors of Hill City Church in Los Angeles, where Deitrick serves as founder/senior pastor and Dominique as executive pastor.

title: Aert van der Neer
text:
Aert van der Neer was a Dutch Golden Age landscape painter born around 1603 in Gorinchem and who died in poverty in Amsterdam on November 9, 1677. He is known for his specialized depictions of small night scenes, illuminated by moonlight or fires, and winter landscapes, often featuring canals or rivers. A contemporary of artists like Aelbert Cuyp and Meindert Hobbema, he shared a similar fate of relative obscurity during his lifetime.

Early in his life, van der Neer worked as a steward for the lords of Arkel, which explains the lack of known artwork from his youth. He later married Lysbeth Camphuysen in 1629, sister to the painters Rafael and Joachim Govertsz Camphuysen, and together they had six children. Despite being an artist, van der Neer struggled financially, barely managing to support his family through the sale of his paintings. He briefly attempted to supplement his income by running a wine tavern in 1659, but was unsuccessful and declared bankruptcy two years later. Upon his death, his paintings were valued at a mere five shillings each, highlighting his lack of recognition at the time. His son Eglon followed in his footsteps and became a portrait painter.

Van der Neer's earliest dated works, from 1639 and 1642, are considered immature and of poor quality. However, his skills developed quickly, as evidenced by pieces from 1643 and 1644. He depicted real locations throughout the Netherlands, including areas around Haarlem, Leiden, and along the Meuse and Rhine rivers. He was particularly drawn to Dordrecht, the home of Aelbert Cuyp, and the two artists developed a friendship and even collaborated on paintings, sometimes contributing different elements to the same canvas. 

Cuyp was the more prominent artist, often enhancing van der Neer’s work with figures and cattle.  Their collaboration is evident in landscapes where Cuyp painted foreground details, such as figures and animals, within van der Neer’s settings. Van der Neer excelled at capturing atmospheric effects, particularly translucence in darkness, using warm browns and steel greys to reveal distant objects. He was also skilled at portraying frozen water, creating lively winter scenes with figures skating, sleighing, and fishing, yet avoiding a harsh, frosty impression. 

While his paintings are not as highly valued as those of Cuyp or Hobbema, they are appreciated for their unique charm and are sought after by collectors. Approximately 150 of his works are publicly accessible, with a significant collection housed in the Hermitage Museum in Saint Petersburg, and others found in the National Gallery and Wallace Collection in England.

title: Karl Urban
text:
Karl Urban is a New Zealand actor born on June 7, 1972, who began his career with roles in New Zealand film and television, including a small part in the series *Pioneer Woman*. He gained wider recognition with his first Hollywood role in the 2002 horror film *Ghost Ship*. Since then, he has appeared in numerous high-profile films, notably playing Éomer in *The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers* and *The Return of the King*, Vaako in two *Riddick* films, and Dr. Leonard “Bones” McCoy in the *Star Trek* reboot series – a role he actively pursued as a longtime fan of the franchise. Other significant film roles include parts in *The Bourne Supremacy*, *Doom*, *Dredd*, *Pete's Dragon*, and *Thor: Ragnarok*.

Urban’s early life was influenced by his father, a German immigrant who ran a leather goods store, and his mother, who worked in the film industry, exposing him to New Zealand cinema. He showed an early aptitude for performance at St Mark's Church School and briefly studied at Victoria University of Wellington before dedicating himself to acting. Before landing Hollywood roles, he worked in local TV commercials and theatre, and even spent time in Australia.

Beyond his film work, Urban has also had success in television. He starred in the sci-fi series *Almost Human* in 2013 and, since 2019, has gained significant acclaim for his portrayal of Billy Butcher in the Amazon Prime Video series *The Boys*. He also played Detective John Kennex in the series *Almost Human*, a futuristic police drama.

Urban’s dedication to his craft is demonstrated by his thorough preparation for roles, like his meticulous approach to embodying Dr. McCoy from *Star Trek*. While considered for the role of James Bond, he ultimately did not take on the part. He has also lent his voice to animated projects, including *The Sea Beast* in 2022, and even had a cameo appearance as a stormtrooper in *Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker*.

In his personal life, Urban was married to Natalie Wihongi, his former makeup artist, from 2004 until their separation in 2014; they have two sons, Hunter and Indiana. He was later in a relationship with actress Katee Sackhoff from 2014 to 2018. He is also involved in philanthropic work, serving as a celebrity ambassador for KidsCan, a New Zealand charity supporting disadvantaged children, and as an official Ambassador for UNICEF Aotearoa New Zealand. He participated in a *Reunited Apart* special alongside other *Lord of the Rings* cast members to raise money for charity.

title: Hayden Panettiere
text:
Hayden Lesley Panettiere was born on August 21, 1989, and began her acting career very young, appearing in commercials at eleven months old. Her first regular television role was as Sarah Roberts on *One Life to Live* from 1994-1997, followed by Lizzie Spaulding on *Guiding Light* from 1996 to 2000, where her character’s battle with leukemia earned her a Special Recognition Award from The Leukemia & Lymphoma Society. She received a Young Artist Award and a Grammy nomination for her voice work in the 1998 Pixar film *A Bug’s Life*, becoming the fifth-youngest Grammy nominee ever. 

Panettiere continued to build her filmography with roles in films like *Remember the Titans* (2000), *Raising Helen* (2004), *Ice Princess* (2005), and *Bring It On: All or Nothing* (2006). She also appeared in television shows like *Ally McBeal* and *Law & Order: Special Victims Unit*.  Her breakthrough role came with the NBC superhero series *Heroes* (2006-2010), where she played Claire Bennet, a character with healing abilities. This role led to appearances at science fiction conventions worldwide. 

From 2012 to 2018, she starred as Juliette Barnes in the ABC/CMT musical drama *Nashville*, a role for which she received two Golden Globe nominations for Best Supporting Actress. She also voiced characters in the *Kingdom Hearts* video game series (2002-2017) and *Until Dawn* (2015).  She appeared in the *Scream* franchise, playing Kirby Reed in *Scream 4* (2011) and reprising the role in a cameo in 2022’s *Scream*. 

Born and raised partly in Palisades, New York, Panettiere is the daughter of actress Lesley R. Vogel and New York City firefighter Alan Lee "Skip" Panettiere. She is of English, German, and Italian descent.  She attended South Orangetown Middle School before being homeschooled with private tutors to accommodate her acting schedule. Sadly, her younger brother, actor Jansen Panettiere, passed away in 2023.

Beyond acting, Panettiere pursued a singing career, releasing songs for Disney films like *Tiger Cruise* and *Ice Princess*, as well as her own single "Wake Up Call" in 2008. She also recorded songs for the *Nashville* soundtrack.  She has also been a spokesperson for Neutrogena and Candie's, and designed handbags for Dooney & Bourke. 

Panettiere is also known for her activism. She has been a supporter of Ronald McDonald House Charities and has advocated for whale conservation, participating in protests against whaling. She has also been an advocate for Washington, D.C. statehood and teen pregnancy prevention. She has spoken publicly about her own experiences with domestic abuse, encouraging others to come forward.  She was in a relationship with boxer Wladimir Klitschko, with whom she has a daughter, after previously dating *Heroes* co-star Milo Ventimiglia.

title: Andreas Ivanschitz
text:
Andreas Ivanschitz, born on October 15, 1983, is a retired Austrian footballer who played as an attacking midfielder throughout an 18-year career. He represented Austria internationally and played for a variety of clubs including Rapid Wien, Red Bull Salzburg, Panathinaikos, 1.FSV Mainz 05, Levante, Seattle Sounders FC, and Viktoria Plzen.

Ivanschitz began his youth career with ASK Baumgarten in Eisenstadt, spending nine years with the local team before being scouted by Rapid Wien in 1998. He signed his first professional contract with Rapid Wien at the age of 16 and made his debut in an Austrian Cup match in October 1999. His league debut followed in 2000. During his time with Rapid Wien, spanning 177 games, he scored 27 goals and helped the team win the Austrian Championship in the 2004–05 season. He was recognized as the Austrian Footballer of the Year in 2003.

In January 2006, Ivanschitz moved to Red Bull Salzburg, and then joined Panathinaikos in August of the same year on a two-year loan, which was later made permanent in 2008. He spent three years in Greece before agreeing to a two-year loan deal with Mainz 05 in July 2009, with an option for a permanent contract. Mainz exercised this option early, securing his services permanently in January 2011. He then transferred to Levante in June 2013, scoring his first La Liga goal in August of that year against Rayo Vallecano. He scored three goals in 29 games during his first season with Levante, including one against Valencia.

Ivanschitz continued his career in Major League Soccer, signing with Seattle Sounders FC in August 2015. His debut was delayed by injury but he eventually made an impact, providing an assist in a match against San Jose Earthquakes. A highlight of his time with Seattle was his contribution to their 2016 MLS Cup victory, successfully converting a penalty in the shootout which ultimately secured the title for the Sounders.

Internationally, Ivanschitz earned 69 caps for Austria, scoring 12 goals, and was part of the Austrian team that participated in Euro 2008. He first appeared for Austria in a friendly match against Greece in 2003.

Beyond football, Ivanschitz comes from a musical family and enjoys playing various instruments. He is also connected to the Burgenland Croat community, and his son, Ilia, is currently a footballer with Red Bull Salzburg. Throughout his career he achieved honours including the Austrian Football Bundesliga title with Rapid Wien in 2005 and the MLS Cup with Seattle Sounders FC in 2016, as well as the individual accolade of Austrian Footballer of the Year in 2003.

title: Blanca Errázuriz
text:
Blanca Elena Errázuriz Vergara, later known as Bianca de Saulles, lived a dramatic life marked by wealth, scandal, and ultimately, tragedy. Born in 1894 in Viña del Mar, Chile, she came from the prominent and politically connected Errázuriz family. Her early life included education at a convent in London, following the death of her mining magnate father when she was just two years old. In 1911, at the age of sixteen, she married John de Saulles, an American businessman fifteen years her senior, after overcoming some initial family objections due to their age and religious differences. They married in France after a ceremony in Paris, having previously lived in New York City.

The couple had one son, John “Jack” de Saulles, in 1912, but their marriage quickly deteriorated due to de Saulles’ infidelities. Blanca filed for divorce in 1916, during which time she befriended Rudolph Valentino, who provided testimony supporting her claims of her husband’s adultery. De Saulles responded by attempting to discredit Valentino, resulting in the actor's arrest on dubious charges and a damaging scandal that impacted his career. Blanca, however, did not offer Valentino gratitude for his support, and ended their association.

Following the divorce finalized in December 1916, a confrontation with her ex-husband led to a fatal shooting. On August 3, 1917, Blanca drove to de Saulles’ home and, after an argument over custody of their son – despite a court ruling in her favor – shot him five times when he attempted to disarm her. She surrendered to police and was charged with first-degree murder. The ensuing trial was a sensation, with Blanca defended by Henry Uterhart and her maid, Suzanne Monteau, providing key testimony. She gained public sympathy, championed by suffragettes who viewed her as a victim of societal chauvinism. 

Ultimately, Blanca Errázuriz was acquitted of all charges in December 1917 by a unanimous “popular” verdict. After the trial, she moved to San Francisco, secured full custody of her son, and eventually returned with him to Chile. She remarried in 1921 to engineer Fernando Santa Cruz Wilson, but they later divorced. In her later years, she became estranged from her son, Jack Jr., who moved to the United States. Suffering from poor health, she died by suicide in 1940 in Viña del Mar, having taken an overdose of barbiturates. Her story inspired the 1918 silent film "The Woman and the Law”, though names were altered for the adaptation. Her brother, Guillermo Errázuriz, also tragically took his own life in 1922 following a heartbreak involving actress Peggy Hopkins Joyce.

title: Tarik Elyounoussi
text:
Tarik Elyounoussi, born in Al Hoceima, Morocco in 1988, is a former professional footballer who played as a forward or winger and represented the Norway national team. He moved to Norway with his family at the age of eleven, beginning his football journey with Nylende in Fredrikstad before moving to Trosvik. He quickly rose to prominence, being considered Fredrikstad’s most significant talent in decades and earning the Norwegian Young Player of the Year award in both 2006 and 2007, alongside a Norwegian Football Cup victory.

In 2008, despite interest from Premier League clubs, Elyounoussi initially agreed to a deal with Le Mans but ultimately signed a five-year contract with SC Heerenveen for €3.5 million. He made an immediate impact, scoring on his debut and contributing crucial goals in both the league and the UEFA Cup. He later returned to Norway, first on loan to Lillestrøm SK in 2010, then permanently to Fredrikstad FK in 2011. 

A move to Rosenborg followed in 2012, lasting until 2013 when he was sold to 1899 Hoffenheim in Germany.  He then joined Greek side Olympiacos in 2016 for an estimated €1 million, playing a key role in securing their seventh consecutive Super League title and scoring his first goal for the club against Veria F.C. A loan spell with Qarabağ in Azerbaijan in 2017 proved less successful, with limited playing time. 

Elyounoussi continued his career with AIK in Sweden in 2018, where he won the Allsvenskan league title. He then moved to Japan to join Shonan Bellmare in 2020, remaining with the club until the end of the 2023 season, making 103 appearances and scoring five goals. 

Internationally, Elyounoussi made a memorable start to his Norway career, scoring just four minutes into his debut against Uruguay in 2008 – one of the fastest debut goals in the national team’s history. He later captained the national team in friendlies against South Africa and Zambia in 2013, scoring the winning goal against South Africa. He is cousins with fellow Norwegian international footballer, Mohamed Elyounoussi. Throughout his career, he achieved honours including the Norwegian Football Cup with Fredrikstad, the KNVB Cup with Heerenveen, the Greek Super League with Olympiacos, and the Swedish Allsvenskan with AIK.

title: Clancy Brown
text:
Clancy Brown, born Clarence James Brown III on January 5, 1959, is a highly prolific American actor known for portraying villains and authoritative figures in a career spanning since the 1980s. He has built a substantial body of work in both live-action and voice-over roles across film and television.

Brown’s early life was shaped by his family’s involvement in the newspaper business; his father, Clarence J. “Bud” Brown Jr., was a newspaper publisher and later a congressman, continuing a legacy begun by Clancy’s grandfather. He graduated from St. Albans School and Northwestern University, with a performance in *The Crucible* at the former. He began his film career with a role in *Bad Boys* (1983) and quickly gained recognition for roles like Rawhide in *The Adventures of Buckaroo Banzai Across the 8th Dimension* (1984), Frankenstein’s monster in *The Bride* (1985), and the Kurgan in *Highlander* (1986). He continued to appear in numerous films including *The Shawshank Redemption* (1994) as Captain Hadley, *Starship Troopers* (1997) as Sgt. Zim, and more recently *Promising Young Woman* (2020) and *John Wick: Chapter 4* (2023). 

Alongside his film work, Brown has maintained a successful television career. Notable roles include Brother Justin Crowe in *Carnivàle* (2003-2005), Waylon "Jock" Jeffcoat in *Billions* (2018-2019, 2023), Kurt Caldwell in *Dexter: New Blood* (2021-2022), and Sal Maroni in *The Penguin* (2024). He frequently appears in guest roles on shows like *ER*, *Lost*, and *The Flash*.

However, Brown is arguably just as renowned for his voice work. Since 1996, he has been the voice of Lex Luthor in numerous DC Comics animated projects, surpassing all other actors in the length of time portraying the character. He is also the iconic voice of Mr. Krabs on *SpongeBob SquarePants* since 1999, and has contributed to the *Avatar: The Last Airbender* franchise, *Star Wars: The Clone Wars* as Savage Opress, and *Thor: Ragnarok* as Surtur. His voice acting extends into video games, including roles in the *Crash Bandicoot* series, *Detroit: Become Human*, and many others. 

Brown has been married to Jeanne Johnson since 1993 and they have two children. His career demonstrates remarkable versatility, allowing him to excel in both on-screen and voice-over performances, often embodying characters that leave a lasting impression.

title: Melvin Van Peebles
text:
Melvin Van Peebles, born Melvin Peebles in Chicago in 1932 and passing away in 2021, was a remarkably versatile American artist – an actor, filmmaker, writer, and composer who remained creatively active into his 80s. His early career was marked by difficulties finding directorial work in the United States due to racial barriers, leading him to begin his filmmaking journey in France. His 1967 feature debut, *The Story of a Three-Day Pass*, based on his own French novel, gained recognition and opened doors, ultimately leading to his first Hollywood film, *Watermelon Man* in 1970. However, he deliberately eschewed further mainstream Hollywood opportunities, choosing instead to finance his own independent projects.

Van Peebles is best known for *Sweet Sweetback’s Baadasssss Song* (1971), a groundbreaking film often credited with launching the blaxploitation genre, although critic Roger Ebert disputed its categorization as exploitation.  He continued a prolific output, creating films like *Don't Play Us Cheap*, based on his own stage play, and writing novels and plays in both English and French. His later films included the French-language *Le Conte du ventre plein* (2000) and the absurdist *Confessionsofa Ex-Doofus-ItchyFooted Mutha* (2008). His son, Mario Van Peebles, followed in his footsteps as a filmmaker and actor, and even portrayed his father in the 2003 biographical film *Baadasssss!*.

Before his filmmaking career took off, Van Peebles had a diverse early life. He earned a B.A. in literature from Ohio Wesleyan University in 1953 and served in the Air Force.  He briefly worked as a cable car gripman in San Francisco, experiences he later wrote about, and added “Van” to his name while living in the Netherlands.  He initially attempted filmmaking with short, low-budget films, learning the craft through trial and error. After struggling to find work in Hollywood, he moved to Europe, eventually landing in France where he found a creative haven. There, he worked as an investigative reporter and writer for publications like *France Observateur* and *Hara-kiri*. 

During the 1960s, Van Peebles also wrote plays and songs, developing a distinctive sprechgesang style. He published several books, including novels and short stories, and saw his play *La Fête à Harlem* staged in Belgium.  His theatrical success continued with the stage musicals *Ain’t Supposed to Die a Natural Death* and *Don't Play Us Cheap*, both of which earned him Tony Award nominations. He also contributed to other Broadway productions as a writer and composer. Beyond theater and film, Van Peebles briefly worked as an options trader on the American Stock Exchange in the 1980s. 

Throughout his life, Van Peebles maintained a strong independent spirit, often prioritizing creative control over commercial success. He was honored with numerous awards, including a Lifetime Achievement Award from the Chicago Underground Film Festival and a Commander of the Legion of Honour from the French government. His work consistently challenged conventions and paved the way for other Black filmmakers, leaving a lasting legacy in American cinema and beyond.

title: Roman Pavlyuchenko
text:
Roman Pavlyuchenko, born in 1981, is a former Russian footballer who now works as a forwards coach for Rodina-2 Moscow. He began his professional career at Dynamo Stavropol, progressing through youth systems before making his debut in 1999. After a stint at Rotor Volgograd, marked by an early red card for violent conduct, he joined Spartak Moscow in 2003, becoming a key player and the team’s top scorer for several seasons. It was at Spartak where he truly established himself, becoming the league’s top scorer in one season and helping the club qualify for the Champions League. He scored 69 goals in 141 appearances for Spartak, gaining a reputation for loyalty and earning the respect of the club's fans.

In 2008, Pavlyuchenko moved to Tottenham Hotspur in the English Premier League for £13.7 million. While he scored goals for Spurs, including a brace against Birmingham City that relegated them, his time was often marked by inconsistency and being behind other strikers in the pecking order. A notable incident occurred when he stormed down the tunnel after being substituted, drawing criticism from his manager. He did, however, prove a reliable goalscorer in domestic cup competitions and played a part in Tottenham’s Champions League qualification.

Pavlyuchenko also enjoyed a decade-long international career with Russia, earning 51 caps and scoring 21 goals. He debuted in 2003 and became a vital part of the national team, notably playing a key role in Euro 2008 where Russia reached the semi-finals. He scored crucial goals during the qualifying campaign, including both goals in a 2-1 victory over England, and continued to find the net during the tournament itself. He was named to the Team of the Tournament for his performances. He later scored a hat-trick against Armenia in Euro 2012 qualifying.

After leaving Tottenham, Pavlyuchenko returned to Russia with Lokomotiv Moscow and later played for Kuban Krasnodar, Ural Yekaterinburg and Ararat Moscow. He even spent time in the Russian Professional Football League and the Amateur Football League, demonstrating a continued passion for the game. He briefly returned to Ararat and then Znamya Noginsk, where he scored a career-high four goals in a single match. His career ended with a ban for misconduct after an on-field altercation, leading to his retirement. Throughout his career, Pavlyuchenko was known for his goalscoring ability and dedication to the sport.

title: Kelli White
text:
Kelli White, born on April 1, 1977, in Oakland, California, was a professional track and field sprinter who achieved initial success before her career was derailed by a doping scandal. She gained prominence by winning two gold medals at the 2003 World Championships in Paris, but these victories were later revoked. She ultimately retired from professional track in 2006. 

White came from a track and field background, as both her parents were sprinters, with her mother, Debbie Byfield, having competed in the 1972 Summer Olympics. She attended James Logan High School in Union City, California, participating in track and field. During her time there, she experienced a violent assault at age 17, suffering facial slashes that required 300 stitches, but remarkably continued to compete in the same season. Though never a state champion, she graduated in 1995 with the fastest 200-meter time and the second-fastest 100-meter time in the North Coast Section. This performance earned her a scholarship to the University of Tennessee, from which she graduated in 1999.

Her athletic achievements were overshadowed by a positive drug test in June 2004, leading to the stripping of her World Championship medals. White admitted her guilt and testified before the Court of Arbitration for Sport, which resulted in the annulment of all her results from December 15, 2000, onwards. She received a two-year ban from the United States Anti-Doping Agency, beginning on May 17, 2004.

The circumstances surrounding her doping were connected to the BALCO doping scandal. After returning to the San Francisco Bay Area following her time at the University of Tennessee, her coach, Remi Korchemny, introduced her to Victor Conte, the head of BALCO. Initially, Conte provided her with substances he claimed were supplements and vitamins. It was later revealed that one of these was a steroid, which she initially refused. However, after a difficult and unsuccessful 2002 season marked by injuries, she began using performance-enhancing drugs. Evidence seized from BALCO ultimately led to her confession of using tetrahydrogestrinone (THG), erythropoietin (EPO), and modafinil.

Following her ban, White actively worked to address the issue of doping in sports. She became the first athlete to directly collaborate with the United States Anti-Doping Agency, offering insights into the culture and processes of doping at elite levels. She also engaged in educational outreach, giving lectures on drug abuse in sports globally. During her period of suspension, she remained involved with track and field by teaching at clinics held at her former high school, James Logan High.

title: Jesse Chacón
text:
Jesse Chacón, born November 9, 1965, is a Venezuelan politician, engineer, and former military officer who has held numerous high-ranking positions within the Venezuelan government. He initially trained as a military officer, graduating from the Military Academy in 1987 with a degree in Military Arts. He later earned a degree in systems engineering from the Polytechnic University of the National Armed Forces in 1996, and completed postgraduate studies in Telematics at institutions in France and Caracas.

Chacón’s early career was significantly marked by his involvement in the November 1992 coup attempt against the government of President Carlos Andrés Pérez, following an earlier coup earlier that year. As a lieutenant, he participated in the occupation of the state television station Venezolana de Televisión (VTV), an action that resulted in the deaths of several station workers. He was subsequently sentenced to 22 years in prison by a military tribunal, but was pardoned two years later by President Rafael Caldera.

Following his pardon, Chacón became involved in the administration of Hugo Chávez, beginning with work at the National Commission of Telecommunications (Conatel) in 1999, where he helped prepare telecommunications legislation. He became the General Director of Conatel in May 2001. In 2003, he was appointed as the first Minister of Communications, and later served as Director of Communications for the “No” campaign during the 2004 recall referendum. 

He then served as Minister of Interior and Justice from 2004 to January 2007, during which time he oversaw the creation of the National Commission on Police Reform (CONAREPOL).  Chacón was subsequently appointed Minister of Telecommunications and Informatics in January 2007, a period during which the Venezuelan state nationalized the CANTV phone and internet provider and the television broadcaster RCTV was shut down. He also served as Minister of the Secretariat of the Presidency in 2008 and again as Minister of Communications (renamed Ministry of the People's Power for Communication and Information) from December 2008 to April 2009.

In April 2009, he became Minister for Science, Technology and Intermediate Industries, but resigned in December of the same year following the arrest of his brother, Arné Chacón, who was connected to an investigation involving intervened financial institutions.  Chacón returned to government service in April 2013 as Minister of Electric Power. By late 2015, he was appointed as Venezuela’s ambassador to Austria by President Nicolás Maduro.

title: Carrie Ann Inaba
text:
Carrie Ann Inaba, born January 5, 1968, is an American entertainer with a multifaceted career encompassing television, dance, choreography, acting, and singing. She is widely recognized as a judge on the ABC show *Dancing with the Stars*, a role she’s held since 2005, and previously co-hosted and moderated the CBS talk show *The Talk* from 2019 until 2021.

Inaba’s career began with a foray into the Japanese music scene in 1986, after winning a talent show in Hawaii. She was groomed as a pop star, releasing three singles, and hosting radio and television programs, though she eventually felt the industry prioritized image over artistry. Returning to the United States, she gained prominence as one of the “Fly Girls” on the sketch comedy show *In Living Color* from 1990 to 1992. She also performed with Prince and was a dancer in Madonna’s 1993 “Girlie Show” World Tour, famously agreeing to shave her head for the opportunity.

Throughout her career, Inaba has appeared in numerous films, often as a dancer, including *Monster Mash: The Movie*, *Austin Powers in Goldmember* where she played Fook Yu alongside Diane Mizota as Fook Mi, and *Showgirls*. She has also had smaller roles in television series like *Jack & Jill* and *Nikki*. Beyond performing, Inaba has worked extensively as a choreographer on programs such as *American Idol*, *The Swan*, and the *Miss America Pageant* for five years. She also contributed to the early seasons of *So You Think You Can Dance*.

Inaba founded EnterMediArts, Inc., a video production company, and has directed, written, and edited films including *Black Water* and documentaries about the Miss America pageant. She also served as a producer for the Broadway show *Burn the Floor* and was honored with the Visionary Award by East West Players for her contribution to the visibility of Asian Americans in entertainment.

Her television presence expanded beyond dancing and choreography with appearances on *The View* and hosting duties on the game show *1 vs. 100*. She was also a recurring guest co-host on *The Talk* before becoming a permanent co-host and moderator in 2019, leaving in 2021 after a leave of absence. 

Inaba’s personal life has included engagements to Artem Chigvintsev, Jesse Sloan (which ended in a broken engagement), and Robb Derringer. She is a passionate animal advocate, founding the Carrie Ann Animal Foundation and actively supporting organizations like the Humane Society and PETA. 

Inaba has openly discussed a number of health challenges, including severe vision impairment, spinal stenosis, Sjögren’s syndrome, lupus, chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, Tourette’s Syndrome as a child, and, most recently, acute gangrenous appendicitis requiring emergency surgery in 2023. She serves as a National Awareness Ambassador for the Sjögren Syndrome Foundation.  Despite her health struggles, she remains committed to raising awareness and funding for research into these conditions.

title: Cicero
text:
Marcus Tullius Cicero, born in 106 BC in Arpinum, was a prominent Roman statesman, lawyer, scholar, philosopher, orator, and writer. He dedicated his life to upholding the principles of the *optimate* faction during a period of intense political upheaval that ultimately led to the establishment of the Roman Empire. Cicero’s extensive body of work, encompassing rhetoric, philosophy, and politics, secured his reputation as one of Rome’s greatest orators and a key innovator of “Ciceronian rhetoric,” profoundly impacting both ancient and modern understanding of the Latin language.

Cicero received a comprehensive education in both Rome and Greece, benefitting from a wealthy equestrian family background and a strong emphasis on Greek language and philosophy within the Roman elite. He translated numerous Greek philosophical concepts into Latin, coining roughly 150 new Latin terms – including words like *evidentia*, *humanitas*, and *qualitas* – to facilitate this process. While celebrated for his legal and oratorical skills, Cicero considered his political career his most significant achievement.

His most famous political act was suppressing the Catilinarian conspiracy in 63 BC during his consulship. Through a series of powerful speeches, he exposed and drove out Lucius Sergius Catilina, a man plotting to overthrow the Republic. However, his subsequent decision to execute five conspirators without trial proved controversial, ultimately leading to his exile in 58 BC, though he was recalled the following year. Disillusioned with Roman politics in the 50s, he served as governor in Cilicia in 51 BC, returning to Italy just before Caesar’s civil war. 

Cicero initially supported Pompey during the war and was pardoned by Caesar after his victory. Following Caesar’s assassination in 44 BC, he became a leading voice in the Senate against Mark Antony, delivering scathing speeches against him and championing Octavian as a counterweight. This opposition proved fatal; after Octavian and Antony formed the Second Triumvirate, Cicero was proscribed and executed in 43 BC while attempting to flee Italy. A gruesome display was made of his severed hands and head, symbols of his vocal opposition to Antony.

Despite his tragic end, Cicero’s legacy endured. The rediscovery of his letters by Petrarch in the 14th century is widely credited with sparking the Renaissance’s renewed interest in classical Roman culture and humanism. His influence reached its peak during the 18th-century Enlightenment, impacting thinkers like John Locke, David Hume, Montesquieu, and Edmund Burke. Today, his works remain crucial primary sources for understanding Roman history, particularly the decline of the Republic, and continue to be studied for their literary and philosophical merit. 

Born to a relatively modest equestrian family, Cicero rose through the ranks of Roman society through his exceptional talent and dedication to public service. He held various positions – quaestor, aedile, praetor, and finally consul – demonstrating his commitment to the *cursus honorum*. His early legal successes, particularly his prosecution of Gaius Verres for corruption, cemented his reputation as a skilled orator and advocate for justice.

title: Marty Mayberry
text:
Marty Mayberry, born on February 9, 1986, and passing away on December 18, 2024, was an Australian Paralympic alpine skier. He competed in standing events as an LW3 classified athlete, utilizing prosthetic legs after losing both legs below the knee due to meningococcal disease contracted during a high school ski trip when he was sixteen. He spent two weeks in a coma and learned of his amputations upon waking in hospital. This life-altering experience profoundly influenced his future, inspiring him to study medicine at Griffith University and the University of Sydney. He actively researched the disease, presenting his experiences at conferences and working at the Kids Research Institute, focusing on the psycho-social impact of meningococcal B on families.

Mayberry’s skiing career began before his illness, and he transitioned to the sport’s disability category by 2004. He quickly rose through the ranks, debuting for the Australian national team in 2005 and representing his country at the 2006 Winter Paralympics in Turin, where he did not medal. Recognizing the need for improvement in his equipment, he collaborated with a prosthetist to develop more effective legs, achieving significant progress with a gold medal at a 2007 World Cup event. He continued to achieve success, earning a bronze medal in 2008 and multiple top-six finishes at the 2009 World Championships.

The peak of his athletic career came with his selection for the 2010 Winter Paralympics in Vancouver. He was honored as Australia’s flag bearer at the opening ceremony. At the Games, Mayberry secured a silver medal in the men’s downhill standing event, tying with another skier for the result. He also finished 24th in the Super-G, was disqualified from the slalom, and did not finish the giant slalom. Prior to the games, he trained extensively in Europe and North America, including winning a gold medal in a downhill event in Aspen, Colorado. 

Following the 2010 Paralympics, Mayberry retired from competitive skiing, receiving an Australian Institute of Sport Sport Achievement Award that year. He lived by the philosophy of being the change he wished to see in the world and, at the time of his death, resided in Brisbane, having previously lived in Byron Bay and Yeerongpilly, Queensland, and Sydney. He was married in 2010 to a woman he met at a music festival.

title: Rui Campos
text:
Rui Campos, also known simply as Rui, was a Brazilian footballer who lived from August 2nd, 1922, to January 2nd, 2002. He is best known for his participation in the Brazil national team during the 1950 FIFA World Cup. Born in São Paulo, Rui enjoyed a professional club career spanning several prominent Brazilian clubs. 

Throughout his career, he played for Bonsucesso, Fluminense, Bangu, São Paulo, and Palmeiras. His time with São Paulo Football Club proved particularly successful, where he established a strong and effective midfield partnership alongside fellow players José Carlos Bauer and Alfredo Noronha. The article highlights this trio’s contribution to the team’s achievements.

Rui’s involvement with the Brazil national team was substantial, accumulating a total of 30 appearances between 1944 and 1950. This period included his selection for and participation in the 1950 FIFA World Cup, a momentous tournament for Brazilian football, and one remembered for its dramatic conclusion. 

Beyond the World Cup, Rui Campos also achieved international success with Brazil by being a part of the team that won the Copa América in 1949. However, his World Cup experience ended in disappointment as Brazil finished as runners-up in the 1950 tournament. While the article does not detail his specific role or performance in these matches, it establishes his presence as a key member of the national squad during this era.

His accomplishments were recognized through several team honours. During his time at São Paulo, he was part of the squads that won the Campeonato Paulista – the São Paulo State Championship – in four separate years: 1945, 1946, 1948, and 1949. These victories cemented his legacy within the club’s history. Combined with his Copa América win with the national team and participation in the 1950 World Cup, Rui Campos had a decorated career representing both club and country.

title: 14th Dalai Lama
text:
Tenzin Gyatso, born Lhamo Thondup on July 6, 1935, is the 14th and current Dalai Lama, the spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism. Recognized as the reincarnation of the 13th Dalai Lama in 1937 and formally enthroned in 1940, he served as Tibet’s spiritual and temporal leader until 1959.
