She further showcased her range with a role in the Netflix anthology *Lust Stories* (2018), playing a sexually dissatisfied wife, earning critical praise.

While her Telugu debut, *Bharat Ane Nenu* (2018), was a commercial success, her subsequent Telugu film *Vinaya Vidheya Rama* was not. 2019 proved to be a breakthrough year with *Kabir Singh* and *Good Newwz*, both becoming major box office hits. She won an IIFA Award for Best Supporting Actress for her performance in *Good Newwz*.  She continued to gain prominence with commercially successful films like *Bhool Bhulaiyaa 2* and *Jugjugg Jeeyo* in 2022.

Advani has received critical acclaim for roles in *Shershaah* (2021), where she played Vikram Batra’s girlfriend, and *Satyaprem Ki Katha* (2023), portraying a troubled married woman, both earning her Filmfare Award nominations for Best Actress.  She has also appeared in films like *Guilty*, *Laxmii*, *Indoo Ki Jawani*, *Govinda Naam Mera*, and most recently, *Game Changer* (2025) though the latter didn't perform as expected. She is currently involved in several upcoming projects including *War 2* and *Toxic: A Fairy Tale for Grown-Ups*.

Beyond acting, Advani is a sought-after brand ambassador, endorsing products like Audi, Galaxy Chocolate, and Colgate, among others. She made her debut at the Met Gala in 2025, notably appearing with a baby bump. She is married to actor Sidharth Malhotra since February 2023, and they have a daughter born in July 2025.

Advani’s background reveals a family with connections to the Indian film industry; actors Ashok Kumar and Saeed Jaffrey are relatives through her maternal side. She holds a Bachelor of Arts degree in mass communication from Jai Hind College, Mumbai. Originally named Alia Advani, she adopted the name Kiara at the suggestion of Salman Khan to avoid confusion with the already established actress Alia Bhatt.  She is regarded as charming and energetic, and has been recognized on lists like The Times of India’s “Most Desirable Woman” and GQ India’s “30 Most Influential Young Indians”. In 2023, she was the most searched personality on Google in India and is among India’s highest tax-paying celebrities.

title: Witold Gombrowicz
text:
Witold Gombrowicz, born in 1904 in Russian Poland and dying in 1969 in France, was a Polish writer and playwright now considered a major figure in Polish literature, though he achieved widespread recognition only late in his life. His work is characterized by psychological depth, paradox, a sense of the absurd, and a rejection of nationalism. He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature four times between 1966 and 1969, and his diaries are widely considered his masterpiece, while *Cosmos* is regarded as his most accomplished novel.

Gombrowicz came from a wealthy gentry family with roots in Lithuania, displaced after his grandfather’s involvement in the January Uprising. This sense of being ‘between’ worlds, neither fully belonging anywhere, became a recurring theme in his life and writing. He studied law at Warsaw University and spent time in Paris, returning to Poland to attempt a legal career but soon turned to writing. Early attempts at novels proved unsuccessful, leading him to short stories collected as *Bacacay*. He gained literary attention with the publication of his first novel, *Ferdydurke* in 1937, which explored themes of immaturity, identity formation, and a critical view of Polish class structures.

Just before World War II, Gombrowicz embarked on a voyage to South America, and the outbreak of war found him in Buenos Aires. He remained in Argentina for over two decades, often facing poverty and struggling for recognition in Argentine literary circles. He published a Spanish translation of *Ferdydurke* in 1947, which later became a significant work in Argentine literature, and continued to write, including the drama *Ślub* (The Marriage) and the novel *Trans-Atlantyk*, which addressed the experience of emigration and national identity. During this period, he also worked as a bank clerk and developed friendships within Buenos Aires’s cultural elite. He began publishing in the Parisian journal *Culture* in 1951, including excerpts from his *Diaries*.

In the 1960s, Gombrowicz gained international acclaim, with translations of his works appearing in numerous languages and his plays staged across Europe. He returned to Europe in 1963, thanks to a Ford Foundation scholarship, eventually settling in Vence, France, with his secretary, Rita Labrosse, whom he later married. Despite his growing renown, his health deteriorated. He gave a series of lectures on philosophy, transcribed by Dominique de Roux, shortly before his death in 1969.

Gombrowicz’s writing consistently critiqued Polish traditions and history, exploring the tension between individual freedom and societal expectations. His style is marked by incisive psychological portraits, a comedic sensibility, and the use of neologisms and symbolic language. Works like *Pornografia* and *Kosmos* delve into complex themes of cultural collapse and the human desire to create meaning. His dramatic work, including *Ivona, Princess of Burgundia* and *Operetka*, often employed grotesque elements to expose the absurdity of power and societal conventions. His *Diaries* are considered a masterpiece, offering a philosophical and personal account of his life and thoughts. Several of his novels, including *Ferdydurke*, *Pornografia*, and *Cosmos* have been adapted into films.

title: Geraldo de Barros
text:
Geraldo de Barros, born in Chavantes, São Paulo, Brazil in 1923 and passing away in 1998, was a highly influential Brazilian artist recognized for his contributions to painting, photography, engraving, graphic arts, and industrial design. He is considered one of the most important Brazilian artists of the 20th century and was a leading figure in the concrete art movement, co-founding Grupo Ruptura.

De Barros began experimenting with photography at age 16, even building his own camera and manipulating negatives. He initially studied figurative and landscape painting with several instructors before becoming drawn to European abstract constructivism, particularly the De Stijl movement of Mondrian and van Doesburg. He continued his artistic education at the Associaçião Paulista de Belas Artes and then, after working at Banco do Brasil to support himself, delved further into photography, co-founding a photography lab with friends and joining the Foto Cine Clube Bandeirante in São Paulo. This period involved studying experimental photographic practices from European and American artists like Moholy-Nagy and Man Ray.

His most celebrated work is the *Fotoformas* series (1946-1952), groundbreaking photographs that utilized multiple exposures, rotated images, and abstract forms. These works aimed to capture the phenomenological experience of Brazil’s rapid urbanization. In 1950, he showcased *Fotoformas* at the Museu de Arte de São Paulo, marking a new direction for photography in Brazil.  

De Barros furthered his artistic exploration through studies abroad, receiving a scholarship to study lithography in Paris and graphic arts at the Ulm School of Design in Germany, where he met Max Bill. This experience led him to abandon photography temporarily to focus on concrete art. He co-founded Grupo Ruptura in 1952, contributing to the writing of their manifesto outlining abstract and concrete art principles. He also established the Escola Paulista photography group.

Beyond fine art, De Barros ventured into industrial design, founding the furniture design company Unilabor in 1954, which allowed him to leave his bank job. Later, he founded Hobjeto with Frei João Batista, though both companies eventually faced bankruptcy due to economic and political instability.  In the 1960s, he collaborated with Nelson Leirner on pop art events. He also founded Galeria Rex as an experiment in the art market. 

After a long period dedicated to concrete art, De Barros returned to photography in 1996, following several strokes that limited his physical abilities. Assisted by photographer Ana Moraes, he created a final series of works titled "Sobras." His work was first exhibited in the United States in 1998, shortly before his death. Since then, his legacy has grown, with retrospectives held in Europe and North America and a documentary film, *Geraldo de Barros: Sobras em Obras*, released in 1999.

title: Roman Šebrle
text:
Roman Šebrle, born in Czechoslovakia in 1974, is widely regarded as one of the greatest decathletes in history. He began his athletic journey playing football but switched to athletics after a serious leg injury sustained during a match in 1987, requiring extensive recovery. He initially focused on high jumping before transitioning to the decathlon, beginning his competitive career in the event in 1991.

Šebrle’s career took off after joining the army sports club Dukla Prague in 1995, where he remained a member throughout his career, maintaining his status as a soldier despite limited military duties. He first achieved a score over 8,000 points in 1996 and began to collect international medals, winning gold at the 1997 World University Games and placing ninth at the World Championships. Success continued with bronze at the 1999 World Indoor Championships and silver at the 2000 European Indoor Athletics Championships. He secured a silver medal at the 2000 Summer Olympics in Sydney, a result surrounded by controversy involving a disputed discus foul.

2001 marked a pivotal year, as Šebrle broke the world record in the decathlon with a score of 9,026 points in Götzis, becoming the first decathlete to surpass 9,000 points. Despite this achievement, injury hampered his performance at the 2001 World Championships. He continued to excel, winning European titles in both indoor and outdoor championships in 2002, and culminating in a gold medal at the 2004 Summer Olympics in Athens, breaking the 20-year-old Olympic record. This victory earned him the title of "World’s Greatest Athlete," a tradition for Olympic decathlon champions, and further recognition as the world’s best athlete by a Wall Street Journal panel in 2008. 

Šebrle’s success wasn’t limited to the Olympics. He earned gold at the 2007 World Championships, silver in 2003, and another silver in 2005. He also dominated the World and European Indoor Championships in the heptathlon, claiming multiple gold and bronze medals. He holds the unique distinction of completing over 40 decathlons with scores exceeding 8,000 points and 20 exceeding 8,500. He was recognized domestically, being named the Best Czech Athlete of the Year five consecutive times between 2002 and 2006, and Czech Sportsman of the Year in 2004. 

A notable incident occurred in 2007 when he was struck by a javelin thrown during training in South Africa, narrowly avoiding a potentially fatal injury. He is married to former Czech athlete Eva Kasalová, and they have two children. Šebrle retired after competing at the 2009 World Championships in Berlin.

title: Maurice Jones-Drew
text:
Maurice Jones-Drew, nicknamed “MJD,” was a professional football running back who played nine seasons in the NFL, achieving significant success after a standout college career at UCLA. Born in Oakland, California, in 1985, he grew up in Antioch and attended De La Salle High School, where his football team achieved a remarkable 151-game winning streak during his three years on the varsity squad. He excelled as a running back, return specialist, and even as a linebacker, famously scoring all four of his team’s touchdowns in a nationally televised game against Long Beach Poly as a junior, including a memorable somersault into the endzone. He was a highly-rated recruit, eventually choosing to play for UCLA.

At UCLA from 2003 to 2005, Jones-Drew consistently led the Bruins in rushing despite being undersized. He demonstrated versatility as both a runner and receiver, and was a standout kick and punt returner. He set an NCAA record for punt return average in 2005 with 28.5 yards per return, and established several UCLA records, including career all-purpose yardage. A particularly impressive performance against Washington saw him rush for 322 yards and five touchdowns in a single game. He earned unanimous All-American honors in 2005 and was the first Bruin since Jackie Robinson to lead the country in punt returning.

Jones-Drew was drafted by the Jacksonville Jaguars in the second round of the 2006 NFL draft. Initially utilized as a kick returner, he eventually became a key part of the Jaguars' offense, first as a third-down back and later as the primary running back following Fred Taylor’s departure. He quickly established himself as a versatile player, excelling in rushing, receiving, and returning. In 2006, he set a franchise record with 166 rushing yards and 303 all-purpose yards in a single game and was a contender for Offensive Rookie of the Year. 

He continued to be a focal point of the Jaguars' offense, earning Pro Bowl selections in 2009 and 2010, and leading the NFL in rushing yards in 2011. During his time in Jacksonville, he often played through injuries, notably a torn meniscus in his knee throughout the 2010 season. After eight seasons with the Jaguars, Jones-Drew finished his NFL career with the Oakland Raiders in 2014. Following his retirement, he transitioned into broadcasting, working as a football analyst for NFL Network and CBS Sports, and is currently the color analyst for the Los Angeles Rams.

title: Zié Ouattara
text:
Zié Mohamed Ouattara is a professional footballer from Ivory Coast, born on January 9th, 2000. He currently plays as a right-back for Radomiak Radom, a club based in Poland. Ouattara began his footballing journey as a youth player with ASEC Mimosas, a club presumably located in Ivory Coast, though the article doesn't specify this. 

His career took a step forward on January 30th, 2018, when he transferred to Vitória S.C., a Portuguese club. However, he didn’t immediately break into the first team. Instead, he initially played for Vitória S.C.’s reserve team, known as Vitória B. His professional debut came on December 9th, 2018, while playing for Vitória B in a LigaPro match against F.C. Penafiel. Unfortunately, his debut wasn’t a winning one, as Vitória B lost the game 3-2. The article does not detail any further appearances or contributions he made for either Vitória S.C.’s first team or its B team.

Beyond his club career, Ouattara has also represented his country at the under-23 level. He first appeared for the Ivory Coast U23 team in March 2019, participating in qualifying matches for the 2019 Africa U-23 Cup of Nations. The article indicates he played in a pair of these qualification games, but doesn’t provide details about his performance in them. 

His involvement in the 2019 Africa U-23 Cup of Nations ultimately resulted in a team achievement, though not a victory. The Ivory Coast U23 team reached the final of the tournament, becoming the runner-up. This signifies a successful, albeit second-place finish, for Ouattara and his teammates in that competition. 

Currently, Ouattara continues his professional career with Radomiak Radom in Poland, building upon the experience he gained with ASEC Mimosas and Vitória S.C. Information regarding his current performance with Radomiak Radom is not included in this article. Further details about his career statistics and personal life are not provided within the scope of this Wikipedia entry.

title: Charles B. McVay III
text:
Charles Butler McVay III was a United States Navy officer whose career was tragically defined by the loss of the USS Indianapolis during World War II and the subsequent, controversial court-martial that followed. Born in 1898 into a naval family – his father was an admiral – McVay graduated from the Naval Academy in 1920 and rose through the ranks, earning a Silver Star for courage early in the war. Before taking command of the Indianapolis in November 1944, he served as chairman of the Joint Intelligence Committee of the Combined Chiefs of Staff. He successfully led the ship through the battles of Iwo Jima and Okinawa, though Indianapolis sustained damage and casualties during the latter when struck by a kamikaze.

In July 1945, the Indianapolis completed a top-secret mission delivering parts for the atomic bombs to Tinian and was en route to report for duty when it was attacked by a Japanese submarine, the I-58, commanded by Mochitsura Hashimoto. Six torpedoes struck the ship, causing it to sink in just twelve minutes. Of the 1,195 men aboard, approximately 879 perished, making it one of the worst maritime disasters in U.S. Navy history. Roughly 900 crewmen were left adrift in the water for four days before rescue arrived, suffering from injuries, dehydration, exhaustion, and shark attacks. The delay in rescue was attributed to Navy protocol regarding radio silence for secret missions, despite the fact that three SOS messages from the ship were received but disregarded for various reasons, including one commander being intoxicated and another dismissing it as a Japanese trick.

Following the sinking, McVay was court-martialed for failing to zigzag and for not ordering the abandonment of ship promptly enough. The court-martial was highly unusual, as he was the only captain in U.S. Navy history to be court-martialed for losing a ship sunk during wartime. Testimony from Commander Hashimoto and American submarine experts suggested that zigzagging likely wouldn’t have prevented the sinking, but McVay was still found guilty. Though initially reprimanded by Admiral Nimitz, the decision was overturned by Admiral King, who insisted on the court-martial. While Secretary Forrestal later remitted his sentence, the ordeal devastated McVay’s career.

For years after the tragedy, McVay was plagued by guilt and received hostile correspondence from grieving families. He eventually took his own life in 1968. However, decades of effort by survivors and others to clear his name finally led to a posthumous exoneration in 2000, with a resolution passed by Congress and signed by President Clinton. This resolution acknowledged the unfairness of his conviction and restored his reputation. Evidence emerged showing that the Navy held information about Japanese submarine activity in the area and that McVay’s request for a destroyer escort had been denied. The story of the Indianapolis and McVay’s fate has been depicted in several films and documentaries, highlighting the tragedy and the long struggle for justice.

title: Nick Kyrgios
text:
Nicholas Kyrgios, born in Canberra, Australia in 1995, is a professional tennis player who has achieved a career-high ranking of world No. 13 in singles and No. 11 in doubles. He has won seven ATP Tour singles titles, including the Washington Open in 2019 and 2022, and reached a major final at the 2022 Wimbledon Championships. Alongside Thanasi Kokkinakis, he won a major doubles title at the 2022 Australian Open. Kyrgios is noted for being one of only three players to have defeated each of the “Big Three” – Novak Djokovic, Roger Federer, and Rafael Nadal – in their first encounter. He is often described as a divisive figure due to his outspoken personality paired with moments of brilliance on the court.

Kyrgios’s family background is diverse; his father, George, is of Greek heritage, and his mother, Norlaila, is Malay and a member of the Pahang royal family, though she relinquished her title when moving to Australia. He has two siblings, Halimah and Christos. His paternal grandparents immigrated to Australia from Greece in 1960. He attended two schools in Canberra, Radford College and Daramalan College, and initially pursued basketball before dedicating himself to tennis at age 14, earning a scholarship to the Australian Institute of Sport two years later. He briefly relocated his training base to Melbourne Park before returning to Canberra, contributing financially to the redevelopment of the Lyneham Tennis Centre.

As a junior player, Kyrgios demonstrated considerable talent, winning the singles title at the 2013 Australian Open and the doubles titles at the 2012 French Open, 2012 Wimbledon Championships and 2013 Wimbledon Championships. He began competing professionally in 2012, winning his first ITF junior tour title in Fiji in 2010. In 2013, he achieved the world No. 1 junior ranking and won the Australian Open junior singles title, defeating Thanasi Kokkinakis in the final.

Kyrgios turned professional in 2012, and quickly rose through the ranks. A breakthrough moment came in 2013 at the French Open when, after initially being in the qualifying competition, he received a main draw wildcard and remarkably defeated Radek Štěpánek, marking his first ATP Tour level win. His progress continued in 2014 with a surprise quarterfinal appearance at Wimbledon, highlighted by a stunning victory over Rafael Nadal, becoming the first male debutant to reach the quarterfinals since 2004. This performance boosted his ranking into the top 100.

The following years saw further development. In 2015, he reached his first Grand Slam quarterfinal at the Australian Open, defeating Andreas Seppi and reaching the quarterfinals. He also reached his first ATP final at the Estoril Open. In 2016, Kyrgios won his first ATP title in Marseille, and later triumphed at the Hopman Cup with Daria Gavrilova. He continued to climb the rankings, reaching a career high of No. 16. In 2017, he reached his first Masters final, losing to Novak Djokovic in Acapulco.

title: Alen Omić
text:
Alen Omić, born on May 6, 1992, is a Slovenian professional basketball player. He began his professional career with Zlatorog Laško in 2009, playing for the club for three seasons until 2012. Following this, he signed a four-year contract with Union Olimpija in August 2012. 

Omić had opportunities to showcase his talent in the NBA Summer League, participating with the Brooklyn Nets in 2014 and the Denver Nuggets in 2015. In 2015, he signed a two-year deal with Gran Canaria, where he quickly made a strong impact and earned a place on the season’s All-EuroCup First Team. He then moved to Anadolu Efes in Turkey in June 2016, signing a two-year contract, but departed in January 2017 to join Unicaja in Spain for the remainder of the season. With Unicaja, he achieved success, winning the EuroCup in April 2017 after a victory over Valencia Basket in the Finals.

The following year, in July 2017, Omić signed with Hapoel Jerusalem in Israel for the 2017–18 season. He later moved to Crvena zvezda in Serbia in January 2018, completing the season with them. A brief stint with Olimpia Milano in Italy followed in January 2019, lasting for the rest of the season. He subsequently joined Joventut Badalona in June 2019, where he averaged 11.1 points and 6.5 rebounds per game. 

In September 2020, Omić signed with JL Bourg Basket in France, performing well with averages of 11.4 points, 9.0 rebounds, and 1.9 assists per game. He returned to a familiar league in November 2021, signing with Cedevita Olimpija of the ABA League. While playing for Cedevita Olimpija in May 2023, he set a new ABA League record for all-time offensive rebounds, reaching a total of 434.  He briefly played for the Guangxi Rhinos in China in August 2023, averaging impressive numbers of 19.43 points, 14.14 rebounds, and 3.57 assists over seven games. He then signed with Metropolitans 92 in France in November 2023, and returned to Cedevita Olimpija in February 2024. As of October 6, 2024, he plays for Budućnost.

Internationally, Omić has represented Slovenia’s senior national team, making his debut at the 2014 FIBA World Cup and also participating in EuroBasket 2015, where Slovenia was eliminated in the eighth finals by Latvia.

title: George Eacker
text:
George I. Eacker was a New York lawyer who achieved lasting notoriety for fatally shooting Philip Hamilton, the eldest son of Alexander Hamilton, in a duel. Born around 1774 in Palatine, New York, he came from a well-established family; his father, Jacob Eacker, was a Revolutionary War veteran and served in public office, and his mother was the daughter of a prominent family. He received a solid education, attending preparatory school in Schenectady and graduating from Columbia College in 1793 before studying law under Henry Brockholst Livingston.

Eacker quickly built a successful legal practice in Manhattan, becoming a prominent attorney by the age of 21. His prosperity allowed him to live comfortably on Wall Street and employ domestic staff. He was active in New York City society, participating as a Freemason, a cavalry captain, and a fire brigade inspector. He did encounter some legal trouble in 1798, appearing in court over an unspecified offense, likely a prior dispute, and posting a bond for good behavior. Later, in 1801, he was appointed a master in the New York Court of Chancery. 

Eacker’s involvement in politics and a controversial oration contributed to the circumstances leading to the duel with Hamilton. He delivered a Fourth of July speech aligned with the Democratic-Republican Party and Aaron Burr, placing him in opposition to Alexander Hamilton and the Federalists. While some claimed the speech criticized Hamilton, others, including Eacker’s brother, maintained it was entirely patriotic and did not mention Hamilton by name. Following the speech, Philip Hamilton and Stephen Price publicly ridiculed Eacker at the Park Theatre, prompting both men to challenge him to a duel.

Eacker first faced Stephen Price in Weehawken, New Jersey, on November 22, 1801, but neither man was injured. The following day, he dueled Philip Hamilton at the same location. Hamilton, following his father’s instructions, refused to fire upon Eacker. Eacker, determined to have the second shot, eventually fired, fatally wounding the 19-year-old Hamilton. Alexander Hamilton was deeply grieved by his son’s death but remained civil towards Eacker. 

Despite the duel’s consequences, Eacker continued his legal career and community involvement. However, he contracted a lingering illness, ultimately diagnosed as tuberculosis, after becoming severely chilled while fighting a fire in January 1802. He died on January 4, 1804, at the age of 30. His funeral was a large affair, attended by military units, Freemasons, and civic leaders. He never married his fiancée, Harriet Livingston, who later married Robert Fulton. Eacker’s story gained renewed attention with his depiction in the 2015 Broadway musical *Hamilton*.

title: Shakira
text:
Shakira Isabel Mebarak Ripoll, born in Barranquilla, Colombia on February 2, 1977, is a Colombian singer-songwriter widely known as the “Queen of Latin Music.” She has profoundly impacted Latin American music and is credited with bringing Hispanophone music to a global audience, earning four Grammy Awards and fifteen Latin Grammy Awards, including three for Song of the Year. 

Shakira began her recording career at age 14 with Sony Music Colombia. Her first two albums, *Magia* (1991) and *Peligro* (1993), were not commercially successful. She achieved prominence with her subsequent albums, *Pies Descalzos* (1995) and *Dónde Están los Ladrones?* (1998). A breakthrough came with *Laundry Service* (2001), her first English-language album, which sold over 13 million copies worldwide and became the best-selling album by a female Latin artist of all time. She continued success with Spanish-language albums *Fijación Oral, Vol. 1* (2005), *Sale el Sol* (2010), *El Dorado* (2017), and *Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran* (2024), all of which topped the Billboard Top Latin Albums chart, making her the first woman to achieve this feat across four different decades. Her English albums *Oral Fixation, Vol. 2* (2005), *She Wolf* (2009), and *Shakira* (2014) also received platinum certifications internationally.

Throughout her career, Shakira has amassed numerous number-one singles and hit songs, including “Estoy Aquí,” “Whenever, Wherever,” “Hips Don't Lie,” “Waka Waka (This Time for Africa),” and “TQG.” She has been a coach on *The Voice* (2013–2014), provided a voice role in *Zootopia* (2016), and served as a judge and executive producer on *Dancing with Myself* (2022). Billboard twice named her the Top Female Latin Artist of the Decade, in the 2000s and 2010s.

Shakira is known for writing or co-writing the majority of her music, both lyrics and music. She is described as an "international phenomenon" whose work bridges Western and Eastern musical styles, incorporating Middle Eastern sounds into Western music and vice versa. She received recognition for her philanthropic work, including the Latin Recording Academy Person of the Year and Harvard Foundation Artist of the Year awards in 2011. She has also served on presidential advisory commissions and been honored by the French government. Her advocacy extends to equitable development, children’s rights, and the interests of marginalized communities.

Shakira’s family history includes Spanish and Lebanese heritage, with her father born in New York City and her grandparents emigrating from Lebanon and Catalonia, Spain. She was raised Catholic and has eight older half-siblings. Early in her life, she demonstrated a passion for writing, starting with poetry at age four. Though her family faced financial hardship when her father went bankrupt, she was able to support them with earnings from her music, buying her parents a car at age 14. 

Her early musical development involved exposure to Middle Eastern music through her father and a rejection from a school choir due to her strong vibrato. She gained early recognition through local talent contests and an audition secured by a theater producer, leading to a record deal at age 13. Her initial albums, *Magia* and *Peligro*, were not commercially successful, but her performance at the Viña del Mar International Song Festival in 1993 helped raise her profile. *Pies Descalzos* (1995) marked her breakthrough, blending various musical influences and achieving platinum status in the U.S., launching a successful international tour and establishing Shakira as a rising star.

title: Carol Chell
text:
Carol Chell was born in July 1941 and is a British television personality known for her work presenting children’s programmes and later, as a television executive. Her initial career path led her to qualify as a teacher, and she began working in education before transitioning to television production in the 1960s, focusing on educational content. She became a familiar face to British children through her long-standing roles on two popular programmes: *Play School* and *Play Away*. 

Chell’s presenting career took off in 1966 when she joined the cast of *Play School*, remaining with the show until 1988. Simultaneously, from 1971 to 1980, she also presented *Play Away*, solidifying her position as a prominent figure in children’s television. Before achieving this widespread recognition, Chell received her education at Nottingham Girls’ High School, a direct grant grammar school, where she lived on Tudor Road in West Bridgford. She furthered her training at the Royal Central School of Speech and Drama.

Prior to her television work, Chell gained experience as a teacher at Pierrepont Secondary Modern School for Girls in Nottingham. Interestingly, a fellow teacher at the school during that time was Brian Clark, who later became a television writer, known for his work on *Telford's Change*. While best known for presenting, Chell also made guest appearances as herself in other programmes. In 1981, she participated in an episode of the BBC quiz show *The Adventure Game*, appearing as one of a group of ‘time-travellers’ attempting to solve puzzles. She also contributed to the ATV schools series *Starting Out* in 1982.

Beyond presenting, Chell moved into television management, taking on the role of head of pre-school programming at The Children's Channel, a satellite television station. She held this position until the channel ceased operations in 1998. Later in her career, she revisited her on-screen presence with an appearance on a celebrity edition of the BBC One game show *Pointless* in 2014, alongside fellow children’s television presenter Johnny Ball.

Chell married Ian Price on October 9, 1965, at St Peter's Church in Tollerton, Nottinghamshire; she was 23 years old at the time. The couple resided in Blackheath, London, while her parents lived in Christchurch, Dorset. Chell and Price have two daughters, Emily and Sophie, and together they have six grandchildren.

title: Vasily Chuikov
text:
Vasily Ivanovich Chuikov was a prominent Soviet military commander who rose to fame for his tenacious defense of Stalingrad during World War II and for accepting the surrender of German forces in Berlin. Born in 1900 to a peasant family near Tula, he began working in a factory at the age of twelve. Following the 1917 Russian Revolution, he joined the Red Army and distinguished himself in the ensuing Civil War, earning awards for bravery. He continued his military education at the Frunze Military Academy, after which he served as a military attaché and intelligence officer, notably in China and the Russian Far East.

Prior to the German invasion of the Soviet Union, Chuikov commanded armies during the Soviet invasion of Poland in 1939 and the Winter War against Finland in 1940. In 1940, he was assigned as a military attaché to China, tasked with supporting Chiang Kai-shek and the Nationalist forces against Japan, a mission directed by Stalin to keep Japan occupied and prevent them from threatening the Soviet Union. He provided substantial military aid to the Nationalists, despite criticism from Communist leaders like Mao Zedong.

In 1942, Chuikov was recalled to the Soviet Union to confront the German advance. He was appointed commander of the 62nd Army and tasked with defending Stalingrad at all costs. Recognizing the Wehrmacht’s superior firepower, he implemented a tactic of keeping Soviet positions as close as possible to the German lines, minimizing the effectiveness of German air support and enabling close-quarters combat. Despite the immense destruction and heavy losses, Chuikov’s army held on, contributing significantly to the eventual Soviet counter-offensive in November 1942, which encircled and ultimately led to the surrender of the German 6th Army in early 1943.

Following Stalingrad, Chuikov’s 8th Guards Army participated in Operation Bagration and the Vistula–Oder Offensive, pushing through Poland. He culminated his wartime service by personally accepting the unconditional surrender of German forces in Berlin on May 2, 1945. 

After the war, Chuikov held several high-ranking positions, including Chief of the Group of Soviet Forces in Germany, commander of the Kiev Military District, Chief of the Soviet Armed Forces, and head of the Soviet Civil Defense Forces. He received the title Hero of the Soviet Union twice, and was also awarded the Distinguished Service Cross by the United States. In 1955, he was promoted to Marshal of the Soviet Union. He died in 1982 and, at his request, was buried at the Stalingrad memorial at Mamayev Kurgan, a poignant testament to the battle that defined his military career. His death was ultimately caused by complications from a war wound sustained in Poland in 1920.

title: Gulshan Kumar
text:
Gulshan Kumar Dua, born in 1956, was a prominent Indian film and music producer who founded the T-Series music label, a cornerstone of the Bollywood industry. His story began with humble roots; his family were Punjabi Hindu refugees who settled in Delhi after the 1947 partition of India, and his father worked as a fruit juice vendor. Gulshan Kumar himself began working with his father from a young age.

Deeply religious, Gulshan Kumar was a devoted worshipper of Shiva and Vaishno Devi. This devotion manifested in a free meal service for devotees visiting the Vaishno Devi Temple, started in 1983 and continuing to this day, now managed by his son. His initial foray into business came with his family’s acquisition of a shop selling records and audio cassettes, which provided the foundation for his future success.

He established Super Cassettes Industries, which rapidly grew into a profitable business, eventually leading him to relocate to Mumbai. His first venture into film production was *Lal Dupatta Malmal Ka* in 1989, but it was *Aashiqui* in 1990, with music by Nadeem-Shravan, that truly launched T-Series to prominence.  He produced several other films including *Bahaar Aane Tak*, *Dil Hai Ke Manta Nahin*, and *Jeena Marna Tere Sang*.

T-Series quickly became a leading music label, significantly contributing to a boom in the Indian music industry in the early 1990s.  The company’s revenue grew dramatically, from ₹20 crore in 1985 to ₹500 crore by 1997, the year of Gulshan Kumar’s death. Today, T-Series continues to dominate the Indian music market, controlling over 60% of it, and has a substantial international presence with exports to 24 countries and a distribution network of over 2500 dealers.

Tragically, Gulshan Kumar was assassinated on August 12, 1997, outside a temple in Mumbai, shot 16 times. The murder stemmed from his refusal to pay extortion money demanded by the D-Company, a Mumbai underworld organization. Despite receiving threats, he refused to comply. Abdul Rauf Merchant was ultimately convicted for the murder in 2002 and sentenced to life imprisonment, though initial accusations also pointed towards film composer Nadeem Saifi, who fled the country.  

Following his death, T-Series was taken over by his younger brother, Krishan Kumar, and son, Bhushan Kumar. His daughters, Tulsi Kumar and Khushalii Kumar, have both become playback singers. A biographical film about his life, *Mogul – The Gulshan Kumar Story*, was announced in 2017, illustrating his lasting legacy in the Indian music industry.

title: Alice Torriani
text:
Alice Torriani, born on March 25, 1984, is an Italian actor, author, and screenwriter. She began her career after graduating from the Paolo Grassi Drama School in Milan in 2007, immediately landing the female lead in a production of Chekhov’s *Three Sisters* directed by Massimo Castri, which launched her on a year-long Italian tour. She followed this with another female lead role in Gabriele Lavia’s adaptation of Dostoyevsky’s *Memoirs from the House of The Dead*, leading to her participation in the film *Ten Winters*, which won both the David di Donatello prize for Best Debut and the Silver Ribbon for Best First Work in 2010.

Her early work also included involvement with the European Project "Prospero" and Alvis Hermanis’s *The Young Ladies of Wilko*, a production touring extensively throughout Europe over two years.  As an actor, Torriani has appeared in several films including *E’ nata una star* and *D.A.D.*, and has consistently sought to hone her skills through workshops with prominent directors like Luca Ronconi and Antonio Latella, as well as studies at acting studios in Los Angeles and New York.

Torriani’s television work includes a guest appearance on the popular Italian series *Montalbano*, and a role in the fourth season of *Un Passo dal Ciello*. However, she is perhaps best known for her portrayal of Andreina Mandelli in *Il Paradiso delle Signore* (Ladies' Paradise), a RAI television adaptation of Emile Zola’s *Au Bonheur des Dames* that began in 2015. She has also shared the stage with celebrated Italian comedian Franca Valeri in the play *Il cambio dei cavalli* and performed in Romeo Castellucci’s *The Four Seasons Restaurant*.

Beyond acting, Torriani has established herself as an author. Her debut novel, *L'Altra Sete* (A Different Thirst), was published in 2015 by Fandango Libri and went on to represent Italy at the Festival Européen du Premier Roman in Germany in 2016. She published a second novel, *Una Vita a Posto*, with the same publisher in 2018.  She has also worked as a screenwriter, co-writing the screenplay for the TV series *Cleaning your Shit* with Giampiero Judica in 2015, and starring in the resulting series when it was filmed in 2017.

title: Félix María Zuloaga
text:
Félix María Zuloaga Trillo (1803-1898) was a Mexican conservative general and politician central to the outbreak of the Reform War in 1858, and briefly served as president of Mexico. His early career involved military service, beginning with a colonelcy in 1834 and campaigns against indigenous groups. He defended the government during the Federalist Revolt of 1840 and participated in revisions to the constitution. During the Mexican-American War, he focused on fortifications, and later served as an alderman in Chihuahua before returning to the military. He initially aligned with the liberal forces under Ignacio Comonfort, even commanding troops for him, but this allegiance shifted dramatically.

The pivotal moment came in 1857 with the drafting of a new constitution, sparking conservative opposition due to its reforms targeting the Church and communal land ownership through the Ley Lerdo. As tensions escalated, Zuloaga, initially loyal to Comonfort, became a key conspirator in the Plan of Tacubaya, which sought to overturn the constitution and establish a new congress. This plan led to the overthrow of Comonfort, with Zuloaga assuming the presidency in January 1858 after Comonfort released Benito Juárez, the rightful constitutional president, and fled the country.

Zuloaga's presidency was marked by immediate conflict with Juárez's liberal government. While Zuloaga’s forces experienced initial military successes, capturing key cities and briefly even imprisoning Juárez, the liberals maintained control over peripheral regions, particularly the strategic port of Veracruz. Despite these victories, Zuloaga faced internal divisions within the conservative ranks – Santanistas, Zuloaguistas, and Fusionists – and struggled with financial difficulties. Attempts to revive a centralized government and suppress dissent further complicated his position.

The tide turned against Zuloaga in December 1858 when a moderate conservative faction, the Fusionists, launched a counter-pronouncement. Unable to quell the rebellion, and facing dwindling support, Zuloaga resigned and sought asylum in the British legation.  Manuel Robles Pezuela then assumed the presidency, attempting a compromise with the liberals.  However, this effort failed, and Miguel Miramon was later elected president with Zuloaga's endorsement, effectively relinquishing his claim to the office.

Zuloaga briefly re-emerged after the war, attempting to reclaim the presidency while conservative guerillas remained active, but this proved unsuccessful. He subsequently left Mexico, returning during the Second Mexican Empire but playing no significant political or military role. Following the Empire's collapse in 1867, he was exiled to Cuba before eventually returning to Mexico, where he lived until his death in 1898.

title: William M. Brodhead
text:
William McNulty Brodhead, born in Cleveland, Ohio in 1941, is a former American politician and lawyer who represented Michigan in the U.S. House of Representatives for four terms. He received his Bachelor of Arts degree from Wayne State University in Detroit in 1965, and subsequently earned a Juris Doctor from the University of Michigan Law School in 1967. He was admitted to the Michigan Bar in 1968 and began practicing law in Detroit.

Brodhead’s political career began with his election to the Michigan House of Representatives in 1970, where he served for two terms, being reelected in 1972. In 1974, with the incumbent Martha W. Griffiths choosing not to seek reelection, Brodhead successfully ran for the Democratic nomination and was then elected to represent Michigan’s 17th congressional district in the U.S. House of Representatives. He served in Congress from 1975 until 1983, spanning the Ninety-fourth Congress and the three that followed. 

During his time in Congress, Brodhead was involved in key committees. He was a member of both the House Ways and Means Committee and the Budget Committee. He also demonstrated leadership within the Democratic party by serving as Chair of the Democratic Study Group, which at that time functioned as the liberal caucus within the House. 

Choosing not to run for reelection in 1982, Brodhead returned to Detroit and resumed his legal career. He joined the law firm of Plunkett & Cooney as a partner, practicing there for two decades until 2003. He continued to practice law independently for another three years, retiring fully in 2006.

Outside of his legal and political work, Brodhead remained active in civic engagement. He dedicated his time to various non-profit organizations, serving on the boards of groups such as Detroit Public Television, Mt. Carmel Hospital, Michigan's Children, and the Citizen's Research Council. He also held positions as Board Chair for the Skillman Foundation, Covenant House Michigan, Focus:Hope, and the Oakland Mediation Center. In 1994, he made an attempt to transition to the Senate, running in the Democratic primary for a U.S. Senate seat but was unsuccessful, losing to Bob Carr.

Currently, Brodhead resides in Northern California with his wife, Kathleen, whom he married in 1965. They have two children and a granddaughter, all of whom live in the same region. He continues his commitment to public service by serving on the board of directors for Covenant House, California.

title: Felician of Foligno
text:
Felician of Foligno was a Christian figure who lived approximately from 160 to 250 AD and is recognized as the patron saint of Foligno, Italy. He was born in Forum Flaminii, now known as San Giovanni Profiamma, located along the Via Flaminia, and came from a Christian family. His early religious education was guided by Pope Eleuterus, and he dedicated his life to spreading the Christian faith throughout the region. He actively evangelized in several cities including Foligno, Spello, Bevagna, Assisi, Perugia, Norcia, Plestia, Trevi, and Spoleto.

Around the year 204 AD, Felician was consecrated as the first Bishop of Foligno by Pope Victor I. Importantly, he was the first bishop to be granted the pallium, a vestment signifying his authority and office. During his more than fifty-year episcopate, he ordained Valentine of Terni as a priest, establishing a further link in the early Christian leadership of the area. He is considered to be among the earliest Christian bishops in northern Italy. 

Later in his life, at the advanced age of 94, Felician faced persecution under the Roman Emperor Decius for his refusal to participate in sacrifices to the Roman gods. He was arrested as a result of his unwavering faith. While imprisoned, he received a visit from one of his devoted followers, Messalina of Foligno. He endured torture and scourging as a consequence of his beliefs. Ultimately, Felician died while being transported from Foligno to Rome for his scheduled execution.

Following his death, a church was constructed over his burial site in Foligno, marking the beginning of his veneration as a saint. Over the centuries, his relics were dispersed. In 970 AD, a significant portion of his remains were moved to Metz, France. Several years earlier, in 965, some relics had been taken to Minden, Germany, mistakenly leading to the belief that Felician had been a bishop of that city and the establishment of a separate feast day for him on October 20th – an error that was even recorded in the Roman Martyrology.  However, some of his relics were eventually returned to Foligno in 1673 and 1674. 

Today, Foligno Cathedral houses a statue depicting Saint Felician, crafted from silver and bronze by the sculptor Giovanni Battista Maini, serving as a visual testament to his enduring importance to the city and its people.

title: Jo Koy
text:
Jo Koy, born Joseph Glenn Herbert on June 2, 1971, is an American stand-up comedian and actor. He gained prominence through frequent appearances on Chelsea Lately and has released six comedy specials with Comedy Central and Netflix. In 2024, he hosted the 81st Golden Globe Awards, a performance that drew significant criticism.

Koy’s background is a blend of cultures; his father, John C. Herbert, was an American serviceman stationed in Japan when he met Koy’s Filipina mother, Josie Harrison. He was also raised with the support of his stepfather, Fredrick Harrison. His family moved several times during his childhood, from Washington state to Las Vegas after high school, to be near his grandmother. He briefly attended the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, but left to pursue a career in comedy. His stage name, “Jo Koy,” originated from a childhood nickname – a mishearing of his aunt calling out “Jo Ko, eat!” (“Ko” meaning “my” in Tagalog).

Koy dedicated roughly 30 years to honing his comedic skills, starting with open mic nights and eventually landing regular gigs, including at the Catch a Rising Star in Las Vegas and by renting the Huntridge Theater to produce his own shows. His frequent appearances on Chelsea Lately increased his visibility in the United States. Beyond stand-up, he hosts the weekly podcast, “The Koy Pond,” where he engages in casual conversation with fellow comedians. 

He has released several successful Netflix specials, including “Jo Koy: Comin’ in Hot” and “Jo Koy: In His Elements,” the latter showcasing Filipino American talent. He also participated in the Rise for Comedy festival, raising funds for a Filipino American nonprofit. His 2020 “Just Kidding” world tour took him across multiple continents.

However, his hosting of the 2024 Golden Globe Awards was largely considered a failure, receiving harsh reviews for an awkward and unfunny monologue. Critics and viewers alike noted dated jokes and a perceived blaming of his writers after some jokes fell flat. Koy acknowledged the backlash but maintained he enjoyed the experience, citing the difficulty of the hosting role and the short timeframe for writing the monologue. Other comedians, like Steve Martin and Whoopi Goldberg, voiced support for him.

Koy draws comedic influence from a range of performers including Bill Cosby, Eddie Murphy, and Robin Williams. He was named one of the "75 Most Influential Filipino-Americans" in 2022. He was previously married to singer Angie King, with whom he has a son, Joseph Jr. He briefly dated Chelsea Handler between 2021 and 2022.  He currently lives in Los Angeles, near his son and ex-wife, and has a passion for Brazilian jiu-jitsu, recently getting a traditional tattoo from a Filipina tattoo artist. His stepfather passed away in 2023, and he publicly honored his service and heroism. While his mother is a Republican supporter, Koy generally avoids political discussion in his routines.

title: Annie Landouw
text:
Annie Landouw, born in Surakarta, Central Java in 1913, was a prominent Indonesian singer and actress best known for her work in the keroncong genre. Her early life was marked by a childhood illness that resulted in the loss of her sight. Following this, she was adopted by her aunt and uncle. Her musical talent emerged in 1927 when she won a singing competition, a Concours concert held at a night fair in Surakarta. This victory led to a recording contract with Beka, prompting her move to Batavia, now Jakarta, where she rapidly gained recognition and popularity.

Landouw’s career progressed quickly, and by 1938 she had become a member of the NIROM radio troupe, performing keroncong music. The following year, she joined Hugo Dumas' Lief Java troupe, further cementing her position in the entertainment world. Concurrent with her radio work, Landouw began contributing to the burgeoning Indonesian film industry. She initially provided vocals for films produced by Tan's Film, beginning with *Fatima* in 1938 and continuing with *Gagak Item* (Black Raven) in 1939. Later in 1939, she made her acting debut in the film *Siti Akbari*. She then appeared in two more films in 1940: *Sorga Ka Toedjoe* (Seventh Heaven) and *Roekihati*.

Landouw’s skill as a keroncong singer brought her widespread fame and a dedicated fan base. In 1940, arrangements were made for eye surgery to potentially restore her sight. Her admirers organized a fundraising effort to assist with the costs, but Landouw ultimately declined their charitable offers. 

After Indonesia achieved independence, Landouw continued to pursue her singing career, but did not appear in any further films. She passed away on August 17, 1982. Her impact on Indonesian culture extends beyond her recordings and performances. Music scholar Peter Keppy has proposed a potential connection between Landouw’s success and a character in Armijn Pane’s 1940 novel *Belenggu*. Keppy suggests that the character of Yah, a famous keroncong singer known as Siti Hayati within the novel, may have been influenced by Landouw’s popularity and persona.

title: Albert Outler
text:
Albert Cook Outler was a prominent 20th-century American Methodist historian, theologian, and pastor, born in Georgia in 1908 and passing away in 1989. He dedicated his life to scholarship and ministry, serving as a professor at Duke University, Yale University, and most notably, Southern Methodist University, where he held a long-term position. His academic work encompassed Christian history, theology, doctrine, and specifically, Wesleyan studies. 

Outler was a significant figure in the ecumenical movement, actively participating in efforts towards Christian unity. He served as a delegate to the Consultation on Church Union and held a position on the Faith & Order board of the World Council of Churches. He also acted as an official observer representing the Methodist tradition at the Second Vatican Council. Along with colleagues like Colin Williams, Frank Baker, and John Deschner, Outler’s scholarship played a vital role in revitalizing contemporary study of John Wesley and establishing Wesley as a significant theological voice. He authored *John Wesley* for "The Library of Protestant Thought" series, a groundbreaking work that positioned Wesley within the broader Western theological tradition, and produced critical editions of Wesley’s Sermons.

A cornerstone of Outler’s theological contribution was his articulation of the “Wesleyan Quadrilateral” – scripture, tradition, reason, and personal experience – as the method by which Wesley approached theology. This framework became central to Methodist understanding, particularly within the United Methodist Church, and informed the theological statement adopted by the newly formed church in 1968. He is credited with uniquely emphasizing the importance of “Tradition” within this Wesleyan system. His focus on early church history and thought also resonated with the paleo-orthodox movement and contemporary evangelicalism, influencing figures like Thomas C. Oden. 

Outler was a prolific writer, producing books and articles not only on Methodist history and theology but also on patrology, psychotherapy, and general theology. His extensive body of work has been compiled into the Albert Outler Library series. His published books range from explorations of Clement of Alexandria and Augustine to analyses of Vatican II and the unity of Christians. He also contributed articles to publications like *The Christian Century* and *Perkins School of Theology Journal*. Resources relating to his life and work, including archival papers, are available online, and some of his writings have been made accessible through LibriVox as public domain audiobooks.

title: Frank Middlemass
text:
Francis George Middlemass was an English actor born in 1919 and passing away in 2006, known for frequently portraying older characters even early in his career. He achieved significant recognition for a number of television roles, most notably as Rocky Hardcastle in the long-running sitcom *As Time Goes By*, Algy Herries in *To Serve Them All My Days*, and Dr. Alex Ferrenby in *Heartbeat*. 

Middlemass’s acting journey began after serving in the army, where he rose to the rank of lieutenant colonel and was wounded during the Dunkirk retreat. He started his stage career in repertory theatre in Penzance before joining the Old Vic Company, with whom he toured extensively across the globe, including performances in *Twelfth Night* alongside Vivien Leigh. He later worked with Ian McKellen’s Actors’ Company and performed alongside Peter O’Toole in *Waiting for Godot*. 

His television career started in 1958 with a role in *Dixon of Dock Green*, and he became a familiar face throughout the 60s, 70s, and 80s with appearances in shows like *Z-Cars*, *The Avengers*, *Doctor at Large*, *War and Peace* (as Kutuzov), *Upstairs, Downstairs*, and *The Sweeney*. He also took on film roles, including a part in Stanley Kubrick’s *Barry Lyndon*. He played a range of characters in numerous television dramas and comedies, including roles in *Juliet Bravo*, *Yes Minister*, and *Miss Marple*.

Beyond television and film, Middlemass had a substantial radio career, most famously as the fourth actor to portray Dan Archer in the radio soap opera *The Archers* – a role he held for four years until the character's death. He also lent his voice to several radio plays and albums, including *The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy*. A committed advocate, he made a BBC Radio appeal for Headway, the National Head Injuries Association, successfully raising considerable funds. 

He was involved with the Royal Shakespeare Company from 1984, performing in productions of *Romeo and Juliet* and *A Midsummer Night's Dream*, among others. Throughout his career, he continued to work on stage, even into his eighties, with roles in *The Importance of Being Earnest* and a one-man show called *Frankly Speaking*. His final television appearances were in the 2005 reunion specials of *As Time Goes By*.  Middlemass never married and lived with his close friend, fellow actor Geoffrey Toone, for forty years until Toone’s death in 2005. He died in 2006 at the age of 87.

title: Profit (gamer)
text:
Park Joon-yeong, known professionally as Profit, is a retired South Korean professional *Overwatch* player born November 19, 1999, in Jinju. He began his career with GC Busan in April 2017, quickly achieving success. GC Busan won OGN APEX Season 4, defeating Cloud 9 KongDoo in the semifinals and RunAway in a close 4-3 final series, where Profit led all players with 134 kills and was named the APEX Finals most valuable player. They also won the 2017 APAC Premier finals against RunAway in China.

In November 2017, Profit and the entire GC Busan roster were signed by the London Spitfire for the inaugural season of the Overwatch League (OWL). Early in the 2018 season, he received a $1,000 fine for an inappropriate gesture during a match, though he apologized and explained it was a response to a backstage joke. The Spitfire reached the Stage 1 Finals, where Profit contributed to 38.2% of his team’s kills in their victory over the New York Excelsior. He finished the regular season as the highest-rated DPS player across all heroes. 

The Spitfire continued to dominate, defeating the Los Angeles Gladiators and Valiant in the playoffs before facing the Philadelphia Fusion in the Grand Finals. Profit played a crucial role in their 3-1 and 3-0 victories, notably securing key final blows while playing Tracer. His performance earned him the Grand Finals Most Valuable Player award. He became a significant figure in the team’s history, and his jersey number 13 was retired by the Spitfire on January 15, 2020.

In October 2019, Profit was traded to the Seoul Dynasty alongside teammates Gesture and Bdosin. During the 2020 season, he became the first OWL player to reach 10,000 total eliminations. The Dynasty reached the Grand Finals but lost to the San Francisco Shock 4-2. He continued with the Dynasty through 2022, winning the Kickoff Clash tournament after defeating the Philadelphia Fusion. He received a Role Star commendation at the end of the regular season and was a finalist for the league’s MVP award. While a role switch to Kiriko didn’t yield a playoff win, the Dynasty had a strong run before being eliminated. Following the disbanding of the Overwatch League and the release of the Seoul Dynasty’s roster in October 2023, Profit announced his retirement from esports on February 20, 2024.

title: Damon Herriman
text:
Damon Herriman, born on March 31, 1970, is an Australian actor with a prolific career spanning film, television, and theatre. He first began acting at the age of eight with television commercials, and quickly gained recognition with a role in the series *The Sullivans* at age ten, earning three Logie Award nominations for his performance. He continued working steadily as a child actor, appearing in series like *The Patchwork Hero*, *Sara Dane*, *For the Term of His Natural Life*, and *Taurus Rising*. He also won a Penguin Award for his work on *The Flying Doctors*.

His early adult work included a role in the Australian cult comedy *The Big Steal*, and he continued to build his resume with appearances in *Love My Way*, *Laid*, and *100 Bloody Acres*. Herriman is also a writer and director, having created several successful short films including *They* and *The Date*, and winning a Best Screenplay award at Flickerfest for *Soar*. He contributed as a performer and writer to the ABC sketch comedy series *The Elegant Gentleman's Guide to Knife Fighting*.

Herriman’s career expanded to the United States in 2004 with a role in the horror film *House of Wax*. He has since worked consistently in American television, with appearances in shows like *The Unit*, *Breaking Bad*, *Wilfred*, and *Vegas*. He portrayed Bruno Hauptmann, the convicted kidnapper of the Lindbergh baby, in Clint Eastwood’s *J. Edgar* and appeared in *The Lone Ranger*.

He is perhaps most recognizable for his roles as Dewey Crowe in the FX series *Justified* and Romeo in the Starz miniseries *Flesh and Bone*. Notably, in 2019, Herriman portrayed Charles Manson in both Quentin Tarantino’s *Once Upon a Time in Hollywood* and the Netflix series *Mindhunter*. That same year, he won the AACTA Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role for his performance in *Judy and Punch*, having previously been nominated for Best Supporting Actor for *The Nightingale* in 2018. 

Beyond acting, Herriman provided the voice for Kabal in the 2021 film *Mortal Kombat* and contributed to the music video for ARO’s “Raining Gold” in 2015. In 2018, he received the Orry-Kelly Award for his contribution to Australia’s national identity through his work.

title: Zhang Yaokun
text:
Zhang Yaokun, born April 17, 1981, was a Chinese footballer who concluded his professional career in November 2018. He began his career with Dalian Shide in 1998, but faced initial setbacks due to an ankle fracture that hampered his progress. After recovering from this injury, he became a vital part of Dalian’s defense, contributing to a period of success for the club. He was a key player in their winning of the Chinese Jia-A League titles in 2001 and 2002, as well as the Chinese FA Cup in 2001. Following a disappointing season for Dalian in 2004, he was loaned to Sichuan Guancheng in 2005, where he quickly became a prominent player. He returned to Dalian the next year and eventually became the team’s captain.

In December 2012, Zhang moved to Guangzhou R&F, making his debut in March 2013 in a match against Liaoning Whowin. He then transferred to Wuhan Zall, a League One side, in February 2017. His time with Wuhan Zall culminated in the team’s promotion to the Chinese Super League, after which he announced his retirement from professional football in November 2018.

Zhang also represented the Chinese national team, receiving a call-up for the 2004 AFC Asian Cup where he appeared as a substitute and played in various defensive positions. He continued to be a regular member of the national squad, contributing to their qualification for the 2007 AFC Asian Cup. During that tournament, he formed the first-choice centre back partnership with Li Weifeng. He also participated in the 2005 East Asian Football Championship, where China won the title.

Throughout his career, Zhang accumulated numerous honors. With Dalian Shide, he won the Chinese Jia-A League four times (1998, 2000, 2001, and 2002), the Chinese FA Cup in 2001, and the Chinese FA Super Cup in 2000 and 2002. More recently, with Wuhan Zall, he secured the China League One title in 2018. Individually, he was recognized for his performance with a place in the Chinese Super League Team of the Year in 2004.

title: Bhāskara I
text:
Bhāskara I was a 7th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer, considered a pivotal figure in the continuation of Aryabhata’s astronomical school. Born in India around 600 AD, and likely an astronomer by profession, he received his education from his father. While details of his life are sparse, references in his writings suggest he may have been born in Saurastra, in present-day Gujarat, and later moved to Aśmaka. He is recognized alongside Brahmagupta as one of the most important Indian mathematicians of his time, both contributing significantly to the study of fractions.

Bhāskara’s most significant contribution lies in his representation of numbers. While positional numeral systems existed before his time, they were expressed through words and allegories – the number one as the moon, two as wings, five as the senses – arranged in reverse order of powers of ten. Bhāskara was the first to openly use the Brahmi numerals in a scientific text, specifically his commentary on Aryabhata’s work, the *Āryabhaṭīyabhāṣya*, written in 629 AD. This commentary is one of the oldest known prose works in Sanskrit dedicated to mathematics and astronomy. He wrote numbers left to right, in descending values, much like our modern decimal system, and explicitly explained the numeral system using the phrase "ankair api" ("in figures this reads") alongside the Brahmi numerals, including a symbol for zero.

Beyond this crucial development, Bhāskara authored two further astronomical texts: the *Mahābhāskarīya* ("Great Book of Bhāskara") and the *Laghubhāskarīya* ("Small Book of Bhāskara"). The *Mahābhāskarīya* is an eight-chapter work covering mathematical astronomy, including planetary longitudes, conjunctions, eclipses, and planetary movements. He also made substantial contributions to mathematical formulas. Notably, he provided a remarkably accurate rational approximation for the sine function, with a relative error of less than 1.9%, which he attributed to Aryabhata. He explored relationships between sine and cosine, and angles in different quadrants. 

Bhāskara also tackled what are now known as Pell's equations, posing problems like finding a square that, when multiplied by eight and increased by one, results in another square. He demonstrated solutions to these types of equations, such as (1,3) and (6,17). He also clearly stated his belief that pi (π) was an irrational number, criticizing the common Jain practice of approximating it as the square root of ten. He was the first to discuss quadrilaterals with four unequal, non-parallel sides. Parts of his *Mahābhāskarīya* were later translated into Arabic, extending his influence beyond India. 

In recognition of his contributions, the Indian Space Research Organisation named the Bhāskara I satellite, launched in 1979, in his honor.

title: Takuma Asano
text:
Takuma Asano, born November 10, 1994, is a Japanese professional footballer currently playing as a forward for La Liga club Mallorca. His younger brother, Yuya Asano, is also a professional footballer with Nagoya Grampus in the J1 League. Asano began his career with Sanfrecce Hiroshima in January 2013, winning the J1 League title in his debut season with a single appearance. He further contributed to the team’s success by winning the Japanese Super Cup in 2014 and a second J1 League title in 2015, during which he scored nine goals in 34 appearances, earning him the J1 League Rookie of the Year award.

In July 2016, Asano signed with Arsenal, but was unable to secure a work permit to play in the Premier League. He was subsequently loaned to VfB Stuttgart until the end of the season, with an option to extend. He played a key role in Stuttgart’s promotion to the Bundesliga, scoring a brace against Karlsruher SC and helping them win the 2. Bundesliga. The loan was extended for another season, before he moved to Hannover 96 on a season-long loan in May 2018.

Asano then transitioned to Serbian club Partizan in August 2019, signing a three-year contract and becoming the first Japanese player in the club’s history. He scored on his debut in the Europa League qualifying rounds and contributed to Partizan’s group stage qualification, playing in all their European matches and scoring against AZ Alkmaar and Astana. While Partizan finished second in the Serbian SuperLiga, and reached the Serbian Cup final, they were unsuccessful in winning either competition. After a period where Partizan didn’t qualify for the Europa League group stage, Asano scored 18 league goals in the 2020/21 season before rescinding his contract in May 2021.

He then joined VfL Bochum in June 2021, making his Bundesliga debut in August. He became a consistent performer for Bochum, contributing crucial goals to help the team avoid relegation, including a brace against Hoffenheim and a goal and assist against Bayer Leverkusen in the final match of the 2022-23 season. He continued with Bochum into the 2023-24 season, scoring multiple goals in draws against Augsburg and Darmstadt 98, and even scoring against Bayern Munich before departing at the end of the season. In July 2024, Asano signed a two-year contract with Spanish side Mallorca, making his debut in August against Real Madrid.

On the international stage, Asano won a gold medal with the Japan U-23 team at the 2016 AFC U-23 Championship, scoring twice in the final. He also represented Japan at the 2016 Summer Olympics. He made his senior debut for Japan in 2015 and scored his first goal in 2016. He was initially overlooked for the 2018 World Cup squad due to a lack of playing time, but famously scored the winning goal against Germany in the 2022 World Cup. Asano has been recognized for his performances, earning the J.League Rookie of the Year award in 2015 and a spot in the Japan Pro-Footballers Association Best XI in 2022. He has won the J1 League twice with Sanfrecce Hiroshima, the 2. Bundesliga with VfB Stuttgart and the AFC U-23 Championship with Japan U23.

title: Neha Sargam
text:
Neha Sargam, originally Neha Dubey, is an Indian actress and singer who has built a career encompassing television, web series, and musical theatre. Her initial claim to fame came through her participation in the popular singing reality show, Indian Idol, though her first attempt in season two was unsuccessful after she forgot the lyrics during a subsequent audition. She returned to the show in 2009 for Indian Idol 4.

Following her appearances on Indian Idol, Sargam transitioned into acting, securing roles in several television serials. She is recognized for portraying Sita in *Ramayan* on Zee TV and for her work in *Chand Chupa Badal Mein* on Star Plus. She’s also appeared in *Doli Armano Ki*, another Zee TV production, taking on a main lead role after a time jump within the show's narrative. Further television credits include cameo appearances in *Punar Vivaah - Zindagi Milegi Dobara* and a role in *Iss Pyaar Ko Kya Naam Doon? Ek Baar Phir*, as well as *Yeh Hai Aashiqui*. She also played the character of Lakshmi in the series *Paramavatar Shri Krishna*.

More recently, Neha Sargam has expanded her work into the realm of web series. In 2020, she took on the role of Saloni Tyagi in seasons two and three of the critically acclaimed *Mirzapur*. 

Beyond traditional television and digital platforms, Sargam has a significant presence in musical theatre. She has been involved in two prominent productions directed by Feroz Abbas Khan. She performed as both an actor and singer in the lead role in *Mughal-E-Azam the musical*, a large-scale production backed by the Shapoorji Pallonji Group. She continued her collaboration with Khan in *Raunaq and Jassi*, another musical, produced by BookMyShow. These theatrical productions showcase her dual talent as a performer capable of both acting and singing.



Further information about Neha Sargam can be found on her IMDb page.

title: Lemuel W. Joiner
text:
Lemuel Whiting Joiner was a 19th-century American politician and pioneer who spent a significant portion of his life in Wisconsin, serving in the state legislature for seven years. Born in Royalton, Vermont, on November 9, 1810, Joiner’s early life involved several relocations. He initially moved to Cincinnati in 1830, then further west to Williamsport, Indiana, in 1834. His final move, in 1845, brought him to Wyoming, Iowa County, Wisconsin, where he established his permanent home and remained for the rest of his life. He passed away on October 22, 1886.

Joiner’s political career began with his election to the Wisconsin State Assembly in 1853, serving for a single year. He then transitioned to the State Senate, where he served three separate terms, totaling six years of Senate service. His first period of representation in the Senate spanned from 1857 to 1858. He was subsequently re-elected and served from 1861 to 1862. After a period away from the legislature, he returned for a final term, representing his constituents from 1869 to 1870. 

Throughout his time in both the Assembly and the Senate, Joiner was affiliated with the Republican Party. The article specifically notes his party affiliation, identifying him as a Republican politician. Beyond his own political endeavors, Joiner’s family also contributed to Wisconsin’s political landscape; his son, Robert Joiner, followed in his father's footsteps and also served in the state legislature, though the specific chamber or years of his service are not detailed in this article. 

Joiner’s life reflects the pattern of many 19th-century Americans, demonstrating movement and settlement as the nation expanded. He transitioned from farming and establishing a life in one location to engaging in public service and representing the interests of his community within the Wisconsin government.

title: Feroze Gandhi
text:
Feroze Jehangir Gandhi was born in Bombay in 1912 to Parsi parents, Jehangir and Ratimai Gandhi. Following his father’s death, he moved with his mother to Allahabad to live with his maternal aunt, a surgeon. He studied at Vidya Mandir High School and Ewing Christian College before attending the London School of Economics, where he earned a B.Sc. degree. He abandoned his studies to join the Indian independence movement, becoming involved with the Nehru family and adopting the surname ‘Gandhi’ as a mark of respect for Mahatma Gandhi.

Feroze was actively involved in the freedom struggle, participating in the Vanar Sena and being imprisoned multiple times for his involvement in protests and campaigns, including nineteen months in jail alongside future Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri. He developed a close relationship with Kamala Nehru and, later, with her daughter Indira. Initially, Indira’s mother rejected his marriage proposal as she was too young, but they eventually married in 1942 in an Adi Dharam Hindu ceremony. The couple was arrested during the Quit India Movement shortly after their wedding and Feroze spent a year in prison.

Following India’s independence, Feroze became the managing director of *The National Herald*, a newspaper founded by Jawaharlal Nehru. He entered politics and was elected to the Lok Sabha representing Rae Bareli in 1952, with Indira playing a key role in his campaign. He quickly established himself as a forceful and independent voice in parliament, unafraid to criticize even his father-in-law’s government.

Feroze became known for exposing financial irregularities and corruption within Indian business and government. In 1955, he revealed a scheme involving Ram Kishan Dalmia, exposing money laundering and misuse of public funds. He later brought to light the Haridas Mundhra scandal in 1958, which involved the Life Insurance Corporation of India and led to the resignation of the Finance Minister, T.T. Krishnamachari. He championed nationalization, suggesting the takeover of companies like TELCO, a move that caused some controversy within the Parsi community.

He suffered a heart attack in 1958 while Indira was on a state visit, and died in 1960 following a second heart attack in Delhi. He was cremated, and his ashes were interred in Allahabad. His widow, Indira Gandhi, later represented the Rae Bareli constituency, as did his daughter-in-law, Sonia Gandhi, for many years. A school and a thermal power station have been named in his honor, recognizing his contributions to the nation.

title: Liam Neeson
text:
Liam Neeson, born in Northern Ireland in 1952, is a highly acclaimed actor with nominations for an Academy Award, a BAFTA Award, three Golden Globes, and two Tony Awards. Recognized as one of Ireland’s greatest film actors, he was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire in 2000. Neeson began his film career in 1978 with *Pilgrim's Progress*, followed by roles in films like *Excalibur*, *The Bounty*, *The Mission*, and *Husbands and Wives*. He achieved significant recognition for his portrayal of Oskar Schindler in Steven Spielberg’s *Schindler’s List* (1993), earning an Academy Award nomination and solidifying his status as a leading man.

Throughout the 1990s, Neeson continued to take on dramatic roles in films such as *Nell*, *Rob Roy*, *Michael Collins*, and *Les Misérables*. He also ventured into blockbuster cinema, playing Qui-Gon Jinn in *Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace*, Ra’s al Ghul in *Batman Begins*, and Aslan in *The Chronicles of Narnia* trilogy.  His filmography includes diverse projects like *Gangs of New York*, *Love Actually*, *Kinsey*, *Chloe*, *Silence*, and *A Monster Calls*. 

A turning point in his career came in 2009 when he began to be recognized as an action star with *Taken* and subsequent action thrillers like *The A-Team*, *The Grey*, *Wrath of the Titans*, *A Walk Among the Tombstones*, and *Cold Pursuit*. He developed a fruitful working relationship with director Jaume Collet-Serra, appearing in four of his films: *Unknown*, *Non-Stop*, *Run All Night*, and *The Commuter*. 

Prior to his film success, Neeson spent two years with the Lyric Players' Theatre in Belfast starting in 1976. He also had a notable stage career in New York, receiving Tony Award nominations for his performances in revivals of Eugene O'Neill's *Anna Christie* and Arthur Miller's *The Crucible*. He also portrayed Oscar Wilde in David Hare’s *The Judas Kiss*.

Born in Ballymena, County Antrim, Neeson grew up Catholic in a predominantly Protestant area, an experience he described as cautious. He attended St Patrick's College and later briefly attended Queen's University Belfast before working at Guinness Brewery.  His early interest in acting was sparked, surprisingly, by observing the theatrical presence of Ian Paisley. Before dedicating himself to acting, he even briefly pursued a career in football. 

Neeson's path to acting included a period of casual labor and teacher training before joining the Lyric Players Theatre. He gained experience in Dublin with the Project Arts Centre and the Abbey Theatre, appearing in productions like Brian Friel’s *Translations*.
