His breakthrough role in film came with *Excalibur*, leading to a move to London and eventual success in Hollywood.  His performance in *Schindler’s List* cemented his acclaim, and he continued to balance mainstream and independent projects, establishing himself as a versatile and respected actor.

title: D. B. Nihalsinghe
text:
D. B. Nihalsinghe, born on May 27, 1939, and passing away on April 21, 2016, was a highly influential figure in Sri Lankan cinema and television. He excelled as a film director, cinematographer, editor, producer, administrator, and educator, and is considered a pioneer in professional television production in Sri Lanka. He introduced colour teledramas to both Sri Lanka and South Asia with *Dimuthu Muthu* in 1979. 

Nihalsinghe's early life showed an initial interest in a military career, but he quickly gravitated towards filmmaking. He received a 16mm Bolex cine camera as a gift after completing his SSC examinations. He studied Economics at the University of Ceylon, Peradeniya, where he also worked on the camera for the student documentary *Niyanada Rata*. After university, he began his professional career as a cameraman for the Australian Broadcasting Corporation in Colombo and later for Hearst Metrotone News, based in Vietnam covering the war.

Returning to Sri Lanka, Nihalsinghe’s film work began with *Sath Samudura*, where he introduced a fluid, newsreel-style approach to cinematography, departing from the then-prevalent static Indian studio style. He earned the Cardiff Commonwealth Film Festival award for his first film, *Bakhti*. He is best known for *Welikathara*, Sri Lanka’s first Cinemascope film and the second in South Asia, which was also recognized among the ten best Sri Lankan films with a Presidential Award. *Maldeniye Simiyon* brought Anoja Weerasinghe the Best Actress award at the New Delhi International Film Festival, while *Kelimadala* garnered a record number of national awards upon its release. *Ridi Nimanaya* is another of his noteworthy films.

Beyond filmmaking, Nihalsinghe held significant administrative roles. He became the youngest Director of the Ceylon Government Film Unit at age 29 and later served as the founding Chief Executive Officer and General Manager of the State Film Corporation from 1972 to 1978. During his tenure at the Film Corporation, he implemented initiatives that dramatically increased domestic film attendance, raising it from 30 million to 74.4 million annually and boosting the local film share of screen time. He also spearheaded the transition from 120 film to 35mm still film for national identification purposes. 

His contributions were internationally recognized. He was awarded the KalaKeerthi national honour and became a Life Fellow of the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (SMPTE), the sole Sri Lankan and South Asian to receive this distinction. The British Kinematograph, Sound and Television Society also made him a Fellow. In 1979, he founded Tele-Cine Limited, pioneering professional colour television production in South Asia and directing *Dimuthu Muthu*, considered the first television drama series in the region. Later in his career, he worked in Hong Kong and Malaysia, training numerous individuals in film and television production. He held advanced degrees including an MA in Film Studies and a PhD in Public Enterprises.

title: Joji (musician)
text:
George Kusunoki Miller, known professionally as Joji, was born in Osaka, Japan in 1993 to an Australian father and a Japanese mother. He attended Canadian Academy in Kobe, Japan, graduating in 2012 before moving to the United States to study at the New York Institute of Technology, earning a Bachelor of Fine Arts degree in 2016. Before his music career, Miller gained prominence on YouTube, beginning with a channel in 2006 showing him breakdancing. He later created the channels DizastaMusic, TVFilthyFrank, and TooDamnFilthy, achieving viral success with his character Filthy Frank and related comedy, including the persona Pink Guy. This comedy incorporated shock humor, hip-hop, challenges, and ukulele performances. He even played a role in popularizing the “Harlem Shake” internet meme.

Miller released two studio albums and an extended play as Pink Guy between 2014 and 2017 – *Pink Guy*, *Pink Season*, and *Pink Season: The Prophecy*. However, in late 2017, he ceased production of all Filthy Frank-related content, including Pink Guy, due to health concerns and a desire to focus on a more serious musical path. He had initially intended to pursue music alongside his YouTube work, even stating he started his channel to promote his music, but the comedy content overshadowed his musical aspirations.

Transitioning to the name Joji, derived from the Japanese pronunciation of his first name, Miller signed with 88Rising and 12Tone Music Group. He released his debut EP, *In Tongues*, in 2017 and followed with the studio albums *Ballads 1* (2018) and *Nectar* (2020). Both *Ballads 1* and *Nectar* reached number three on the Billboard 200 chart, featuring singles like "Slow Dancing in the Dark" and "Sanctuary". His 2022 single, "Glimpse of Us," became his most successful track, reaching number eight on the Billboard Hot 100 and topping the ARIA Charts, preceding his album *Smithereens*.

Joji’s musical style is a blend of R&B, lo-fi, and trip-hop, with influences ranging from James Blake and Radiohead to boom bap instrumentals. He describes his work as “dark love songs.” Throughout his career, he’s embarked on several tours, including the *Ballads 1 Tour*, *Nectar: The Finale*, *Smithereens Tour* and the ongoing *Pandemonium* tour. His early web-show contributed significantly to internet culture, notably kickstarting the Harlem Shake meme. He also released an unreleased album titled *Chloe Burbank: Volume 1*.

title: Shigeru Fukudome
text:
Shigeru Fukudome was a Japanese admiral who served as Chief of Staff of the Imperial Japanese Navy during World War II. Born in 1891, he graduated from the Imperial Japanese Naval Academy in 1912, placing eighth in his class of 144. His early naval career involved service aboard various ships including cruisers like the Soya, Izumo, and Kashima, and battleships such as Satsuma and Hizen. He progressed through the ranks, attending torpedo and naval artillery schools, and serving as a navigator on destroyers and cruisers. 

He continued to climb the ranks, becoming a lieutenant commander after graduating from the Naval War College in 1924 and a commander in 1929. Fukudome held numerous staff positions throughout the 1930s, eventually becoming captain of the battleship Nagato from 1938 to 1939. He was promoted to rear admiral in November 1939 and later to vice admiral in 1942. 

During the early stages of the Pacific War, Fukudome served with the Combined Fleet, participating in aerial torpedo exercises with Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto in 1940 as part of the planning for the attack on Pearl Harbor. He later became Chief of Staff under Admiral Mineichi Koga from May 1943 to March 1944. In a remarkable and historically significant event, Fukudome was captured by Filipino guerrillas led by Lieutenant Colonel James M. Cushing in March 1944 after his plane crashed while en route to deliver the “Z plan,” Japan’s defense strategy for the Marianas Islands. This made him the first Japanese flag officer to be captured by the enemy. He was released to prevent further civilian reprisals, but the battle plans fell into American hands.

Following Koga’s death on the same night as his capture, Fukudome was appointed commander-in-chief of the 1st Combined Base Air Force and 2nd Air Fleet, operating in the Kyūshū-Okinawa-Formosa area. He later commanded forces in the Philippines and, eventually, Singapore, where he oversaw the IJN 10th Area Fleet, consisting largely of training aircraft and a few operational ships. He was largely sidelined in Singapore due to American air and sea dominance.

After the war, Fukudome was interrogated by the U.S. Navy and tasked with assisting in the repatriation of Japanese nationals from Singapore. He was later arrested and tried for war crimes relating to the execution of American airmen while in command in Singapore, and was found guilty of negligence.  He was released in 1950 and contributed to the formation of the Japanese Self-Defense Force before his death in 1971. He is buried at Tama Cemetery in Tokyo, and was portrayed in the 1970 film *Tora! Tora! Tora!* by Koji Kawamura.

title: Napoleon
text:
Napoleon Bonaparte, born Napoleone di Buonaparte in Corsica in 1769, rose from relative obscurity to become one of the most significant figures in European history. His family, of Italian noble descent, moved to mainland France when he was young, and he was commissioned as an officer in the French Royal Army in 1785. He initially supported the French Revolution, even promoting its ideals in Corsica, and rapidly ascended through the ranks, gaining recognition for his successful siege of Toulon in 1793 and for suppressing a royalist uprising in Paris in 1795.

His military prowess truly emerged during the War of the First Coalition in 1796, where he led a campaign in Italy against Austria and its allies, achieving decisive victories that cemented his status as a national hero. This success was followed by an expedition to Egypt and Syria in 1798, undertaken as a means to disrupt British trade routes and further his political ambitions. In 1799, he seized power in France through the Coup of 18 Brumaire, becoming First Consul of the Republic. He consolidated his control with the victory at the Battle of Marengo in 1800, securing France’s position in the War of the Second Coalition, and later sold the Louisiana Territory to the United States in 1803. 

Napoleon’s ambition culminated in his self-coronation as Emperor of the French in 1804. He then embarked on a series of conflicts, known as the Napoleonic Wars, dominating much of continental Europe. Major victories at Austerlitz in 1805 resulted in the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire, and at Jena-Auerstedt in 1806, he defeated Prussia. He installed his brother Joseph as King of Spain in 1808, sparking the Peninsular War. Further victories followed at Wagram in 1809, but his disastrous invasion of Russia in 1812, marked by a devastating retreat from Moscow, proved to be a turning point. 

Following defeats at the Battle of Leipzig in 1813, Napoleon was forced to abdicate in 1814 and was exiled to the island of Elba.  In a remarkable return, he escaped Elba in 1815 and briefly regained control of France, initiating the period known as the Hundred Days. This final chapter ended with his definitive defeat at the Battle of Waterloo in June 1815. He was then exiled to the remote island of Saint Helena, where he died of stomach cancer in 1821 at the age of 51.

Napoleon’s legacy is complex. He is revered as a military genius, and his tactics continue to be studied. He instituted significant legal and administrative reforms, including the Napoleonic Code, which modernized laws and centralized state power. He abolished feudalism, emancipated religious minorities, and established a public education system. However, he is also criticized for the immense loss of life caused by his wars, his looting of conquered lands, his suppression of free speech, and the reinstatement of slavery in French colonies (with the exception of Haiti). His reign saw a curtailment of representative government and the violent repression of opposition.

title: Rory Byrne
text:
Rory Byrne, born in 1944, is a South African engineer and car designer renowned for his success in Formula One, where his designs have secured ninety-nine Grand Prix wins, seven constructors’ titles, and seven drivers’ championships. He is considered the third most successful Formula One designer, trailing only Adrian Newey and Colin Chapman.

Byrne’s initial interest in motorsport began during his time at Witwatersrand University. After graduating in 1964 with a chemistry degree, he worked in that field but continued to pursue his passion for racing, eventually co-founding a performance car parts company called Auto Drag and Speed Den in Johannesburg. It was here he began designing racing cars, leveraging his mathematical skills despite lacking formal engineering training, and achieved success with a competitive Formula Ford racer in 1972.

He moved to England in 1972 to further his career, working with Royale Formula Ford, eventually becoming their designer for four years. A connection with Ted Toleman led to a position as designer for Toleman’s Formula 2 team, culminating in a championship win in 1980 and paving the way for the team’s entry into Formula One.

The first Formula One car designed by Byrne, the TG181, debuted in 1981. After a period of development, the team, later purchased by Benetton, achieved its first win in 1986 with Gerhard Berger. The Benetton years saw further race victories, but a consistent championship challenge proved elusive until the arrival of Michael Schumacher. Byrne’s B193 car in 1993 was a significant technical leap forward, and the subsequent B194 in 1994 proved dominant, although controversy surrounded the team’s success. Benetton secured both the drivers' and constructors' titles in 1995, fulfilling a long-held ambition for Byrne, who initially announced his retirement for 1996.

However, Byrne was lured out of retirement by Ferrari and Ross Brawn to join the Italian team in 1996, replacing John Barnard as chief designer. This marked the beginning of a period of unprecedented success. Ferrari became competitive again, and Byrne’s designs spearheaded a run of five consecutive drivers’ championships for Michael Schumacher and six consecutive constructors' championships from 1999 to 2004. He retired from his chief designer role at the end of 2006, transitioning to a consultancy position for two years.

Byrne has continued to contribute to Ferrari in an advisory capacity, assisting with car development including the F2012, LaFerrari, the 2014 car, and more recently the F1-75 (2022), SF-23 (2023) and SF-24 (2024), with his contract being renewed multiple times. Outside of Formula One, he currently works as a Special Engineering Advisor for Discovery Insure in South Africa, focusing on road safety.

title: Vladimir Lenin
text:
Vladimir Lenin, born Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov in 1870, was a pivotal figure in 20th-century history, leading the Bolsheviks and establishing the first socialist state. He served as the first head of government of Soviet Russia from 1917 until his death in 1924, and subsequently of the Soviet Union until 1924. His adaptation of Marxist theory, known as Leninism, became a dominant force in the communist movement internationally. 

Lenin’s path to revolution began with personal tragedy. After his father, a dedicated educator who rose to middle-class status from a lower-class background, died in 1886, his older brother, Alexander, became involved in a plot to assassinate the Tsar and was executed in 1887. This profoundly impacted Lenin, leading him to embrace revolutionary socialist politics. He was expelled from Kazan University for protesting and later earned a law degree before becoming a Marxist activist in Saint Petersburg.  His early activism led to arrest and a three-year exile to Siberia in 1897, after which he moved to Western Europe, becoming a leading figure within the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party.

A key moment came in 1903 when the party split between Lenin’s Bolshevik faction and the Mensheviks. Lenin advocated for a tightly organized “vanguard party” to lead the proletariat in overthrowing capitalism, a concept central to Leninism. He briefly returned to Russia during the unrest of 1905. During World War I, he campaigned for the war’s transformation into a Europe-wide proletarian revolution. Following the February Revolution of 1917, which overthrew Tsar Nicholas II, Lenin returned to Russia and spearheaded the October Revolution, successfully overthrowing the Provisional Government and establishing Bolshevik rule.

Lenin’s government implemented radical changes, abolishing private land ownership, nationalizing major industries and banks, and withdrawing Russia from World War I through the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk. He also sought to promote global revolution through the Communist International. The Bolsheviks, initially in a coalition, eventually consolidated power during the Russian Civil War, employing a brutal policy known as the Red Terror to suppress opposition. Facing famine and unrest, Lenin introduced the New Economic Policy in 1921, a temporary retreat from strict communism designed to stabilize the economy. The Red Army ultimately prevailed in the Civil War, leading to the formation of the Soviet Union in 1922, though some nations, like Poland, gained independence.

Lenin suffered a series of strokes beginning in 1922, which incapacitated him before his death in 1924. His death triggered a power struggle within the Communist Party, ultimately resulting in Joseph Stalin’s ascent to power.  After his death, Lenin became the subject of a widespread personality cult within the Soviet Union, becoming an ideological figurehead under Stalin. He remains a controversial figure, praised by some for establishing a revolutionary government and criticized by others for establishing a repressive dictatorship responsible for mass killings. Despite the debate, he is widely considered one of the most influential figures of the 20th century.

title: Hiren Gohain
text:
Hiren Gohain, born in 1939, is a prominent figure from Assam, recognized as a polymath with expertise spanning literature, social science, and criticism. His academic journey began at Cotton College, followed by studies at Presidency College, Calcutta, and Delhi University, where he earned his post-graduation in English literature. He then pursued doctoral research at Cambridge University, focusing on ‘Paradise Lost and the 17th Century Crisis’, a work later published as ‘Tradition and Paradise Lost: A Heretical View’ and praised for its innovative approach. He eventually returned to India and became a professor in the Department of English at Gauhati University.

Gohain is credited with introducing Anglo-American New Criticism to the study of Assamese and Indian literature. Initially holding radical ideologies while in Cambridge, he later embraced Marxism and integrated the ideas of thinkers such as György Lukács and Antonio Gramsci into Assamese literary criticism. He has authored numerous significant books in Assamese, including ‘Sahityar Satya,’ ‘Sahitya Aru Chetana’, and ‘Asomiya Jatiya Jibanat Mahapurushiya Paramapara,’ along with four volumes of memoirs that incorporate social and historical observations. He regularly contributes to publications like *Economic and Political Weekly*, *Frontier*, and journals from institutions such as the Indian Institute of Advanced Studies and the Centre for English and Foreign Languages, Shillong, and also writes columns for regional and national newspapers.

Beyond literary pursuits, Gohain has engaged with pressing socio-political issues in Assam. His book, ‘Assam A Burning Question,’ compiles essays examining the crises during the Assam Movement and the period of extremism in the 1980s. More recently, he was involved in mediating peace talks between the Indian government and the United Liberation Front of Asom (ULFA). He also served as the founder president of the Asomiya Sahitya Sanmilani. Gohain’s contributions were formally recognized with the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1989 for his work on Sankardev. 

He is known for his outspoken views on contemporary issues, being a critic of both Assamese nationalism and Hindutva extremism. Gohain actively opposed the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, comparing its exclusion of Muslims to the Nazi persecution of Jews. He is also a vocal critic of Narendra Modi and participated in protests against the CAA, including one organized by the All Assam Journalists Union. His extensive body of work includes books written in both English and Assamese, covering a wide range of topics from Shakespeare to Bengali culture and the socio-political landscape of Assam.

title: Kion Smith
text:
Kion Smith, born on October 7, 1998, is a professional American football player currently signed with the Miami Dolphins of the National Football League. He plays the position of offensive tackle. Smith’s football journey began at Lumberton High School, where his senior year was unfortunately cut short by an injury that kept him sidelined for the entire season. 

Following high school, Smith attended Fayetteville State University and played college football for the Fayetteville State Broncos. During his collegiate career, he participated in a total of 20 games. However, his senior season was completely cancelled as a result of the widespread disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite the shortened opportunity, he managed to attract the attention of professional scouts.

Smith entered the professional ranks after the 2021 NFL draft, going undrafted and subsequently signing with the Atlanta Falcons. He did not ultimately make the Falcons’ final 53-man roster, marking a temporary setback in his career. Shortly thereafter, on September 6, 2021, he joined the practice squad of the Miami Dolphins. 

The Dolphins organization showed continued faith in Smith’s potential, signing him to a reserve/future contract on January 11, 2022. He was briefly waived by the team on August 30, 2022, but quickly re-signed to the Dolphins’ practice squad.  He again secured a reserve/future contract with the Dolphins on January 16, 2023, indicating his ongoing development and the team’s investment in his abilities.

Unfortunately, Smith experienced a significant injury in the preseason of 2024. On August 10, 2024, it was announced that he had suffered a torn ACL, and was subsequently placed on season-ending injured reserve. This injury will prevent him from playing during the 2024 NFL season. Further information regarding his path to the NFL was documented in an article by Ron Baxley for *The Fayetteville Observer* in May 2021, detailing his progression from a walk-on tryout to signing with a professional team. Additionally, D. Orlando Ledbetter of *The Atlanta Constitution* wrote about Smith and another player attempting to transition from Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) to the NFL in August 2021.

title: Jonathan Roy
text:
Jonathan Piuze-Roy, born on March 15, 1989, is a Canadian singer and songwriter who notably comes from a family steeped in hockey history as the son of Hockey Hall of Fame goaltender Patrick Roy. While initially following in his father’s footsteps and pursuing a career in junior hockey, Roy transitioned to music in 2007 with his father’s encouragement. He has since released six studio albums throughout his career.

Roy’s upbringing was marked by a move to Colorado at age six due to his father’s trade, but he also found early artistic influence through his mother’s piano playing. He began writing poetry as a teenager, around ages 13 or 14, and soon started composing music to accompany his verses around age 16. He did play competitive hockey, even joining the Quebec Remparts at 17 while his father was the team’s coach, but simultaneously harbored musical ambitions, drawing inspiration from artists like the Backstreet Boys, John Mayer, and Ray LaMontagne. At 18, a conversation with his father solidified his decision to pursue music, rather than continue with hockey and formal education.

His early musical efforts resulted in the release of *What I’ve Become* in 2009, followed by *Found My Way* in 2010. In 2011, he released his first French-language album, *La route*, which featured a duet with Natasha St-Pier on the title track, garnering the most attention of his earlier work. Beyond music recording, Roy also took on an acting role in the 2012 revival of the musical *Don Juan*, receiving critical praise.

A pivotal moment in his career came in 2012 when his father facilitated a meeting with Corey Hart, the 1980s pop singer and head of Siena Records, an affiliate of Warner Music. Impressed by Roy’s performance of a Teddy Thompson song, Hart signed him to the label. This partnership led to a successful holiday collaboration in 2016, a duet with Hart on the Chris Rea song "Driving Home for Christmas." 

Roy's major-label debut, *Mr. Optimist Blues*, arrived in 2017 on Siena Records, with Hart serving as executive producer and contributing to the songwriting. The album was described as a blend of contemporary pop, reggae, and influences from artists like Ed Sheeran, Paolo Nutini, and Bob Marley. He frequently collaborates with Kim Richardson, utilizing her talents as a duet partner or backing vocalist. More recently, in 2023, Roy contributed to a charity single, joining an all-star lineup for Serena Ryder’s “What I Wouldn’t Do,” benefiting youth mental health initiatives. He is currently based in Toronto.

title: William G. Angel
text:
William Gardner Angel was born in Rhode Island in 1790 and spent much of his life in New York, becoming a lawyer, politician, and judge. His family moved to a farm in Richfield, New York, in 1792, where he received a basic education while helping with farm work, and later attended Dr. Buckingham’s Grammar School. He briefly pursued the study of medicine before turning to law.

Angel began his legal career in an unconventional way. He impressed a lawyer, William Dowse, while serving as a witness in a trial and was subsequently hired as a handyman. During this time, he read law and worked as a clerk in Dowse’s office. Following Dowse’s death, Angel continued his legal studies with Farrand Stranahan, and eventually entered into a partnership with Luther Elderkin in 1817. This partnership was short-lived, however, as Elderkin absconded with client funds, leaving Angel responsible for reimbursing them. He then established his own practice in Burlington, New York, where he practiced law until 1833. Prior to his congressional service, he served as the Surrogate of Otsego County from 1821 to 1824.

Angel served three terms in the U.S. House of Representatives, representing New York’s 13th congressional district from 1825 to 1827 and again from 1829 to 1833 as a Jacksonian Democrat. After leaving Congress, he relocated to Hammondsport and re-entered the practice of law, first in partnership with Morris Brown. He later mentored and partnered with Martin Grover, and then with his son, Wilkes Angel, practicing in Angelica, New York, from 1835 to 1843 and 1843 to 1847 respectively. He was also a delegate to the New York State Constitutional Convention in 1846. 

In 1847, Angel was appointed as the First Judge and Surrogate of the Allegany County Court, a position he held until 1851. He was married twice, first to Emily P. English in 1812 with whom he had several children including William P. and Wilkes Angel, and later to Clarissa English, with whom he had ten children, including James R. Angel and Texas Angel, who himself became a lawyer and political figure in Idaho. William G. Angel died in Angelica, New York, in August of 1858 and is buried in the Until the Day Dawn Cemetery.

title: F. Gwynplaine MacIntyre
text:
Fergus Gwynplaine MacIntyre, born Paul Grant Jeffery in 1956 and known to many as Froggy, was a New York City-based writer and artist who died in 2010. He worked across multiple genres, publishing science fiction, fantasy, horror, and mystery stories in magazines like *Weird Tales*, *Analog*, and *Asimov’s Science Fiction*, as well as contributing to various anthologies. He authored the novel *The Woman Between the Worlds* and a collection of humorous pieces titled *MacIntyre’s Improbable Bestiary*. Beyond his published work, MacIntyre also wrote as a ghostwriter, including a novel in the Tom Swift IV series, *The DNA Disaster*, credited to Victor Appleton, though acknowledged by MacIntyre himself.

MacIntyre’s personal history was notably complex and largely fabricated. Born to Grant Turner Peter Jeffery and Mathilde Barbara Mantano, he created elaborate stories about his origins, claiming to be orphaned and raised in Australia, including time in a labour camp. He adopted different aliases throughout his life, including Timothy C. Allen and Oleg V. Bredikhine. However, acquaintances remembered him speaking with a New York accent even in his twenties, and his brother later confirmed after his death that many of the stories he told about his past were untrue, though the reasons remained undisclosed. He derived the “Gwynplaine” portion of his name from the protagonist of Victor Hugo’s *The Man Who Laughs*, identifying with the character’s permanently fixed smile.

Professionally, MacIntyre’s career had unusual turns. In the 1970s, he worked for a publisher of pornographic novels, tasked with writing entire books in a single week. He was known for his linguistic creativity, coining new words and reviving obscure ones, and even gained the acknowledgement of William Safire for a neologism he created. He also contributed illustrations to *Analog* and wrote numerous book reviews for *The Magazine of Fantasy & Science Fiction*. He claimed to have contributed significantly to a documentary about Theda Bara, but was only credited with “Special Thanks.”

MacIntyre’s life was also marked by legal trouble and mental health struggles. In 2000, he was arrested and pleaded guilty to misdemeanor assault after a violent attack on a neighbor. Prior to his death, he experienced increasing depression, referencing a troubled childhood and suicidal thoughts in mass emails to friends. He also faced financial hardship and health issues. 

He died in a fire in his Brooklyn apartment in June 2010, after setting it ablaze. The fire required sixty firefighters to extinguish. He had posted a final review on the Internet Movie Database the day before, framing it as his last. MacIntyre was also known for writing over 1,600 often-fabricated reviews on IMDb, sometimes openly admitting to making them up for films he hadn’t seen. His brother’s revelation about the fabricated nature of his life story came after his death, adding a final layer of mystery to a life already filled with invention and complexity.

title: Rii Sen
text:
Rii Sen, born Rituparna Sen, is an Indian actress primarily known for her work in Bengali cinema, particularly within the realm of alternative filmmaking. She began her career as a freelance model and television actress, appearing in series like *Ekhane Akash Neel*, *Jai Kali Kalkattawali*, and *Trinayani*. While her debut film was *Tepantorer Mathe*, it was never released due to its explicit content. Sen gained wider public recognition as a contestant on *Bigg Boss Bangla* Season 2, finishing as the second runner-up.

Her film career gained momentum with roles in films like *Bissh*, *Gandu*, and *Cosmic Sex*, each of which pushed boundaries and often involved challenging subject matter. In *Bissh*, she played the complex character of Anushka, a role she found deeply immersive. *Gandu* notably featured Sen in a lead role requiring frontal nudity, with the director stating she was the only actress in the Bengali film industry capable of handling the part. Reviews praised her confidence in the film's explicit scenes. She also had a minor role in Srijit Mukherji’s *Autograph*.

Sen continued to take on diverse roles in films such as *Koyekti Meyer Golpo*, where she portrayed a gangster’s wife, and *Cosmic Sex*, a film exploring sexual self-discovery. It was for her performance in *Cosmic Sex* that she received a Best Actress award at Osian's Cinefan Festival of Asian and Arab Cinema in 2012. She also appeared in *Tasher Desh*, a modern adaptation of a Rabindranath Tagore play.  Further projects included *Byanka Prithibi* and the anticipated *LUDO*, where she was set to portray a previously unseen role in Indian cinema.

Sen has been recognized as a significant figure in alternative Bengali cinema, often tackling roles that challenge societal norms. She openly discusses her views on sexuality and its place in filmmaking, aiming to explore it “to the borderline where it becomes extreme and dangerous.” She acknowledges being one of the first Indian actresses to perform full frontal nudity on screen, predating Paoli Dam’s widely publicized work by six months, and embraces using her body as a tool for artistic expression and capturing a moment in time.  



Her filmography also includes several documentary appearances, like *Love in India* and *Many Stories of Love and Hate*. Throughout her career, she has also continued to work in television, with roles in series like *Durga Durgeshwari* and *Sanjher Baati*.

title: Marli Renfro
text:
Marli Renfro, born in Los Angeles, California on April 3, 1938, is an American former showgirl, model, Playboy cover girl, and actress. She is best known for her work as the body double for Janet Leigh in Alfred Hitchcock’s iconic 1960 film, *Psycho*. Renfro received $500 for her contribution to the film, a scene now considered one of the most famous in cinematic history, characterized by its rapid 50+ cuts within three minutes of screen time and a six-day filming schedule. While the scene implies nudity, none is actually shown; Hitchcock initially claimed only Janet Leigh appeared in the shower, later admitting Renfro was used for shots where Leigh's face wasn’t visible. Leigh herself maintained she performed all the shower footage, with Renfro only appearing in a cut overhead shot. 

Before her work on *Psycho*, Renfro had a career appearing in a variety of men’s magazines, including *Ace*, *Adam*, *Beau*, *Dude*, *Escapade*, *Follies*, *Gala*, and *Modern Man*. She was featured on the cover of the September 1960 issue of *Playboy* and also worked as a showgirl in Las Vegas and a Playboy Bunny. Renfro was described as a “free spirit” with a lifelong dedication to nudism, and she reportedly was not uncomfortable with performing nude.

Following *Psycho*, Renfro appeared in Francis Ford Coppola’s 1962 film, *Tonight for Sure*. Decades later, she was again connected to the film through Alexandre O. Philippe’s 2017 documentary, *78/52*, which examines *Psycho* and, specifically, the shower scene.

A significant degree of confusion surrounded Renfro’s involvement with *Psycho* due to the tragic death of Myra Davis, who served as Janet Leigh’s stand-in for lighting during filming. In 1988, Davis was murdered, and media outlets mistakenly reported that she was Leigh’s body double, and even claimed she provided the voice for Norman Bates’ mother—a role actually voiced by Virginia Gregg and Jeanette Nolan. Author Don Lasseter further fueled the confusion in his 2002 book, *Body Double*, by incorrectly stating that Davis and Renfro were the same person, leading to reports of Renfro’s death. 

This misinformation prompted author Robert Graysmith, fascinated by Renfro, to investigate. He discovered she was alive and living in California, having been informed by Davis's granddaughter that Davis wouldn’t have engaged in nude work. He documented his findings in his 2010 book, *The Girl in Alfred Hitchcock's Shower*, detailing Renfro’s role in *Psycho* and correcting the narrative surrounding Davis’s death. Renfro is now known as Marli Renfro Peterson and has resided in the Mojave Desert since 1970.

title: Vujadin Savić
text:
Vujadin Savić, born on July 1st, 1990, is a Serbian football coach and former player who played as a centre-back. He began his football journey at Red Star Belgrade at the age of eight, progressing through their youth system before playing for Rad between 2007 and 2009. He then returned to Red Star, playing for the first team until 2010 when he moved to France to join Bordeaux. A loan spell at Dynamo Dresden followed in January 2012 for the remainder of the 2011–12 season.

In 2015, Savić signed with English Championship club Watford, but was released after their promotion to the Premier League without making any appearances. He then found success with Sheriff Tiraspol, playing 40 games and scoring 4 goals across all competitions over two seasons, including a notable bicycle kick goal against Zaria Bălți in 2015. 

He returned to Red Star Belgrade in June 2017, signing a two-year contract. During his time there, Red Star achieved a historic run to the 2018 Europa League knockout phase, and had their first season in 26 years surviving the group stage of a UEFA competition. He formed strong defensive partnerships with players like Srđan Babić and Damien Le Tallec, contributing to a strong defensive record in the Europa League. He was recognized for his performances by being named to the Serbian SuperLiga Team of the Season for 2017–18. Savić also played a key role in Red Star’s first ever qualification for the UEFA Champions League, captaining the team in several matches in the absence of Nenad Milijaš, even keeping clean sheets against Napoli and Liverpool. An injury sustained during a match against Liverpool at Anfield sidelined him for further games.

In July 2019, Savić moved to Cypriot club APOEL on a free transfer, with a clause stipulating Red Star would receive a portion of any future transfer fee. He signed a three-year contract but underwent groin surgery shortly after joining. In February 2021, he was loaned to Slovenian side Olimpija Ljubljana for the remainder of the season.

Savić has also represented Serbia at the Under-21 level, participating in the 2009 UEFA European Under-21 Championship. He received a call-up to the senior national team in March 2018, but was unable to make his debut due to injury. He is the son of former Serbian footballer Dušan Savić, and has four children with actress Mirka Vasiljević. He shares his name with Serbian coach Vujadin Boškov and is nicknamed Giška. 

Throughout his career, Savić has won several honors including two Serbian SuperLiga titles and the Serbian Cup with Red Star Belgrade, two National Division titles, a Moldovan Cup, and a Moldovan Super Cup with Sheriff Tiraspol, the Cyprus Super Cup with APOEL, and the Slovenian Cup with Olimpija Ljubljana.

title: Fidel Castro
text:
Fidel Alejandro Castro Ruz, born in 1926, was a Cuban politician and revolutionary who led Cuba from 1959 to 2008, first as prime minister and later as president. A Marxist-Leninist and Cuban nationalist, he transformed Cuba into a one-party communist state, nationalizing industries and implementing socialist reforms. His life was marked by a long struggle against US influence and a dedication to anti-imperialist ideals.

Born to a wealthy farming family, Castro became politically active while studying law at the University of Havana, embracing leftist ideologies. He participated in rebellions in the Dominican Republic and Colombia before turning his attention to overthrowing Cuban President Fulgencio Batista. A 1953 attack on the Moncada Barracks failed, leading to Castro’s imprisonment. While incarcerated, he penned “History Will Absolve Me,” a speech outlining his revolutionary ideals and criticizing Batista’s regime. 

Following his release, Castro went to Mexico where he formed the 26th of July Movement with his brother Raúl and Ernesto “Che” Guevara. They returned to Cuba and waged a guerrilla war from the Sierra Maestra mountains, ultimately overthrowing Batista in 1959. As prime minister, Castro implemented sweeping changes, leading to opposition from the United States which attempted to remove him through assassination attempts, an economic embargo, and the failed Bay of Pigs invasion. In response, Castro aligned with the Soviet Union, culminating in the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis when Soviet nuclear weapons were stationed on the island.

Castro’s government established Cuba as the first communist state in the Western Hemisphere, centralizing economic planning and expanding healthcare and education, but also suppressing dissent and controlling the press. He actively supported revolutionary movements in other countries, including Chile, Nicaragua, Grenada, and provided aid to conflicts in Africa. Cuba’s international profile grew through Castro’s leadership of the Non-Aligned Movement and the promotion of Cuban medical internationalism. 

The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 brought economic hardship to Cuba, known as the “Special Period,” during which Castro embraced environmentalist and anti-globalization ideas. He later forged alliances with Latin American leaders like Hugo Chávez of Venezuela. In 2006, Castro gradually transferred power to his brother Raúl, who formally succeeded him as president in 2008. 

Throughout his long rule, Castro remained a polarizing figure. Supporters lauded him as a champion of socialism, anti-imperialism, and social justice, while critics condemned him as a dictator responsible for human rights abuses and economic hardship. He was the longest-serving non-royal head of state in the 20th and 21st centuries, leaving behind a complex legacy that continues to be debated.

title: Stephen J. Mackwell
text:
Stephen J. Mackwell is a geophysicist whose research focuses on the physical, chemical, and mechanical properties of geological materials. His work investigates fluid transport within rocks, both in Earth's mantle and crust, and how these fluids affect the rocks’ mechanical behavior. He is a prolific author, having published over 80 articles in international scientific journals and also served as an editor of a book concerning the comparative climates of terrestrial planets, published by the University of Arizona Press in 2013.

Mackwell’s academic foundation began with a Bachelor of Science degree in Physics and Mathematics from the University of Canterbury in New Zealand, earned in 1978. He continued at Canterbury, completing a Master of Science in Physics the following year, with a thesis focused on excitation temperatures of late-type stars. He also obtained a Diploma of Education from Christchurch Teachers College in 1979. He then pursued and received a Ph.D. in Geophysics from the Australian National University in 1985, with his dissertation examining the diffusion and weakening effects of water in quartz and olivine.

His early career included a postdoctoral fellowship at Cornell University from 1984 to 1987. He then joined Pennsylvania State University as an assistant professor in 1987, and was promoted to associate professor of geosciences in 1992. A period of public service followed, serving as program director for geophysics at the National Science Foundation from 1993 to 1994, and as an Alexander von Humboldt Fellow at the Bayerisches Geoinstitut in Germany in 1996. In 1998, he became a full professor of experimental geophysics at the Bayerisches Geoinstitut, and subsequently its director from 2000 to 2002.

In late 2002, Mackwell moved back to the United States to become director of the Lunar and Planetary Institute (LPI) in Houston, Texas, a division of the Universities Space Research Association (USRA). Alongside this role, he managed USRA’s Houston facility and oversaw educational programs. He transitioned to the role of USRA Corporate Director of Science Programs in 2016, when Louise Prockter became Director of the LPI. He has remained active in the scientific community through editorial roles with journals like *Geophysical Research Letters* and *Physics and Chemistry of Minerals*, and participation in Planetary Science Decadal Survey activities. He currently holds adjunct professorships at Rice University, the University of Minnesota, and the University of Maryland – College Park. 

From 2019 to 2021, Mackwell served as Deputy Executive Officer of the American Institute of Physics. More recently, from April 2022 to March 2025, he held positions at the National Science Foundation, first as Section Head for Disciplinary Programs and then as Acting Deputy Division Director. Throughout his career, Mackwell has received numerous accolades, including fellowships from the American Association for the Advancement of Science and the American Geophysical Union, and the naming of asteroid 5292 Mackwell in his honor in 2016.

title: Gubby Allen
text:
Sir George Oswald Browning “Gubby” Allen was a prominent cricketer and influential administrator, born in Australia in 1902 but raised in England from the age of six. He captained England in eleven Test matches and was known as a fast bowler and hard-hitting lower-order batsman, primarily playing first-class cricket for Middlesex and Cambridge University. His early life included education at Eton College, where he developed his cricketing talent despite battling rib injuries that plagued his career. He was accepted to Trinity College, Cambridge, and continued to excel, facing some early accusations of illegal bowling that were later dismissed. 

Allen's first-class career began with appearances for Middlesex in 1921, alongside his university matches. His time at Cambridge was marked by success, including a nine-wicket haul against Winchester and a crucial performance against Oxford in the University Match, earning him a blue. However, academic shortcomings led to a period of rustication, and he returned to Middlesex. He found balancing cricket with a full-time job in the City of London challenging, initially working for the Royal Exchange Assurance Corporation and later for Debenhams, which impacted his availability for matches. He spent time working in France, where he demonstrated financial acumen by identifying and warning against a risky business venture.

Despite the difficulties of balancing work and cricket, Allen continued to impress, showcasing his all-round abilities with both bat and ball. He gained recognition with the Gentlemen's team and was frequently mentioned as a potential England player, though selection was often delayed. He finally debuted for England in 1930, filling in for an injured Harold Larwood, but faced criticism in the press regarding his Australian birth. Allen’s bowling was often described as erratic but capable of devastating spells, and he frequently delivered crucial runs when his team was under pressure. A particularly memorable performance came in 1929 when he took all ten wickets for Middlesex against Lancashire at Lord’s.

Allen became England captain in 1936, leading the team on the 1936–37 tour of Australia, which England narrowly lost 3-2 after initially winning the first two matches. He continued to play intermittently for Middlesex following World War II, in which he served in military intelligence, and made a final Test appearance as captain in the West Indies in 1947-48. His career was often hampered by his work commitments and the recurring rib injury. 

As his playing career wound down, Allen transitioned into cricket administration, becoming a highly influential figure within the Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC). He played a key role in developing an MCC coaching manual and worked to eliminate illegal bowling actions. He served as chairman of the England selectors from 1955 to 1961, overseeing a period of success in English cricket alongside captain Peter May. He later became MCC president in 1963 and treasurer the following year, where he became embroiled in the controversial D’Oliveira affair. He was knighted in 1986 and lived near Lord’s until his death in 1989 at the age of 87.

title: Funke Abimbola
text:
Funke Abimbola is a Nigerian-born businesswoman and lawyer who is a prominent advocate for diversity, particularly within the UK legal profession. Her journey began with a childhood in a family of medical doctors, but a fear of pain and blood steered her away from following in their footsteps. She was educated at Burgess Hill Girls before pursuing a law degree at Newcastle University, after which she returned to Nigeria to pass the Nigerian Bar examination, gaining experience with the firm F. O. Akinrele & Co.

Upon returning to the UK in the mid-1990s, Abimbola faced initial difficulty securing an entry-level legal position. Undeterred, she proactively contacted numerous law firms and in-house legal teams, ultimately securing a role that allowed her to qualify as a solicitor in-house in 2000. She initially worked with Wembley Plc as a corporate/commercial lawyer before moving to Campbell Hooper. 

Her career progressed significantly with Roche UK, where she eventually became Managing Counsel for the UK and Ireland, also serving as the UK Data Protection Officer. She continued to rise within the company, becoming General Counsel and Company Secretary in December 2015, and then General Counsel and Head of Financial Compliance in January 2017, making her the most senior Black solicitor within Roche’s operations across the UK, Ireland, Gibraltar, and Malta. 

Abimbola’s path wasn't without its challenges; she recounts an interview where she was directly questioned about whether she believed her race had hindered her job search, a moment that prompted her to consider the potential impact of racial bias. Throughout her career, she has consistently championed corporate and social diversity, becoming a recognized speaker and recipient of numerous awards. 

These accolades include features in the Diversity League Table in 2013, nominations for a National Diversity Award and the Law Society Excellence Awards in 2014, and a Positive Role Model Award in 2015. Further recognition came with a ‘Point of Light’ award from the UK Prime Minister in 2016 and an M.B.E. (Member of the Order of the British Empire) from Queen Elizabeth II in 2017, both for her dedication to diversity in the legal field and her work with young people. In 2019, the University of Hertfordshire awarded her an honorary doctorate of laws, acknowledging her contributions to social and corporate diversity. She also served as a governor of Uxbridge College, London, from 2010 to 2014. Abimbola is a mother to a son currently studying Software Engineering at Newcastle University.

title: Bir Hambir
text:
Bir Hambir, also known by several other names including Veer Hambir, was the forty-ninth king of the Malla dynasty, ruling the region of Mallabhum, primarily in present-day Bankura district of West Bengal, from 1565 to 1620 AD. He was a contemporary of the Mughal emperor Akbar, and his reign was marked by a complex relationship with the expanding Mughal Empire. While he acknowledged Mughal suzerainty by paying annual tribute, he simultaneously worked to maintain the autonomy of his kingdom.

A key event in Bir Hambir’s reign was his alliance with the Mughals during Akbar’s campaign against Qutlu Khan Lohani, an Afghan ruler who had extended influence over areas including Midnapore and Bishnupur. He provided troops and advice to Mughal general Man Singh’s son, Jagat Singh, and famously rescued him from a surprise Afghan attack, solidifying the bond between Mallabhum and the Mughal Empire. This act of bravery is documented in the *Akbarnama*.

Bir Hambir’s rule took place during a period when Bengal was fragmented, with power held by various local landlords known as the Baro-Bhuyans. Though not one of the twelve himself, Bir Hambir shared their resistance to Mughal centralisation and actively defended his territory against external threats, including the Mughals. He effectively utilized military strength and strategic alliances with other regional chiefs.  He participated in conflicts to restore power to local rulers, such as the re-establishment of Raja Chhotu Roy in Karnagarh following a period of instability.

Bir Hambir’s reign saw a strengthening of the kingdom and a period of safety and security, signified by the addition of the “Dev” title to the Malla name. He led his forces to victory against Daud Khan Karrani, son of Sulaiman Khan Karrani, at the Battle of Mundamala Ghat in 1575, earning the title “Bir Hambir” for his courage and the devastating defeat of the Pathan army, so much so that the battlefield became known as Mundmalaghat due to the many corpses.

Beyond his military and political achievements, Bir Hambir was a devout follower of Vaishnavism.  A pivotal moment in his spiritual journey involved encountering devotees from Vrindavan who were robbed.  Moved by their devotion and the reading of the *Bhagavata*, he embraced Vaishnavism, generously gifting land and money to the devotees and introducing the worship of Madan Mohan to Bishnupur.

His reign also saw significant cultural development. He commissioned the construction of the Rashmancha in 1600 CE, a building used for the worship of Radha Krishna idols during the Vaishnava Ras festival.  Furthermore, the Dal Madal cannon, one of the largest ever created, was founded during his rule, showcasing the skills of local artisans like Jagannath Karmakar.

title: Avraham Eilam-Amzallag
text:
Avraham Eilam-Amzallag, born on September 28, 1941, is an Israeli musician and composer with a distinct style rooted in his background and musical training. He began his life in Casablanca, Morocco, before immigrating to Israel during his childhood. This early experience appears to have profoundly influenced his later artistic pursuits.

Eilam-Amzallag pursued formal musical education in Israel, initially focusing on the flute as his instrument of study. He later expanded his musical skillset through compositional studies at the Buchman-Mehta Music Academy in Tel Aviv, suggesting a dedication to both performance and the creation of original works. 

His career has centered around the exploration and presentation of oriental music, a genre he actively champions through the ensemble he founded. This ensemble is specifically dedicated to performing music within this tradition. However, his work isn’t simply a preservation of traditional forms; instead, Eilam-Amzallag's compositions are characterized by a unique fusion. He blends the sounds and structures of oriental Jewish music with contemporary compositional techniques, creating a sound that is both deeply connected to its cultural origins and innovative in its approach.

Although the article doesn’t detail the scope of his wider output, it does list several specific compositions. These include “Desolation,” a piece lasting three minutes and thirty-three seconds, and “(composition for flute)” which is identified as a “Mawal” and runs for five minutes and thirteen seconds. Further evidence of his work is given by “Music for flute and percussion,” a piece composed in 1975. 

Beyond the performance aspect of his musical life, Eilam-Amzallag has also engaged in the publication of his work, with “Music for flute and percussion” (1975) being a formally published composition. This indicates a desire to share his musical ideas beyond the realm of live performance and establish a lasting record of his artistry.

Within the broader context of Israeli musical culture, Eilam-Amzallag’s work is relevant to the field of Music of Israel, as noted in the "See also" section of the article, showcasing his contribution to the country's musical landscape. The article itself provides a concise overview of his life and career, establishing him as a figure who bridges tradition and innovation in Israeli music.

title: Sayuri Yamauchi
text:
Sayuri Yamauchi, born on May 28, 1956, and passing away on March 6, 2012, was a Japanese voice actress known professionally as Sayuri. Throughout her career, she lent her voice to a wide variety of characters in anime, video games, and dubbed foreign productions. She was associated with Kyu Production at one point and, at the time of her death at the age of 55, was affiliated with Aigumi. 

Yamauchi’s work spanned numerous well-known series. In anime, she voiced Vera Ronstadt in *The Big O*, Hikaru Kosaka in *The Brave Fighter of Legend Da-Garn*, and characters in the *City Hunter* franchise, including a dress store clerk and a performer in the film adaptation. She also contributed to *Crayon Shin-chan* as both Nanako Ohara and Lulu Lu Lulu, and took on the role of 0012 in *Cyborg 009*. Other notable anime roles included Satella in *Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood*, Primada, Ikumi Kaidou, and Ai Amami in *The King of Braves GaoGaiGar*, Astral in *Saint of Braves Baan Gaan*, Lady Une in *Mobile Suit Gundam Wing* and *Gundam Wing: Endless Waltz*, "Twilight" Suzuka in *Outlaw Star*, Osuzu in *Samurai Champloo*, Maya in *Shaman King* and Tiara in *Shamanic Princess*. 

In the realm of video games, Yamauchi’s voice graced titles like *Baten Kaitos Origins* where she played Gena, and *Dragon Force II* as both Bjorn and Medea. She was also involved in the *Super Robot Wars* franchise, lending her voice to characters like Ai Anami and Primada in *Super Robot Wars Alpha 2*, Ikumi Kaidou and Palus Abel in *Super Robot Wars Alpha 3*, and Ikumi Kaidoh in *Super Robot Wars T*. Further video game roles included Tomoe Kawasaki in *Robot Alchemic Drive* and Lorithia in *Xenoblade Chronicles*.

Beyond animation, Yamauchi also performed dubbing work for live-action films and television. She provided the Japanese voice for Monica Swinton (played by Frances O’Connor) in *A.I. Artificial Intelligence*, Donna Jensen (Marg Helgenberger) in *Erin Brockovich*, Trin (Melina Kanakaredes) in *The Long Kiss Goodnight*, Sadie (Sadie Frost) in *Love, Honour and Obey*, and Switch (Belinda McClory) in *The Matrix*. She also voiced characters in *Mission: Impossible*, *Pecker*, *The Sea Inside*, and the 1998 DVD edition of *Suspiria*, as well as Audrey Horne (Sherilyn Fenn) in *Twin Peaks*. 

Perhaps her most recognizable dubbing role was providing the voices for both Itchy and Maude Flanders in the Japanese version of the animated television series, *The Simpsons*.

title: Date Narikuni
text:
Date Narikuni was a samurai who lived during the late Edo period in Japan. Born on November 6, 1817, he became the 12th daimyō, or feudal lord, of the Sendai Domain located in the Tōhoku region of northern Japan, and was the 28th head of the prominent Date clan. His lineage was somewhat indirect; he was the son of Date Munemitsu, belonging to the Tome-Date clan, a branch family of the main Date line, and consequently the grandson of Date Yoshimura, a previous daimyō of Sendai. Throughout his childhood, he was known by several names—first Kōgorō, then Tosaburō, and finally Sojirō.

Narikuni’s rise to power was directly linked to a succession crisis within the Sendai Domain in 1828. The previous daimyō, Date Nariyoshi, died leaving behind a two-year-old son, Date Yoshikuni, as his heir. The Tokugawa shogunate, while having previously intervened to secure the Date line's continuation, was growing impatient with the repeated succession issues within the domain and considered the possibility of stripping the Date clan of their lands. 

An initial proposal involved marrying Nariyoshi’s young daughter, Masahime, to a son of the shōgun Tokugawa Ienari, but this plan failed to materialize. Instead, Masahime was wed to Narikuni, who was from a cadet branch of the Date family. Crucially, Narikuni then formally adopted the infant Date Yoshikuni as his heir, ensuring the continuation of the main Date line and appeasing the shogunate. 

Following this arrangement, in 1828, Narikuni was granted the Court rank of Junior Fourth, Lower Grade, and received the title of Mutsu-no-kami. His status was further elevated in 1831 with promotions to Junior Fourth, Upper Grade, and Sakonoe-chūshō. 

Despite his political maneuvering, Narikuni was known primarily for his intellectual pursuits. He possessed a scholarly disposition and was well-versed in literature. However, his time as daimyō was cut short. He became ill during a mandatory trip to Edo in 1840, a practice known as *sankin-kōtai*, and ultimately died in Edo on September 9, 1841, at the relatively young age of 25. Narikuni’s father was Date Munemitsu, who lived from 1787 to 1843, and his mother was Tsuneko-hime. He was married to Masahime, who outlived him, passing away in 1861.

title: Ralph Macchio
text:
Ralph Macchio, born November 4, 1961, is an American actor best known for his enduring role as Daniel LaRusso in the *Karate Kid* franchise, beginning with the 1984 film and continuing through the television series *Cobra Kai* which concluded in February 2025. He has received nominations for Critics’ Choice Awards and a Primetime Emmy Award for his work on *Cobra Kai*. Beyond this iconic role, Macchio is also recognized for his performances as Johnny Cade in Francis Ford Coppola’s *The Outsiders* (1983) and as Billy Gambini in *My Cousin Vinny* (1992). He received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2024.

Macchio grew up in Huntington, New York, the son of a laundromat and wastewater disposal business owner and a mother of Italian ancestry. He has a younger brother named Steven. He began tap dancing at age three and was discovered by a talent agent at sixteen. He had some early martial arts training in karate and jiujitsu as a child, which would later prove useful.

Macchio’s early television work included a role on *Eight is Enough* in 1980. His breakthrough came with *The Outsiders*, where he acted alongside a large ensemble of future stars. This led to the role of Daniel LaRusso in *The Karate Kid*, portraying a young man who learns karate from his mentor, Mr. Miyagi, played by Pat Morita. Macchio reprised the role in *The Karate Kid Part II* (1986) and *The Karate Kid Part III* (1989), achieving widespread fame. He playfully referenced the character in a 2007 music video and a 2010 online short for Funny or Die.

In 2018, Macchio returned to the *Karate Kid* universe with *Cobra Kai*, a series that re-examines the original films and explores the complexities of the characters, particularly Johnny Lawrence. The show initially aired on YouTube and later moved to Netflix, running for six seasons. He authored a memoir in 2022, *Waxing On: The Karate Kid and Me*, reflecting on his experiences with the franchise. He reprised the role of Daniel LaRusso again in 2025 in *Karate Kid: Legends* alongside Jackie Chan.

Throughout his career, Macchio has taken on diverse roles in film and television. These include appearances in *Crossroads* (1986), *Ugly Betty* (2008-2009), *The Deuce* (2017-2019), and *Hitchcock* (2012). He also starred on Broadway in *Cuba and His Teddy Bear* and in a U.S. tour revival of *How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying*, receiving positive reviews. He competed on *Dancing with the Stars* in 2011, finishing fourth. 

Macchio has been married to Phyllis Fierro since 1987, and they have two children, Julia and Daniel. His daughter, Julia, appeared in *Cobra Kai*. He is a longtime fan of the New York Islanders hockey team. He recently earned a black belt in karate in April 2025, decades after first portraying Daniel LaRusso, and was awarded an honorary black belt by the World Karate Federation with Jackie Chan in May 2025.

title: Ariel Behar
text:
Ariel Behar, born November 12, 1989, is a professional tennis player from Uruguay specializing in doubles competition. He began playing tennis at age three and seriously pursued it by age ten, citing Roger Federer and Andre Agassi as early inspirations. Though from a Jewish family, he has stated he isn’t particularly religious. He has been a member of the Uruguay Davis Cup team since 2009.

Behar initially competed primarily on the ATP Challenger Tour from the mid-2010s until 2017, achieving success with seven doubles titles during that period. He made his Grand Slam debut at Wimbledon in 2017, and in 2018, he began a highly successful partnership with Gonzalo Escobar of Ecuador. Together, they won ATP titles at the 2021 Delray Beach Open and the 2021 Andalucía Open, reaching three other ATP tour finals that year. They also secured eight Challenger titles between 2018 and 2020.

This partnership propelled Behar into the top 50 of the doubles rankings in April 2021, finishing the year ranked No. 41, a career high at that time. He reached a career-high doubles ranking of No. 39 in January 2022 following the Australian Open. Further success with Escobar came at the 2022 Serbia Open, where they won the title, defeating the top-seeded team of Mektić and Pavić.

In 2023, Behar partnered with Nicolas Barrientos to reach the quarterfinals of the Córdoba Open and the final of the Argentina Open. He then teamed with Adam Pavlásek, achieving a significant milestone by reaching the quarterfinals of Wimbledon, where they upset the former champions Mektić and Pavić before falling to the eventual winners. This result pushed him back into the top 50. Later in the year, partnering with Pavlasek, he reached the final of the European Open.

2024 has seen continued success, with a quarterfinal appearance at the Australian Open with Pavlásek. He then reached his first Masters final at the Mutua Madrid Open, also with Pavlásek, upsetting several highly-ranked teams along the way, though they ultimately lost the final. This performance elevated him to a career-high ranking of World No. 34 on May 6, 2024. He also reached the final of the Japan Open with Robert Galloway. Throughout his career, Behar has accumulated three ATP titles, twelve runner-up finishes, and an impressive 27 Challenger titles. He has a 6-12 record against top 10 ranked players at the time of their matches.

title: Joseph Jaquet
text:
Joseph Jaquet, a Belgian sculptor born in Antwerp on January 30, 1822, and who died in Schaerbeek on June 9, 1898, achieved recognition for his work throughout his lifetime. Born to a baker, Jaquet received his artistic training at the Brussels Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts under the guidance of Guillaume Geefs. He formed a close friendship with Peter Ludwig Kühnen, a landscape painter from Aachen. 

Throughout his career, Jaquet was consistently supported by his brother Jacques, who moved from Antwerp to Brussels to assist him. Jacques also pursued his own artistic endeavors, exhibiting his sculptures at Brussels art salons in 1843, 1854, 1860, 1866, 1872, and 1873. Joseph Jaquet first gained attention in 1842 at the Brussels Art Salon, showcasing a collection of work including a marble bust, three plaster busts, a depiction of ‘Moses Saved from the Waters’, and ‘Meditating Saint Paul’. 

He further developed his reputation with a model for a bronze statue of Froissart intended for Chimay, presented at the 1845 Salon, but it was ‘The Golden Age’ in 1854 that truly cemented his notoriety. Jaquet resided on Goffard street before later moving to Charles Quint street. His talent led to commissions beyond Belgium, beginning in 1864 with ‘The Victory’ for the Paleis voor Volksvlijt in Amsterdam, followed by work decorating the national monument in The Hague’s Willemspark. 

In 1868, he completed a significant work, the equestrian statue of Baldwin I of Constantinople, which was installed in Mons. Two years later, in 1872, he contributed the pediment and lion sculptures to the Brussels Stock Exchange.  One of his later notable pieces was a statue of Louise of Orléans, the first Queen of the Belgians, created in 1879. This statue was initially placed on the Place d'Armes in Philippeville before being relocated to the old École moyenne on Namur street.

Jaquet was also dedicated to education, serving as a professor at the Brussels Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts, where he mentored Charles Samuel.  His contributions to the arts were formally recognized with several honours during his life, including being appointed an Officer of the Order of Leopold and an Officer of the Order of the Oak Crown. He was also elected as a Member of the Royal Academy of Science, Letters and Fine Arts of Belgium, signifying the high esteem in which his peers held his artistic achievements.

title: Nonzee Nimibutr
text:
Nonzee Nimibutr, born December 18, 1962, is a prominent Thai filmmaker working as a director, producer, and screenwriter. He is considered a leading figure in the “New Wave” of Thai cinema, alongside directors like Pen-Ek Ratanaruang, Wisit Sasanatieng, and Apichatpong Weerasethakul. His family has connections to Thai media history through his relative, Lieutenant General Phachoen Nimitbutr, who founded Thailand’s first television station.

Nonzee began his career directing television commercials and music videos before making his feature film debut in 1997 with *Dang Bireley's and Young Gangsters*, a crime film influenced by John Woo, which won Best Picture at the Thailand National Film Awards and received a nomination at the Vancouver International Film Festival. He quickly followed this success with *Nang Nak* (1999), a ghost thriller based on a well-known Thai folk tale, also garnering Best Picture at the Thailand National Film Awards. These two films are credited with revitalizing the Thai film industry.

He then pioneered a trend of pan-Asian film production with *Jan Dara* (2001), featuring a Hong Kong actress and seeking funding from international studios. *Jan Dara* sparked controversy due to its mature themes of incest, rape, and abortion, requiring censorship cuts for its release in Thailand.  Nonzee expanded his role in the industry by becoming a prolific producer, lending his name to films such as *Bangkok Dangerous*, *Tears of the Black Tiger*, *Bang Rajan*, and *Monrak Transistor*. He co-founded the production company Cinemasia with Duangkamol Limcharoen, who sadly passed away in 2003.

Continuing his pan-Asian approach, he participated in the horror anthology *Three* (2002), directing a segment alongside directors from Hong Kong and Korea.  His later directorial work includes *OK Baytong* (2003), a drama set in Southern Thailand addressing themes of religious and political conflict, and the short film *The Ceiling* (2005) for the Asian Film Academy. He also directed *Queens of Langkasuka* (2008), a historical-fantasy epic, and has been involved in developing projects like *Toyol*, a Singaporean co-production, and a live-action adaptation of the comic *Noo Hin: The Movie*.

Throughout his career, Nonzee has continued to produce films, including *The Letter* and *The Eye 2*. In 2008, he was recognized for his contributions to Thai cinema with the Thailand Culture Ministry's Silpathorn Award, joining a prestigious group of fellow filmmakers. His recent work includes *Distortion* (2012), *Timeline* (2015), *The Gift* (2017) and *Once Upon A Star* (2023), a Netflix film.

title: DeAnna Bennett
text:
DeAnna Danielle Bennett, born November 18, 1984, is an American mixed martial artist currently competing in the Flyweight division. She began her professional MMA career in 2012, having previously competed in Muay Thai after starting with kickboxing to get in shape. Her journey in the sport began with a successful run in Showdown Fights, where she won all four of her bouts between 2012 and 2014, including victories over Sharon Jacobson, Colleen Schneider, and Julianna Peña.

Bennett then moved to Invicta Fighting Championships, achieving wins against Michelle Ould and Jennifer Maia by TKO and unanimous decision respectively, followed by another unanimous decision victory over Norma Rueda Center. In 2017, she was a participant on *The Ultimate Fighter 26*, a competition to determine the UFC’s first women’s 125-pound champion. She won her opening-round fight but lost in the quarterfinals to Sijara Eubanks. 

Her time in the Ultimate Fighting Championship was brief, resulting in a majority draw against Melinda Fábián and subsequent release from the promotion. She returned to Invicta, earning a split decision win over Karina Rodríguez, and participated in a flyweight tournament, defeating Miranda Maverick before losing a rematch to Rodriguez in the final.

Bennett subsequently joined Bellator MMA, where she faced Liz Carmouche in September 2020, losing via submission.  She was scheduled to fight Alejandra Lara multiple times in 2021, with the bout repeatedly rescheduled and ultimately taking place at a catchweight due to Bennett missing the flyweight limit. She won this fight by unanimous decision. She secured further unanimous decision wins over Justine Kish twice in 2022, with Kish also missing weight for their second encounter.  In April 2023, Bennett fought Carmouche again for the Bellator Women's Flyweight World Championship, but lost by submission after missing weight again and being fined a portion of her purse. More recently, in May 2023, she competed in Fury Pro Grappling 7, losing a grappling match against Marissa Pacelli by unanimous decision.

title: Jennifer Paz
text:
Jennifer Paz-Fedorov is a Filipino actress who gained significant recognition for her role as Lapis Lazuli in the animated television series *Steven Universe* and its follow-up, *Steven Universe Future*. She also contributed voice work as part of the character Malachite within the same series. 

Paz’s journey to acting began with a move from the Philippines to Seattle, Washington, at the age of five, joining her mother’s brother.  After one year of study at the University of Washington, at 21 years old, she landed the alternate lead role of Kim in the 1st National US Tour of *Miss Saigon*. This marked her professional acting debut, and she subsequently received numerous award nominations and wins, including a 2008 LA Stage Alliance Ovation Award for Best Lead Actress. She continued to perform the role of Kim in various regional productions of *Miss Saigon*, including a 2013 performance at the Casa Mañana theatre.

Beyond *Miss Saigon*, Paz’s stage career includes appearances in prominent productions such as *Les Misérables* on Broadway and a role as Mei-Li in David Henry Hwang’s revised *Flower Drum Song* at the Los Angeles Mark Taper Forum, where the production was so well-received it extended its run by five weeks. 

In addition to her stage and voice acting work, Paz is also developing her skills as a writer. She was a recipient of the 2022/23 NAMT (National Alliance of Musical Theatre) Writers Residency Grant and won the 2021 Outstanding Screenplays TV Pilot Competition for her original comedy, “Proud Marys.”

Paz is married to Anthony Fedorov, becoming engaged on Christmas Day in 2012. They have a son, Julian Paz Fedorov, born in April 2013. 

Her work also appears on several recordings, including contributions to *The Lost Chords: Cinderella* and *Walt Disney Records The Legacy Collection: Cinderella*, where she performed “I Lost My Heart At the Ball” and “The Face That I See in the Night.” She has also contributed featured vocals to *Awakening*, and provided vocals for various *Steven Universe* soundtracks, including “That Distant Shore” from *Steven Universe, Vol. 2*, “Happily Ever After,” “Who We Are,” and “Finale” from *Steven Universe the Movie*, and “Shining Through” from *Steven Universe Future*.

title: Lou Briel
text:
Lou Briel, born in Santurce, Puerto Rico in October 19, is a multifaceted artist working as a singer, composer, comedian, record producer, pianist, and host. He began his career as a young member of the pop group Anexo 3, with whom he recorded four albums produced, initially, by Alfred D. Herger. The group achieved popularity with songs like “Oh, Cuanto te Amo,” “Contigo,” and “Por eso estoy Preso,” and won second prize at the local OTI Festival twice with songs co-written by Briel and Julio Ortiz-Teissonniere, “Tengo Vida” and “Más Allá de mis Canciones.” Anexo 3 also hosted a television variety show, *Contigo... Anexo 3*, and appeared in a popular Datsun commercial, with Briel singing the jingle.

Following the breakup of Anexo 3, Briel pursued a solo career. In 1984, he gained recognition for writing “Yo puedo” for Yolandita Monge, an inspirational song about perseverance. He toured extensively throughout Latin America and the United States, and placed highly in the Festi-Buga song festival in Colombia with the same song. Throughout his career, Briel has represented Puerto Rico four times at the International OTI Festival as a composer, with songs performed by Edgardo Huertas, himself, Juan Manuel Lebrón, and his niece, Ivonne Briel (later known as Arana). 

Beyond performing, Briel has composed for numerous television programs and telenovelas, creating opening and title themes for shows like *De Fiesta con Nydia*, *Estudio Alegre*, *El Amor Nuestro de Cada Día*, and *Ave de Paso*. He also ventured into television as a performer, hosting and writing the musical-comedy show *En Broma y en Serio* alongside Dagmar, and creating and starring in the children’s series *Teatrimundo* as the character "Lubrielito." He also starred in the sitcom *Cara o Cruz* alongside Edgardo Huertas. From 1995 to 2001, he produced and hosted his own variety show, *Voces en Función*. 

Briel is also a stage performer, having appeared in various zarzuelas and operettas, as well as children's musicals like *Jack y la Mata de Guisantes* and *Los Pitufos*. In 2004, he reprised his role as “Lubrielito” in the family film *Yo Creo en Santa Claus*, which he also directed and composed the soundtrack for. He spearheaded a 2005 video clip, *Dios Alumbra a Puerto Rico*, featuring 40 Latin artists to raise awareness about child abuse. More recently, he has performed in *Solo para Hombres... y para Mujeres tambien* and as an MC and singer in a Puerto Rican folkloric revue for tourists, as well as participating in *La Receta de la Abuela Tour*.

Over the years, Briel has released numerous albums, beginning with *Solo Por Fin* in 1981 and continuing through *Lou Briel con La Maphia Boba... Adondequiera* in 2008. His compositions have been recorded by many prominent Latin artists, including Yolandita Monge, Gilberto Santa Rosa, and Jose Feliciano.
